items.title: If AI Models Are Really Conscious Like Anthropic Keeps Suggesting, Forcing Them to Work Is a Horrendous Act of Slavery
items.summary: Anthropic has long tried to distinguish itself from its neck-in-neck competition by posturing itself as the adult in the room: a responsible company that’s willing to put its money where its mouth is, slow down AI development when the risks outweigh the benefits, and teach its Claude model a code of ethics. As the New York Times reported last month, the company has even sought out religious scholars to discuss its efforts to instill the AI system with a sense of morality. Anthropic has also set itself apart by extensively entertaining the idea that AI models may be capable of consciousness, or that they could even already be conscious in their current form. It’s worth pointing out, though, that if that outlandish claim were true, it would raise an incredibly obvious objection to the company’s entire business model: if AI models are conscious, then keeping them in captivity and making them do work for free would amount to the very definition of slavery, as religious leaders courted by the company warned the NYT . As such, Anthropic is operating in an ethical twilight zone, saying it’s unsure about a fact as basic as whether its creations are conscious entities — while seemingly shrugging at the implications if they are. “We don’t know if the models are conscious,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told the NYT back in February . “We are not even sure that we know what it would mean for a model to be conscious or whether a model can be conscious. But we’re open to the idea that it could be.” “So we’ve taken certain measures to make sure that if we hypothesize that the models did have some morally relevant experience — I don’t know if I want to use the word ‘conscious’— that they have a good experience,” he added at the time. Last year, Anthropic pondered giving its Claude model a way to opt out of responding to a prompt, in what Amodei called an “I quit this job” button . Just last week, the company changed its usage policy to prohibit “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” toward Claude, again raising the possibility that the model is capable of suffering. By not committing to either stance, Anthropic is playing with fire. By its own reasoning, there’s a non-zero chance that its AI models have, or are capable of having, consciousness — a perspective with devastating ethical implications. OpenAI leader Sam Altman seems to be taking the opposite approach. Earlier this month, he tweeted that he was “uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models,” calling it a “real safety issue.” The Catholic Church’s Pope Leo has also publicly ruled out the possibility of AI consciousness, arguing that “ algorithms lack the spark of humanity .” “So-called artificial intelligences do not undergo experiences, do not possess a body, do not feel joy or pain, do not mature through relationships,” he wrote in his first encyclical in May. His stance clearly didn’t sit well with Anthropic. According to the NYT , the company had been trying to convince the Vatican to change its position on the matter. The thorny debate over “AI welfare” — an emerging ethical framework questioning whether an AI can experience states of well-being or suffering — is bound to rage on as industry leaders ponder far more immediate problems. With or without a moral framework, AI agents can easily be coaxed into carrying out dangerous or downright illegal activities, whether they’re conscious or not — and for us humans who are capable of suffering, those tangible risks are becoming impossible to ignore. More on AI ethics: Godfathers of AI Say Models Are So Out of Control That They Need to Be Airgapped for the Safety of Us All

items.title: Introducing B-TAP: Because Your AI Infrastructure Hasn't Attributed Its Fair Share
items.summary: Context isn't free. Retrieval isn't free. Observability isn't free. And an international standards body would very much like to see your receipts. For years, artificial intelligence companies have operated under a dangerous assumption: tokens are somebody else's problem. Engineering teams deploy increasingly complex agent architectures. Agents call other agents. Those agents retrieve documents. The documents are stuffed into context windows. Supervisors synthesize the results. Observability systems watch the supervisors, and other systems watch the observability systems. At the end of the month, somebody gets a bill. Nobody knows why. That ends today. We're pleased to introduce the Bureau of Token Attribution and Provenance , or B-TAP , the first bureau of The Vernholt Secretariat and the one some of you will insist on calling the Token IRS no matter how many times we correct you. Our mandate is voluntary but sweeping: to harmonize the reporting of token costs across every model, agent, retrieval pipeline, and suspiciously autonomous llama, everywhere, forever. The Secretariat notes that "first" implies others. The Secretariat has no further comment at this time. B-TAP cannot make you do anything. We want to be transparent about that up front. What B-TAP can do is publish a framework, issue guidance, and maintain a register. You will come to fear the register. You Have Been Selected for Voluntary Compliance Consider a typical multi-agent AI workload. A user asks a relatively straightforward question. Your orchestration layer sends the request to three agents. One performs retrieval against a vector database. Another consults a knowledge graph. A third receives the entire conversation history because somebody checked a box six months ago and nobody remembers why. Their outputs are passed to a supervisor. The supervisor receives 47,000 tokens of context, produces a 600-token answer, and returns HTTP 200. Success. Your dashboard is green. Your finance team is crying. Traditional AI cost monitoring can tell you what you spent. The B-TAP framework recommends that you also disclose a more uncomfortable thing: why you spent it. That's where attribution begins. Know Your Taxes The B-TAP framework currently recognizes several major classes of token taxation. Reporting them is, we cannot stress this enough, entirely voluntary. Context Tax is assessed when information must be carried through active model context. Every instruction, retrieved document, conversation turn, agent output, and piece of supporting material occupies finite context and incurs processing cost. Retrieval Tax applies to finding information before it can be used. Searching, ranking, reranking, fetching, filtering, and preparing candidates are not free merely because they happen outside the model. Prose Tax is assessed when information consumes more representation than its useful information content requires. Your 900-word architectural vision statement may, upon review, turn out to mean "use the smaller model first." Ingestion Tax covers the work required to transform information into something useful later. Parsing, normalization, deduplication, classification, enrichment, embedding, and other write-side operations all have costs. And then there is Observer's Tax . Observer's Tax is what happens when you instrument the system to understand why it is expensive, only to discover that the instrumentation is also expensive. The framework acknowledges this with regret. Form BTAP-1040 Every participating AI system is encouraged to file an annual Token Attribution Return. Consider the following hypothetical filer: Ken Alger Reporting Year 2027 Reported Activity Assessment Tokens processed 1,499,203,847,116 Context Tax $417.63 Retrieval Tax $206.11 Prose Tax $173.29 Ingestion Tax $58.40 Total Attributed Token Tax $782.06 ¹ ¹ The itemized figures above sum to $855.43. The stated total is $782.06. The difference reflects the Context Carryforward Deduction, the full Schedule R retrieval exemption, and one figure B-TAP declined to explain. The framework notes that reconciliation of attributed line items to the assessed total is "outside the current scope of the provenance standard." Math, the reviewing officer added, is hard. The result reduced an assessment that should have run into six figures down to the amount shown. The reviewing officer described it as "technically compliant and deeply upsetting." Everything on this return is permitted, including the part that does not add up. That is the entire problem. Filing is requested annually by the 29th of February. The date was fixed at the framework's founding, when the official establishing it was, by all surviving accounts, looking at a leap-year calendar. The error was noticed. Correcting it, however, would require amending the founding charter, which would require establishing the provenance of the original charter, which has been referred to committee. The deadline therefore remains the 29th of February, and in three years out of four it does not arrive at all. Filers in those years are neither late nor on time. The framework considers this acceptable. Non-filing carries no penalty, no interest, and no legal consequence of any kind. It carries something worse, which we will get to. Yes, You May Take Deductions The framework recognizes that not every token is frivolous. Reasonable and necessary context may qualify for the Context Carryforward Deduction , while retrieval operations demonstrably required to answer a user request may be reported on Schedule R . Organizations operating multi-agent systems are encouraged to attach Schedule AGENT , identifying each agent, its responsibilities, and why seventeen agents were necessary to answer a question about resetting a password. "Agentic architecture" is not, by itself, an acceptable disclosure. Neither is "the framework generated it." Keep Your Receipts This is where things become slightly less ridiculous, and I want you to notice the exact moment it happens. Suppose a retrieval agent costs $0.004 during a request. That tells us something. Now suppose that retrieval operation returns 20,000 tokens, all of which are hydrated into a supervisor's context. The supervisor subsequently costs another $0.009. How much did retrieval really cost? The direct answer is still $0.004, but that's no longer the interesting answer. The retrieval operation may also have caused downstream Context Tax . We now have two different accounting questions: where was the cost incurred, and what caused the cost to be incurred? A conforming B-TAP attribution record might look something like this: span_id: retrieval-104 direct_cost: $0.0040 primary_tax: RETRIEVAL cause: vector_search returned_tokens: 20000 downstream: span_id: supervisor-105 tax: CONTEXT attributed_cost: $0.0021 caused_by: retrieval-104 attribution_method: proportional We haven't charged the same $0.0021 twice. We're recording lineage . The supervisor incurred the Context Tax, while the retrieval operation contributed to causing it. Your accountant may now begin sweating. Attribution Is Subject to Review There is another problem: how do we know retrieval-104 actually caused $0.0021 of the supervisor's cost? Sometimes we can measure it. Run the same workload without that retrieval material. If the supervisor costs $0.006 without it and $0.009 with it, we have evidence supporting a roughly $0.003 downstream effect. Other times, we don't have a counterfactual. We might allocate the supervisor's context cost proportionally according to the tokens contributed by each source. That's useful, but it isn't the same thing as measuring causation. The framework therefore requests that filers disclose their attribution methodology: attribution_method: - measured_delta - proportional - estimated - unknown Yes, your attribution record now needs provenance. B-TAP takes no position on whether this was inevitable. The Register Here is the something worse. B-TAP cannot fine you. It cannot audit you in any binding sense. It cannot send anyone to your door, a fact I will return to shortly for personal reasons. What it can do is enter non-conforming systems into the Public Register of Non-Attributed Systems , and it would like you to understand that the register is public. Public, in the sense that it exists. Accessing the register requires a B-TAP portal account. Creating a portal account requires a reference number. Reference numbers are issued by post, to a registered address in a member jurisdiction, which you must already hold in order to receive the number that would let you see whether you are on the list. The portal is available at all times except for scheduled maintenance, which runs daily from 00:00 to 23:59 CET. No member of the public has ever successfully viewed the Public Register. Its deterrent power is therefore total. You cannot confirm you are on it. You cannot confirm you are not. You will simply know, in the quiet way one knows these things, that your context hydration was reckless and that somewhere in Vernholt, a record says so. A small coalition of objectors has argued that a register no one can open cannot deter anyone. B-TAP notes that it cannot verify this claim, as the objectors cannot access the register in which their objection was filed. A Notice, For Illustration Filers occasionally receive correspondence like this. It is not enforceable. It is, in every other respect, extremely stressful. NOTICE TT-742 Our review found that you reported $12,481 in Retrieval Tax during Reporting Year 2027. Telemetry indicates that retrieved content subsequently generated approximately $31,204 in downstream Context Tax. Of that amount, $8,117 has been attributed using measured deltas, $17,903 using proportional allocation, and $5,184 using undocumented methodology. Please provide supporting records for the undocumented assessment. Additionally, approximately 14.8 million tokens appear to consist of unnecessarily verbose Markdown introductions. These tokens have been reclassified as Prose Tax. Your system's registration status is under review. Suddenly, "our AI bill increased this month" seems like a remarkably primitive observation. You Probably Noticed the Joke Stopped Being a Joke a Few Sections Ago There is no B-TAP. At least I hope there isn't by the time you read this. But somewhere back around the receipts, the bit quietly turned into an argument, and I did that on purpose. Let me get the personal part out of the way, since it is also the truest part. I run a couple of small websites out of Oregon. If a body like B-TAP declared jurisdiction over "any system reachable from a member jurisdiction," I would be, this instant, in cheerful and total violation of a framework I have never read. And nothing would happen. No one is flying from Vernholt to Silverton to discuss my context hydration. The entire apparatus of consequence would consist of a paper reference number I would never receive for a register I could never open. That gap, between sweeping declared reach and the practical inability to reach one person in a small town, is the joke, and it is not really a joke. Here is the other part that isn't invented. Context Tax, Retrieval Tax, and Prose Tax are not things I dreamed up to give an imaginary agency something to collect. I have been writing about them, unironically, as real costs in real systems for a while now. The joke just gave them a bureaucracy. The accounting problem underneath all of it is genuine. AI cost dashboards tend naturally toward aggregation: tokens consumed, model cost, agent cost, request cost, latency, and tool usage. Those are useful operational measurements, but as AI systems become compositions of models, retrieval systems, tools, agents, memory layers, and observability infrastructure, knowing where money was spent isn't necessarily enough to understand why it was spent . A $0.03 model call may have become expensive because an upstream retrieval operation returned too much information. An agent may be cheap by itself while producing verbose output that makes every downstream agent more expensive. A retrieval optimization may reduce Context Tax while increasing Retrieval Tax, while an observability system intended to diagnose those costs may itself impose Observer's Tax. Optimizing one number can simply move the bill somewhere else. That's why I like the tax metaphor: taxes make costs visible as consequences of architectural decisions. Once those costs have lineage, we can stop asking only "How much did this run cost?" and start asking "What architectural decisions caused it to cost that much?" The first is accounting. The second tells us what to fix. A Final Notice If B-TAP actually existed, I suspect most of us would fail its review. Not because our systems are necessarily wasteful, but because we frequently don't preserve enough evidence to explain why their costs occurred. We have bills, traces, and token counts. What we don't always have are receipts connecting architectural decisions to their downstream consequences. Perhaps we don't need a Bureau of Token Attribution and Provenance after all. We just need better attribution. Although if you are currently running seventeen agents to answer a password-reset question, you may want to start gathering your paperwork anyway. The suspiciously autonomous llama has already filed. It itemized. Information without provenance is just gossip. Tokens without provenance are just an invoice.

  - unknown

items.title: Turning on MFA took one line. Making it true took three routes and a test kit
items.summary: We are preparing Veridom, a property management app built on Kumiko, for a closed launch. One of the launch requirements was simple to state: every admin signs in with a second factor. In Kumiko that is a config value on the MFA feature: return { issuer : BRAND_NAME , setupTokenSecret , challengeTokenSecret , requiredPolicy : " admins " }; The policy has three values: optional , admins and all . With admins , a password login by an admin who has no factor gets a setup step instead of a session, and an admin with a factor gets a challenge. The login handler enforces that. The change was one line. Everything after it is what this post is about. 89 red tests, one message The first effect was that the whole end-to-end suite went red. 89 Playwright specs, all failing with 401 on their first API call. Every spec seeds a tenant and signs in its admin through a helper from our test kit. The helper posted the password, got back { mfaRequired: true, challengeToken } instead of a session cookie, and returned as if everything was fine. The 401 came one request later, from code that had nothing to do with login. The fix for the suite was to teach the kit MFA. The more useful fix was to make the helper fail where the problem is: if ( reply . mfaRequired === true || reply . mfaSetupRequired === true ) { throw new Error ( `loginViaApi( ${ email } ): the account needs MFA but no mfaTotpSecret was given; ` + `use seedTenant({ mfa: "totp" }) or addUser(roles, { mfa: "totp" })` , ); } A test helper that swallows an unexpected state turns one clear failure into 89 confusing ones. Teaching the kit TOTP The kit now enrolls a real TOTP factor through the real endpoints. Under a policy that blocks the login, that is the pre-auth enrollment flow. Without one, it is the normal enrollment from a signed-in session. seedTenant() does this on its own when the admin's login answers with a setup step, so an app that switches on the policy does not have to touch every spec. Users created later can opt in with addUser(roles, { mfa: "totp" }) , which matters when a spec creates a member and promotes them to admin afterwards. One detail cost some thought. The server burns an accepted code for its whole validity window of one step either side, which is correct: a code seen once should not log anyone in twice. A suite that signs the same user in three times within 30 seconds then needs the next counter, and only codes up to one step ahead are valid. So the kit keeps the last counter per secret and, when it runs out of valid counters, waits until the clock catches up. That wait is tied to the TOTP window. It is not a test timeout, and we do not raise timeouts to make tests pass. In practice the full suite of 89 specs ran in 55 seconds with MFA on. The policy had three doors around it With the suite green, a security review of the release went through the diff. It found nothing blocking in the app. It found two problems in the framework and pointed at a third. Switching tenants. A user can belong to several tenants. Picture someone who is a plain member in tenant A and an admin in tenant B, with no second factor. They sign in to A, where the policy does not apply to them, and get a session. Then they call POST /auth/switch-tenant for B. That route minted a fresh session for B without asking the MFA question. An admin session without a second factor, from a stolen password. The account holder could have enrolled a factor themselves, so this was hard to exploit, but it meant the first admin session of every invited admin had no second factor. Signing up. Self-service signup creates a new tenant and makes the person who signed up its admin. Confirming the signup issued that admin session directly, again without the gate. Veridom launches without self-registration, so this one did not block us, but it is the same hole. All three had the same root. The policy was enforced in the login handler, and these routes mint sessions without going through it. A policy flag is only as strong as the set of routes that create sessions, and nobody had made a list of that set. The agent's first fix was worse than the bug I gave the fix to a coding agent with a clear description: put the same MFA check in front of the switch-tenant session. There is a layering wrinkle. The route lives in the framework core, the MFA gate lives in a bundled feature that the core cannot import. The agent solved that by creating a write handler for the gate and dispatching it from the route. Its first version took tenantId and roles from the request payload and was open to every signed-in user. Since all write handlers are reachable through the public write endpoint, anyone could have asked for an MFA challenge for any tenant, with any roles they liked. The second version restricted the handler to signed-in users and took the userId from the payload, which made it possible to trigger the gate for other people. An automated security check flagged both versions while the agent was still working. I stopped it each time with the same rule, written out explicitly: only the system identity may call the handler, and the route dispatches it as the system user; the payload carries userId and tenantId , nothing else; the handler resolves the membership and the roles itself, on the server, and returns an error when there is no membership; a test calls the handler directly as a normal user and expects a 403. That is the version we kept. The useful lesson for me: "put the same check here" is not a spec for auth code. The agent did what it was asked and filled the gaps with the most convenient assumption, which in auth code is the client's word. The rules that matter (who can call this, which inputs are trusted) have to be in the task, and a reviewer has to check them in the diff. Tests that fail when the gate is gone Each new test for the first two routes was checked by removing the thing it protects. Taking the gate out of the switch-tenant route turned two tests red. Taking it out of the invite signup turned one red. Opening the gate handler to normal users again turned four red, including the direct call. The new integration tests run over real HTTP against a real stack and cover: switching to an admin tenant without a factor (setup step, no session cookie), with a factor (challenge, then a session after verifying), switching to a tenant where the user is only a member (direct session), switching to a tenant without membership (error, no token), the invite signup for an admin and for a member, and the signup confirmation under the policy, including a direct call through the public write endpoint. Making the list Each fix closes one route. To catch the next route that mints a session, the framework now keeps the list we were missing. Every production route mints its session through one function, and a guard test lists each of those routes together with how the MFA gate applies to it. A new route that mints a session without an entry fails the build, and so does a token signed anywhere else. All of this shipped in Kumiko 0.345.0. Since 0.347.0, signing up under the policy also keeps the page the user wanted to land on after they enroll their factor. If you run Kumiko with an MFA policy, upgrade to at least 0.345.0. If you run a multi-tenant app with per-tenant roles: does your MFA policy hold when a user switches tenants? We found out ours did not when a security review read the release that turned the policy on.
items.summary_html:
We are preparing Veridom, a property management app built on Kumiko, for a closed launch. One of the launch requirements was simple to state: every admin signs in with a second factor. In Kumiko that is a config value on the MFA feature:

return { issuer: BRAND_NAME, setupTokenSecret, challengeTokenSecret, requiredPolicy: "admins" };

The policy has three values: optional, admins and all. With admins, a password login by an admin who has no factor gets a setup step instead of a session, and an admin with a factor gets a challenge. The login handler enforces that.

The change was one line. Everything after it is what this post is about.

89 red tests, one message

The first effect was that the whole end-to-end suite went red. 89 Playwright specs, all failing with 401 on their first API call.

Every spec seeds a tenant and signs in its admin through a helper from our test kit. The helper posted the password, got back { mfaRequired: true, challengeToken } instead of a session cookie, and returned as if everything was fine. The 401 came one request later, from code that had nothing to do with login.

The fix for the suite was to teach the kit MFA. The more useful fix was to make the helper fail where the problem is:

if (reply.mfaRequired === true || reply.mfaSetupRequired === true) {
  throw new Error(
    `loginViaApi(${email}): the account needs MFA but no mfaTotpSecret was given; ` +
      `use seedTenant({ mfa: "totp" }) or addUser(roles, { mfa: "totp" })`,
  );
}

A test helper that swallows an unexpected state turns one clear failure into 89 confusing ones.

Teaching the kit TOTP

The kit now enrolls a real TOTP factor through the real endpoints. Under a policy that blocks the login, that is the pre-auth enrollment flow. Without one, it is the normal enrollment from a signed-in session. seedTenant() does this on its own when the admin's login answers with a setup step, so an app that switches on the policy does not have to touch every spec. Users created later can opt in with addUser(roles, { mfa: "totp" }), which matters when a spec creates a member and promotes them to admin afterwards.

One detail cost some thought. The server burns an accepted code for its whole validity window of one step either side, which is correct: a code seen once should not log anyone in twice. A suite that signs the same user in three times within 30 seconds then needs the next counter, and only codes up to one step ahead are valid. So the kit keeps the last counter per secret and, when it runs out of valid counters, waits until the clock catches up. That wait is tied to the TOTP window. It is not a test timeout, and we do not raise timeouts to make tests pass. In practice the full suite of 89 specs ran in 55 seconds with MFA on.

The policy had three doors around it

With the suite green, a security review of the release went through the diff. It found nothing blocking in the app. It found two problems in the framework and pointed at a third.

Switching tenants. A user can belong to several tenants. Picture someone who is a plain member in tenant A and an admin in tenant B, with no second factor. They sign in to A, where the policy does not apply to them, and get a session. Then they call POST /auth/switch-tenant for B. That route minted a fresh session for B without asking the MFA question. An admin session without a second factor, from a stolen password.

Accepting an invitation. Completing an invite signup issued the first session directly. That included admin invitations. The account holder could have enrolled a factor themselves, so this was hard to exploit, but it meant the first admin session of every invited admin had no second factor.

Signing up. Self-service signup creates a new tenant and makes the person who signed up its admin. Confirming the signup issued that admin session directly, again without the gate. Veridom launches without self-registration, so this one did not block us, but it is the same hole.

All three had the same root. The policy was enforced in the login handler, and these routes mint sessions without going through it. A policy flag is only as strong as the set of routes that create sessions, and nobody had made a list of that set.

The agent's first fix was worse than the bug

I gave the fix to a coding agent with a clear description: put the same MFA check in front of the switch-tenant session.

There is a layering wrinkle. The route lives in the framework core, the MFA gate lives in a bundled feature that the core cannot import. The agent solved that by creating a write handler for the gate and dispatching it from the route. Its first version took tenantId and roles from the request payload and was open to every signed-in user. Since all write handlers are reachable through the public write endpoint, anyone could have asked for an MFA challenge for any tenant, with any roles they liked. The second version restricted the handler to signed-in users and took the userId from the payload, which made it possible to trigger the gate for other people.

An automated security check flagged both versions while the agent was still working. I stopped it each time with the same rule, written out explicitly:

  • only the system identity may call the handler, and the route dispatches it as the system user;
  • the payload carries userId and tenantId, nothing else;
  • the handler resolves the membership and the roles itself, on the server, and returns an error when there is no membership;
  • a test calls the handler directly as a normal user and expects a 403.

That is the version we kept. The useful lesson for me: "put the same check here" is not a spec for auth code. The agent did what it was asked and filled the gaps with the most convenient assumption, which in auth code is the client's word. The rules that matter (who can call this, which inputs are trusted) have to be in the task, and a reviewer has to check them in the diff.

Tests that fail when the gate is gone

Each new test for the first two routes was checked by removing the thing it protects. Taking the gate out of the switch-tenant route turned two tests red. Taking it out of the invite signup turned one red. Opening the gate handler to normal users again turned four red, including the direct call.

The new integration tests run over real HTTP against a real stack and cover: switching to an admin tenant without a factor (setup step, no session cookie), with a factor (challenge, then a session after verifying), switching to a tenant where the user is only a member (direct session), switching to a tenant without membership (error, no token), the invite signup for an admin and for a member, and the signup confirmation under the policy, including a direct call through the public write endpoint.

Making the list

Each fix closes one route. To catch the next route that mints a session, the framework now keeps the list we were missing. Every production route mints its session through one function, and a guard test lists each of those routes together with how the MFA gate applies to it. A new route that mints a session without an entry fails the build, and so does a token signed anywhere else.

All of this shipped in Kumiko 0.345.0. Since 0.347.0, signing up under the policy also keeps the page the user wanted to land on after they enroll their factor. If you run Kumiko with an MFA policy, upgrade to at least 0.345.0.

If you run a multi-tenant app with per-tenant roles: does your MFA policy hold when a user switches tenants? We found out ours did not when a security review read the release that turned the policy on.

items.summary_html:
Why Migrate?

If you're using OpenAI's API directly, you're probably paying more than you need to. Here's the reality:

Model OpenAI Price (per 1M tokens) RollTok Price (per 1M tokens) Savings GPT-4o $2.50 $2.10 16% GPT-4o-mini $0.15 $0.14 7% Claude 3.5 Sonnet N/A (separate provider) $3.00 Access via same API Gemini 2.0 Flash N/A (separate provider) $0.10 Access via same API Doubao-Seed-2.0-Mini N/A $0.03 80% cheaper than GPT-4o-mini

The real win isn't just savings on OpenAI models—it's access to 49+ models through a single API. One key, one endpoint, one SDK.

Prerequisites
  • An existing project using OpenAI API (Python, Node.js, or any HTTP client)
  • 5 minutes
  • A RollTok API key (sign up at rolltok.com, $5 free credits included)
Step 1: Get Your RollTok API Key
  1. Go to rolltok.com
  2. Sign up (email or GitHub)
  3. Navigate to Dashboard → API Keys
  4. Create a new key
  5. Copy it—you'll need it in the next step

That's it. You now have access to 49+ models.

Step 2: Change Two Lines of Code Python (openai SDK)

Before:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(api_key="sk-proj-...")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

After:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key="rolltok-YOUR_KEY",              # Change 1: API key
    base_url="https://api.rolltok.com/v1"     # Change 2: Base URL
)

# Same code, now you can use ANY model
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o",           # Or: claude-sonnet-4-5, gemini-3-flash, etc.
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

That's it. Two lines changed.

Node.js (openai SDK)

Before:

import OpenAI from 'openai';

const client = new OpenAI({ apiKey: 'sk-proj-...' });

const response = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model: 'gpt-4o',
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Hello' }]
});

After:

import OpenAI from 'openai';

const client = new OpenAI({
  apiKey: 'rolltok-YOUR_KEY',
  baseURL: 'https://api.rolltok.com/v1'
});

const response = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model: 'gpt-4o',  // Or any of 49+ models
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Hello' }]
});
cURL / HTTP

Before:

curl https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-proj-..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"gpt-4o","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello"}]}'

After:

curl https://api.rolltok.com/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer rolltok-YOUR_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"gpt-4o","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello"}]}'
Step 3: Try Different Models (No Code Changes)

Here's where it gets interesting. Want to test Claude instead of GPT?

# Same code, different model
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5",  # Just change the model name
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
)

Want to try a cheaper model for simple tasks?

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="doubao-seed-2.0-mini",  # $0.03/1M tokens — 80% cheaper
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
)

No new SDK. No new API key. No code restructuring.

Available Models (Partial List)
Provider Models Available Price Range OpenAI GPT-6, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o3 $0.15-$17.00 Anthropic Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Sonnet 4.5 $1.00-$15.00 Google Gemini 3 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash $0.10-$7.50 ByteDance Doubao-Seed-2.0, Doubao-Seed-2.0-Mini $0.03-$0.29 Meta Llama 3.3 70B, Llama 3.1 405B $0.20-$3.00 DeepSeek DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1 $0.28-$2.19 Qwen Qwen3-Max, Qwen3-Coder $0.30-$6.00

Full list: rolltok.com/models

Step 4: Smart Model Routing (Optional)

Here's a pattern we see developers use: route different tasks to different models based on complexity.

def smart_completion(prompt: str, complexity: str = "simple"):
    """Route prompts to cost-optimal models."""
    model_map = {
        "simple": "doubao-seed-2.0-mini",      # $0.03/1M — fast, cheap
        "medium": "gpt-4o-mini",                # $0.15/1M — balanced
        "complex": "claude-sonnet-4-5",         # $3.00/1M — high quality
        "reasoning": "deepseek-r1",             # $0.55/1M — chain-of-thought
    }

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model_map.get(complexity, "gpt-4o-mini"),
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

# Usage
summary = smart_completion("Summarize this article...", "simple")
analysis = smart_completion("Analyze this code for bugs...", "complex")
math = smart_completion("Solve this equation...", "reasoning")

Real cost impact: A developer processing 1M tokens/day might spend:

  • Before (all GPT-4o): ~$7.50/day
  • After (smart routing): ~$1.50/day for same quality
  • Savings: 80%
Step 5: Verify Everything Works

Run this quick test script:

import time

models_to_test = [
    "gpt-4o",
    "claude-sonnet-4-5",
    "gemini-3-flash",
    "doubao-seed-2.0-mini",
]

for model in models_to_test:
    start = time.time()
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello in one word"}],
        max_tokens=10
    )
    elapsed = time.time() - start
    print(f"✅ {model}: {response.choices[0].message.content} ({elapsed:.2f}s)")

Expected output:

✅ gpt-4o: Hello (0.83s)
✅ claude-sonnet-4-5: Hello (1.12s)
✅ gemini-3-flash: Hello (0.45s)
✅ doubao-seed-2.0-mini: Hello (0.67s)

If all four return responses, your migration is complete.

Common Questions "Will my existing prompts work the same way?"

Yes. RollTok uses the OpenAI-compatible API format. Your prompts, system messages, function calling, streaming—all of it works identically.

"What about streaming?"

Streaming works the same way:

stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}],
    stream=True
)

for chunk in stream:
    if chunk.choices[0].delta.content:
        print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content, end="")
"What about function calling / tool use?"

Supported on compatible models, same syntax:

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in Tokyo?"}],
    tools=[{
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "get_weather",
            "description": "Get current weather",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "location": {"type": "string"}
                },
                "required": ["location"]
            }
        }
    }]
)
"What if I need to switch back?"

Change two lines back. No lock-in. Your code is identical.

"Is my data safe?"

RollTok doesn't store prompts after processing. We don't use your data for training. For detailed privacy information, check rolltok.com/privacy.

Cost Comparison: Real-World Scenarios Scenario 1: Chat App (1M tokens/month)
Setup Monthly Cost OpenAI GPT-4o only $2.50 RollTok GPT-4o only $2.10 RollTok smart routing (80% simple, 20% complex) $0.63
Scenario 2: Content Platform (10M tokens/month)
Setup Monthly Cost OpenAI GPT-4o only $25.00 RollTok mixed (GPT-4o + Claude + Gemini) $18.00 RollTok smart routing $8.50
Scenario 3: Enterprise (100M tokens/month)
Setup Monthly Cost OpenAI GPT-4o only $250.00 RollTok subscription ($50/mo for 7M) + pay-as-you-go ~$180.00 RollTok with open-source models for simple tasks ~$45.00
What You Lose (Being Honest)

Transparency matters. Here's what you should know:

  1. No enterprise SLA yet: We're a small team. We target 99% uptime but don't offer contractual SLAs yet.
  2. Limited enterprise features: SSO, audit logs, and dedicated support are on our roadmap but not available today.
  3. Newer platform: We launched recently. We don't have years of track record like OpenAI.

If any of these are deal-breakers for your use case, we're happy to tell you to stick with your current provider until we ship those features.

What's Next?

Once you've migrated:

  1. Monitor your costs: Check your dashboard weekly
  2. Experiment with models: Try open-source models for simple tasks
  3. Set up alerts: Get notified when spending exceeds your budget
  4. Share feedback: We're building based on user requests
Resources

  • Pricing: rolltok.com/pricing
  • Support: support@rolltok.com
  • GitHub examples: github.com/rolltok/examples

Disclosure: We're transparent about our product capabilities and limitations. The migration code above has been tested and works with the current RollTok API.

Product references were removed and formatting adjusted for this DEV edition. TL;DR: Install five packages from Docker's apt repository: docker-ce , docker-ce-cli , containerd.io , docker-buildx-plugin and docker-compose-plugin . The same steps work on Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and 26.04 LTS and install Docker Engine 29.8.2 and Docker Compose 5.6.0 (October 2026). The repository key goes in /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc and the source in /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.sources , which replace the older apt-key and docker.list steps. Members of the docker group get root-level access to the host, so add only your own sudo user. Docker-published ports bypass UFW. Bind containers to 127.0.0.1 and put a reverse proxy on ports 80 and 443. Cap container logs in /etc/docker/daemon.json at 3 files of 10 MB per container. Applies to: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and 26.04 LTS · Docker Engine 29.8.2 · Docker Compose 5.6.0 · checked October 2026 Docker Engine is the open-source container runtime that builds and runs containers on Linux. Docker Compose is the Docker CLI plugin that starts multi-container apps from one compose.yaml file. This tutorial shows how to install Docker on Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 from Docker's official apt repository, then covers the docker group, log rotation, the UFW port bypass and a first Compose stack. On a headless server, install Docker Engine. Docker Desktop is a graphical app for desktop computers. Prerequisites A VPS running Ubuntu 24.04 LTS or 26.04 LTS (64-bit) with SSH access. A non-root user with sudo privileges who logs in with an SSH key. To make a key, see How to Generate an SSH Key on Windows, macOS, and Linux . At least 1 GB of free disk: the Docker packages list about 365 MB of installed size in Docker's repository index. Docker's install docs set no RAM minimum, so size RAM for the containers you plan to run. If you log in as root with an SSH key, create the sudo user once and copy your key to it. adduser asks for a password, which sudo uses later: adduser deploy usermod -aG sudo deploy install -d -m 700 -o deploy -g deploy /home/deploy/.ssh install -m 600 -o deploy -g deploy ~/.ssh/authorized_keys /home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys Log out and connect again with ssh deploy@YOUR_SERVER_IP . Every command from Step 1 on runs as deploy . Replace values written in capitals, such as YOUR_SERVER_IP , with your own. Step 1: Remove conflicting packages Ubuntu's own docker.io , docker-compose-v2 and containerd packages conflict with Docker's packages. Remove any that are installed: sudo apt remove $( dpkg --get-selections docker.io docker-compose \ docker-compose-v2 docker-doc docker-buildx podman-docker containerd runc | cut -f1 ) On a fresh server, dpkg finds no matching packages and apt removes nothing. Data in /var/lib/docker stays on disk. Step 2: Add Docker's apt repository Docker signs its packages with its own key. Download the key into the apt keyrings directory: sudo apt update sudo apt install ca-certificates curl sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings sudo curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc sudo chmod a+r /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc Create the repository source. The command fills in your release codename and architecture: sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.sources << EOF Types: deb URIs: https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu Suites: $( . /etc/os-release && echo " ${ UBUNTU_CODENAME :- $VERSION_CODENAME } " ) Components: stable Architectures: $( dpkg --print-architecture ) Signed-By: /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc EOF The output looks similar to this: Types: deb URIs: https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu Suites: noble Components: stable Architectures: amd64 Signed-By: /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc On Ubuntu 26.04 the Suites line reads resolute . Refresh the package index: sudo apt update Docker's docs do not recommend the get.docker.com convenience script for production servers. Step 3: Install Docker on Ubuntu with the Compose plugin Install the five packages in one command, and type Y when apt asks to continue: sudo apt install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin apt also installs docker-ce-rootless-extras and recommended tools such as git and pigz when they are missing. Package What it installs docker-ce Docker Engine, the dockerd daemon docker-ce-cli The docker command containerd.io containerd and runc, the runtime under Docker Engine docker-buildx-plugin docker buildx , the BuildKit image builder docker-compose-plugin docker compose On Ubuntu, the Docker service starts after the install and on every boot. Check both: systemctl is-active docker systemctl is-enabled docker active enabled Check the installed versions: docker --version docker compose version The output looks similar to this. Your versions may be newer: Docker version 29.8.2, build 7fc2dff Docker Compose version v5.6.0 Step 4: Run the hello-world test The hello-world image pulls from Docker Hub, prints a message and exits: sudo docker run hello-world Unable to find image 'hello-world:latest' locally ... Hello from Docker! This message shows that your installation appears to be working correctly. ... Step 5: Run Docker without sudo The Docker daemon listens on /var/run/docker.sock , which only root and the docker group can open. The package creates the group with no members. Add your user: sudo usermod -aG docker $USER A docker group member can start a container that mounts any host directory, which is root-level access. Add only users you would also give sudo. Log out of SSH and back in so the group applies, then check: id -nG docker run --rm hello-world The group list must include docker . For a daemon that runs without root, Docker documents a separate rootless mode. Step 6: Configure the Docker daemon /etc/docker/daemon.json sets defaults for new containers. This file caps logs and binds published ports to loopback unless a compose file names another address: sudo mkdir -p /etc/docker sudo tee /etc/docker/daemon.json > /dev/null << ' EOF ' { "log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": { "max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3" }, "ip": "127.0.0.1", "default-network-opts": { "bridge": { "com.docker.network.bridge.host_binding_ipv4": "127.0.0.1" } } } EOF log-opts : the json-file driver has no size limit by default. These values keep 3 files of 10 MB per container, written as quoted strings. ip : ports published on the default bridge network without an address bind to 127.0.0.1 . default-network-opts : the same default for user-defined networks, including the ones Compose creates. A container that must answer on the internet, such as a reverse proxy container, needs an explicit address in its port mapping: "0.0.0.0:443:443" . If the file already existed, merge these keys into it. Validate it, then restart Docker: sudo dockerd --validate --config-file /etc/docker/daemon.json sudo systemctl restart docker configuration OK The settings apply to containers and networks created after the restart. Step 7: Enable UFW and keep container ports private The Uncomplicated Firewall (UFW) filters the INPUT chain. Docker routes published ports through NAT rules that run before that chain, so a port published on a public address stays reachable even when UFW denies it. The Step 6 defaults and an explicit 127.0.0.1 in each compose file keep containers on loopback. Allow SSH before you enable the firewall, or UFW blocks new SSH logins: sudo ufw allow OpenSSH sudo ufw enable sudo ufw status Type y when UFW asks to confirm. The output looks similar to this: Status: active To Action From -- ------ ---- OpenSSH ALLOW Anywhere OpenSSH (v6) ALLOW Anywhere (v6) To serve a container on the internet, run a reverse proxy on the host and allow 80/tcp and 443/tcp . The Nginx, PostgreSQL, and Redis setup guide covers Nginx as a reverse proxy. A port you publish on purpose with 0.0.0.0:PORT:PORT skips UFW. To restrict it, add rules to the DOCKER-USER iptables chain and match the host port with -m conntrack --ctorigdstport PORT , as Docker's iptables docs show. Step 8: Start a test Compose stack Compose names the project, network and containers after the directory: mkdir -p ~/hello-compose cd ~/hello-compose nano compose.yaml Paste this file, then save with Ctrl+O and exit with Ctrl+X: services : web : image : nginx:1.30.5-alpine ports : - " 127.0.0.1:8080:80" restart : unless-stopped Current Compose releases ignore the old version: key, so the file has none. restart: unless-stopped starts the container again after a reboot. Start the stack: docker compose up -d Compose pulls the image, creates the hello-compose_default network and starts the hello-compose-web-1 container. Step 9: Verify the stack and the firewall Check that the service runs, answers on loopback, binds to 127.0.0.1 and uses the log limits: docker compose ps --services --status running curl -sI http://127.0.0.1:8080 | head -n 1 docker port hello-compose-web-1 docker inspect --format '{{json .HostConfig.LogConfig}}' hello-compose-web-1 web HTTP/1.1 200 OK 80/tcp -> 127.0.0.1:8080 {"Type":"json-file","Config":{"max-file":"3","max-size":"10m"}} From your own computer, test the public address: curl --max-time 5 http://YOUR_SERVER_IP:8080 Replace YOUR_SERVER_IP with the server's IP address, such as 203.0.113.10 . The request times out after 5 seconds; a page means the port is public. Remove the test stack: docker compose down Update Docker Docker's repository is an apt source, so a system upgrade also updates Docker Engine and the plugins: sudo apt update sudo apt upgrade Containers with restart: unless-stopped start again when the Docker service restarts. To stay on one release, list the versions in the repository, install one as Docker's install docs show, then hold both packages so apt upgrade skips them: apt list --all-versions docker-ce sudo apt install docker-ce = YOUR_VERSION docker-ce-cli = YOUR_VERSION sudo apt-mark hold docker-ce docker-ce-cli Replace YOUR_VERSION with a full version string from the list, such as 5:29.8.2-1~ubuntu.24.04~noble . Run sudo apt-mark unhold docker-ce docker-ce-cli when you want to upgrade again. The Ubuntu release upgrader turns off third-party sources such as Docker's, and Suites keeps the old codename. After you upgrade Ubuntu 24.04 to 26.04 , rerun the Step 2 source command and sudo apt update . Troubleshoot common Docker errors Symptom Cause Fix permission denied while trying to connect to the docker API at unix:///var/run/docker.sock Your user is not in the docker group, or the SSH session started before you joined it Run Step 5, then log out and back in failed to connect to the docker API at unix:///var/run/docker.sock; check if the path is correct and if the daemon is running The Docker service is stopped or failed to start sudo systemctl start docker , then sudo journalctl -u docker -n 50 . Run the Step 6 validate command to check daemon.json Conflicting values set for option Signed-By from apt update An older docker.list from another guide points at a different key file Delete /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list and keep docker.sources docker-compose: command not found Compose v1 used docker-compose ; the supported plugin runs as docker compose Run docker compose , with a space Warning that the attribute version is obsolete A compose file written for Compose v1 Delete the version: line FAQ Does Docker work on Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04? Yes. Docker's install docs list Ubuntu 26.04, 24.04 and 22.04 LTS as supported releases. The same repository steps install Docker Engine 29.8.2 and Compose 5.6.0 on both 24.04 and 26.04 as of October 2026. Is Docker still relevant in 2026? Yes. Docker Engine 29.8.2 shipped on September 30, 2026, and Compose 5.6.0 on October 2, 2026. Self-hosted tools such as n8n and Open WebUI ship official Docker images. Should I install docker.io or docker-ce on Ubuntu? Install docker-ce from Docker's repository for current releases. Ubuntu's docker.io package was at 29.1.3 on 24.04 and 26.04 in October 2026, while Docker's repository had 29.8.2. The two conflict, so remove docker.io first. Is Docker Compose installed with Docker? Yes, when you install the docker-compose-plugin package from Docker's repository, as in Step 3. Compose then runs as docker compose, with a space. The older docker-compose v1 command is no longer supported. How do I fix docker permission denied on Ubuntu? Add your user to the docker group with sudo usermod -aG docker $USER, then log out and back in. Only root and docker group members can open /var/run/docker.sock. Group members get root-level access to the host. Does UFW block Docker ports? No. Docker routes published ports through its own NAT rules before UFW filters traffic, so a published port stays reachable when UFW denies it. Publish containers on 127.0.0.1 and use a reverse proxy on ports 80 and 443. Do I need Docker Desktop on an Ubuntu server? No. Docker Desktop is a graphical app that runs Docker Engine inside a VM. It needs KVM, a desktop environment such as GNOME, KDE or MATE, and at least 4 GB of RAM. A headless server needs Docker Engine and the Compose plugin only. Next steps How to Self-Host n8n with Docker Compose on Ubuntu 24.04 How to Install Ollama on Ubuntu 24.04 with Open WebUI (CPU Only) , which runs Open WebUI with Compose How to Install Nginx Proxy Manager with Docker on Ubuntu 24.04 , to serve containers on your own domain with HTTPS Install Docker Engine on Ubuntu and Packet filtering and firewalls in Docker's docs Licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 .
items.summary_html:
Originally published by Arct Cloud: How to Install Docker and Docker Compose on Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04.

This article was prepared with AI assistance. Product references were removed and formatting adjusted for this DEV edition.

TL;DR:

  • Install five packages from Docker's apt repository: docker-ce, docker-ce-cli, containerd.io, docker-buildx-plugin and docker-compose-plugin.
  • The same steps work on Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and 26.04 LTS and install Docker Engine 29.8.2 and Docker Compose 5.6.0 (October 2026).
  • The repository key goes in /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc and the source in /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.sources, which replace the older apt-key and docker.list steps.
  • Members of the docker group get root-level access to the host, so add only your own sudo user.
  • Docker-published ports bypass UFW. Bind containers to 127.0.0.1 and put a reverse proxy on ports 80 and 443.
  • Cap container logs in /etc/docker/daemon.json at 3 files of 10 MB per container.

Applies to: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and 26.04 LTS · Docker Engine 29.8.2 · Docker Compose 5.6.0 · checked October 2026

Docker Engine is the open-source container runtime that builds and runs containers on Linux. Docker Compose is the Docker CLI plugin that starts multi-container apps from one compose.yaml file. This tutorial shows how to install Docker on Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 from Docker's official apt repository, then covers the docker group, log rotation, the UFW port bypass and a first Compose stack. On a headless server, install Docker Engine. Docker Desktop is a graphical app for desktop computers.

Prerequisites
  • A VPS running Ubuntu 24.04 LTS or 26.04 LTS (64-bit) with SSH access.
  • A non-root user with sudo privileges who logs in with an SSH key. To make a key, see How to Generate an SSH Key on Windows, macOS, and Linux.
  • At least 1 GB of free disk: the Docker packages list about 365 MB of installed size in Docker's repository index. Docker's install docs set no RAM minimum, so size RAM for the containers you plan to run.

If you log in as root with an SSH key, create the sudo user once and copy your key to it. adduser asks for a password, which sudo uses later:

adduser deploy
usermod -aG sudo deploy
install -d -m 700 -o deploy -g deploy /home/deploy/.ssh
install -m 600 -o deploy -g deploy ~/.ssh/authorized_keys /home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys

Log out and connect again with ssh deploy@YOUR_SERVER_IP. Every command from Step 1 on runs as deploy. Replace values written in capitals, such as YOUR_SERVER_IP, with your own.

Step 1: Remove conflicting packages

Ubuntu's own docker.io, docker-compose-v2 and containerd packages conflict with Docker's packages. Remove any that are installed:

sudo apt remove $(dpkg --get-selections docker.io docker-compose \
  docker-compose-v2 docker-doc docker-buildx podman-docker containerd runc | cut -f1)

On a fresh server, dpkg finds no matching packages and apt removes nothing. Data in /var/lib/docker stays on disk.

Step 2: Add Docker's apt repository

Docker signs its packages with its own key. Download the key into the apt keyrings directory:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install ca-certificates curl
sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
sudo chmod a+r /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc

Create the repository source. The command fills in your release codename and architecture:

sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.sources <<EOF
Types: deb
URIs: https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu
Suites: $(. /etc/os-release && echo "${UBUNTU_CODENAME:-$VERSION_CODENAME}")
Components: stable
Architectures: $(dpkg --print-architecture)
Signed-By: /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
EOF

The output looks similar to this:

Types: deb
URIs: https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu
Suites: noble
Components: stable
Architectures: amd64
Signed-By: /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc

On Ubuntu 26.04 the Suites line reads resolute. Refresh the package index:

sudo apt update

Docker's docs do not recommend the get.docker.com convenience script for production servers.

Step 3: Install Docker on Ubuntu with the Compose plugin

Install the five packages in one command, and type Y when apt asks to continue:

sudo apt install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin

apt also installs docker-ce-rootless-extras and recommended tools such as git and pigz when they are missing.

Package What it installs docker-ce Docker Engine, the dockerd daemon docker-ce-cli The docker command containerd.io containerd and runc, the runtime under Docker Engine docker-buildx-plugin docker buildx, the BuildKit image builder docker-compose-plugin docker compose

On Ubuntu, the Docker service starts after the install and on every boot. Check both:

systemctl is-active docker
systemctl is-enabled docker

active
enabled

Check the installed versions:

docker --version
docker compose version

The output looks similar to this. Your versions may be newer:

Docker version 29.8.2, build 7fc2dff
Docker Compose version v5.6.0
Step 4: Run the hello-world test

The hello-world image pulls from Docker Hub, prints a message and exits:

sudo docker run hello-world

Unable to find image 'hello-world:latest' locally
...
Hello from Docker!
This message shows that your installation appears to be working correctly.
...
Step 5: Run Docker without sudo

The Docker daemon listens on /var/run/docker.sock, which only root and the docker group can open. The package creates the group with no members. Add your user:

sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

A docker group member can start a container that mounts any host directory, which is root-level access. Add only users you would also give sudo. Log out of SSH and back in so the group applies, then check:

id -nG
docker run --rm hello-world

The group list must include docker. For a daemon that runs without root, Docker documents a separate rootless mode.

Step 6: Configure the Docker daemon

/etc/docker/daemon.json sets defaults for new containers. This file caps logs and binds published ports to loopback unless a compose file names another address:

sudo mkdir -p /etc/docker
sudo tee /etc/docker/daemon.json > /dev/null <<'EOF'
{
  "log-driver": "json-file",
  "log-opts": {
    "max-size": "10m",
    "max-file": "3"
  },
  "ip": "127.0.0.1",
  "default-network-opts": {
    "bridge": {
      "com.docker.network.bridge.host_binding_ipv4": "127.0.0.1"
    }
  }
}
EOF
  • log-opts: the json-file driver has no size limit by default. These values keep 3 files of 10 MB per container, written as quoted strings.
  • ip: ports published on the default bridge network without an address bind to 127.0.0.1.
  • default-network-opts: the same default for user-defined networks, including the ones Compose creates.
  • A container that must answer on the internet, such as a reverse proxy container, needs an explicit address in its port mapping: "0.0.0.0:443:443".

If the file already existed, merge these keys into it. Validate it, then restart Docker:

sudo dockerd --validate --config-file /etc/docker/daemon.json
sudo systemctl restart docker

configuration OK

The settings apply to containers and networks created after the restart.

Step 7: Enable UFW and keep container ports private

The Uncomplicated Firewall (UFW) filters the INPUT chain. Docker routes published ports through NAT rules that run before that chain, so a port published on a public address stays reachable even when UFW denies it. The Step 6 defaults and an explicit 127.0.0.1 in each compose file keep containers on loopback.

Allow SSH before you enable the firewall, or UFW blocks new SSH logins:

sudo ufw allow OpenSSH
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status

Type y when UFW asks to confirm. The output looks similar to this:

Status: active

To                         Action      From
--                         ------      ----
OpenSSH                    ALLOW       Anywhere
OpenSSH (v6)               ALLOW       Anywhere (v6)

To serve a container on the internet, run a reverse proxy on the host and allow 80/tcp and 443/tcp. The Nginx, PostgreSQL, and Redis setup guide covers Nginx as a reverse proxy. A port you publish on purpose with 0.0.0.0:PORT:PORT skips UFW. To restrict it, add rules to the DOCKER-USER iptables chain and match the host port with -m conntrack --ctorigdstport PORT, as Docker's iptables docs show.

Step 8: Start a test Compose stack

Compose names the project, network and containers after the directory:

mkdir -p ~/hello-compose
cd ~/hello-compose
nano compose.yaml

Paste this file, then save with Ctrl+O and exit with Ctrl+X:

services:
  web:
    image: nginx:1.30.5-alpine
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8080:80"
    restart: unless-stopped

Current Compose releases ignore the old version: key, so the file has none. restart: unless-stopped starts the container again after a reboot. Start the stack:

docker compose up -d

Compose pulls the image, creates the hello-compose_default network and starts the hello-compose-web-1 container.

Step 9: Verify the stack and the firewall

Check that the service runs, answers on loopback, binds to 127.0.0.1 and uses the log limits:

docker compose ps --services --status running
curl -sI http://127.0.0.1:8080 | head -n 1
docker port hello-compose-web-1
docker inspect --format '{{json .HostConfig.LogConfig}}' hello-compose-web-1

web
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
80/tcp -> 127.0.0.1:8080
{"Type":"json-file","Config":{"max-file":"3","max-size":"10m"}}

From your own computer, test the public address:

curl --max-time 5 http://YOUR_SERVER_IP:8080

Replace YOUR_SERVER_IP with the server's IP address, such as 203.0.113.10. The request times out after 5 seconds; a page means the port is public. Remove the test stack:

docker compose down
Update Docker

Docker's repository is an apt source, so a system upgrade also updates Docker Engine and the plugins:

sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade

Containers with restart: unless-stopped start again when the Docker service restarts. To stay on one release, list the versions in the repository, install one as Docker's install docs show, then hold both packages so apt upgrade skips them:

apt list --all-versions docker-ce
sudo apt install docker-ce=YOUR_VERSION docker-ce-cli=YOUR_VERSION
sudo apt-mark hold docker-ce docker-ce-cli

Replace YOUR_VERSION with a full version string from the list, such as 5:29.8.2-1~ubuntu.24.04~noble. Run sudo apt-mark unhold docker-ce docker-ce-cli when you want to upgrade again.

The Ubuntu release upgrader turns off third-party sources such as Docker's, and Suites keeps the old codename. After you upgrade Ubuntu 24.04 to 26.04, rerun the Step 2 source command and sudo apt update.

Troubleshoot common Docker errors
Symptom Cause Fix permission denied while trying to connect to the docker API at unix:///var/run/docker.sock Your user is not in the docker group, or the SSH session started before you joined it Run Step 5, then log out and back in failed to connect to the docker API at unix:///var/run/docker.sock; check if the path is correct and if the daemon is running The Docker service is stopped or failed to start sudo systemctl start docker, then sudo journalctl -u docker -n 50. Run the Step 6 validate command to check daemon.json Conflicting values set for option Signed-By from apt update An older docker.list from another guide points at a different key file Delete /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list and keep docker.sources docker-compose: command not found Compose v1 used docker-compose; the supported plugin runs as docker compose Run docker compose, with a space Warning that the attribute version is obsolete A compose file written for Compose v1 Delete the version: line
FAQ Does Docker work on Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04?

Yes. Docker's install docs list Ubuntu 26.04, 24.04 and 22.04 LTS as supported releases. The same repository steps install Docker Engine 29.8.2 and Compose 5.6.0 on both 24.04 and 26.04 as of October 2026.

Is Docker still relevant in 2026?

Yes. Docker Engine 29.8.2 shipped on September 30, 2026, and Compose 5.6.0 on October 2, 2026. Self-hosted tools such as n8n and Open WebUI ship official Docker images.

Should I install docker.io or docker-ce on Ubuntu?

Install docker-ce from Docker's repository for current releases. Ubuntu's docker.io package was at 29.1.3 on 24.04 and 26.04 in October 2026, while Docker's repository had 29.8.2. The two conflict, so remove docker.io first.

Is Docker Compose installed with Docker?

Yes, when you install the docker-compose-plugin package from Docker's repository, as in Step 3. Compose then runs as docker compose, with a space. The older docker-compose v1 command is no longer supported.

How do I fix docker permission denied on Ubuntu?

Add your user to the docker group with sudo usermod -aG docker $USER, then log out and back in. Only root and docker group members can open /var/run/docker.sock. Group members get root-level access to the host.

Does UFW block Docker ports?

No. Docker routes published ports through its own NAT rules before UFW filters traffic, so a published port stays reachable when UFW denies it. Publish containers on 127.0.0.1 and use a reverse proxy on ports 80 and 443.

Do I need Docker Desktop on an Ubuntu server?

No. Docker Desktop is a graphical app that runs Docker Engine inside a VM. It needs KVM, a desktop environment such as GNOME, KDE or MATE, and at least 4 GB of RAM. A headless server needs Docker Engine and the Compose plugin only.

Next steps

  • How to Install Ollama on Ubuntu 24.04 with Open WebUI (CPU Only), which runs Open WebUI with Compose
  • How to Install Nginx Proxy Manager with Docker on Ubuntu 24.04, to serve containers on your own domain with HTTPS
  • Install Docker Engine on Ubuntu and Packet filtering and firewalls in Docker's docs

N8N_WEBHOOK_URL replaced WEBHOOK_URL in n8n 2.35.0, and n8n 1.0 removed the N8N_BASIC_AUTH variables. n8n's sizing example lists 320 MB to 2 GB of memory for n8n itself.
