items.title: What’s new in Windows 11: Everyday experiences, reimagined
items.summary: Every day, your PC helps you get things done, stay connected, capture ideas and make time for what you enjoy. That’s why Windows 11 continues to evolve, starting with a faster, more dependable and refined experience. Throughout the year, we’ve worked with the Windows Insider community on improvements to Windows that are now beginning to roll out broadly, with more to come. That same care shapes our latest Windows experiences, building on these foundational improvements with new possibilities that make everyday moments on your PC simpler and more intuitive. From new features for gamers, to a modernized Photos experience, to more seamless phone to PC integration, Windows is built to support the way you work, create, play and connect. A faster, more responsive Windows experience Responsiveness shapes nearly every experience on your PC. It’s the difference between staying in your flow and waiting for your device to catch up. That’s why we’ve continued to invest across Windows , from the platform and shell to the apps people use every day, to make Windows feel faster, more responsive and more efficient. The result is a Windows experience that’s up to 20% more responsive , with improvements you can feel as soon as you boot into your PC and extending to Start, File Explorer, Search, Snipping Tool, Microsoft 365, Edge and more 1 . A big part of that work is making smarter use of memory and system resources. We’ve improved memory management and efficiency across Windows to help keep more of your PC’s resources focused on what you’re actively doing. That work can make an especially meaningful difference on PCs with 8GB of memory. Windows can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage, helping your PC stay responsive as you open more apps or browser tabs. Windows is also making additional memory-saving improvements that reduce background memory use. For example, on PCs with 8GB of memory or less, Widgets load only when you open them, making more than 200 MB of memory available for your apps and other work 2 . It’s one example of the broader work underway to reduce the Windows memory footprint and deliver a fast, responsive experience across the PCs people use every day, an area we’ve made an explicit focus for Windows. But a great Windows experience isn’t only about speed. It’s also about making your PC feel dependable, less disruptive and more your own. We’re giving you more flexibility to personalize Start and your taskbar , including choosing where it appears on your screen, while making Widgets cleaner and quieter so you have more control over what gets your attention. And we’ve improved Windows Update to give you greater control over when updates happen and better coordinate updates to reduce restarts, while continuing to reduce the time it takes to apply an update. We’re also improving the everyday interactions you depend on. Bluetooth headphones work more reliably on Windows, with smoother pairing, reconnection, audio and calls, including an AirPods pairing experience that’s up to 15 seconds faster 3 . And we’ve made signing in with Windows Hello easier, faster and more reliable, with improvements to both face and fingerprint recognition. Alongside that work, we’re partnering with our hardware ecosystem through the Driver Quality Initiative to improve driver stability, reliability, security and performance across Windows devices. The result is a Windows experience that feels faster, more responsive and more thoughtfully designed around you, whether you’re opening an app, finding a file, connecting your headphones, arranging your taskbar the way you want or simply getting back to what you were doing. From searching to doing, faster https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2TOTiZhIrVo For hundreds of millions of people each day, Windows search on the taskbar is where intent begins. It’s one of the quickest ways to get started, whether finding a file, opening an app, or changing a setting. This release builds on the search quality improvements we delivered in recent months, with clearer results and more control over suggestions. Now, we are carrying those improvements forward with a new interface and expanding search from a place for finding information into a place for getting things done. Finding the right result is often only the first step. After finding what you’re looking for, you often need to navigate to another destination to complete the task. Actions allow you to complete common Windows tasks directly from the search results. When searching for a system setting like dark mode or night light, you can now make the relevant change without opening Settings or searching for the right sub-menu. Search can also help with managing your workspace, like minimizing or arranging open windows, and coming soon, the ability to interact with your connected phone. These actions are designed to make common tasks faster and more intuitive: simply search and act directly from the taskbar. The new Windows Search experience is available to Windows Insiders today and will roll out more broadly later this year. Learn more about the new Windows Search experience . Move between your phone and PC seamlessly https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uxNHn_-vmRg When you’re in the middle of something on your PC, your phone’s messages, apps and files should be within reach too. Windows 11 brings more of your phone experience to your desktop, so you can reply to a message, answer phone calls, open apps, and keep going without reaching for another device 4 . Preview messages and notifications from your Android phone or iPhone in Start to see what needs your attention. When a conversation needs a reply, open it in a window focused on your chat, send your response and get back to what you were doing. Quick Settings keeps useful phone controls close, whether you want to silence or ring a misplaced phone. With a supported Android phone, open your phone apps in separate, resizable windows on your desktop, with room to work on the larger screen alongside your other apps. Browse your phone files in File Explorer and open what you need without switching devices. And when you take a photo on your phone, a notification on your PC lets you open it with one click, ready for a closer look. When you do move between devices, Resume helps you pick up supported activities where you left off instead of finding your place again. It’s your phone and PC working together, so you can stay connected from the screen you’re already using. From capture to creation, faster https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=62yLzOLBXOw Spend less time searching for your photos and more time enjoying them. The new Microsoft Photos app brings images from your PC and connected libraries into one fast, beautiful Gallery, with more of your collection in view. Whether you’re revisiting a favorite trip or browsing everyday snapshots, it’s easier to see what you have and rediscover moments worth keeping close. Find a favorite by describing it in your own words or bring memories together in albums to share. Bring out the best in a favorite photo with a new Editor that loads faster and gives you easy-to-use, precise editing tools on your PC’s larger display. From a quick crop to fine-tuning colors, you have room to see the details and make the adjustments you want. Quickly remove a distracting object from the background, or use Relight to correct lighting and explore a different look. The Photos app now launches up to 20% faster and the redesigned Viewer opens photos with less clutter and more room for your pictures to shine 5 . When you find a photo you want to pass along or put on display, everyday actions like sharing and printing are within easy reach. Learn more about the new Photos experience . The most PC games, and the best place to play 6 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zB3Uao5BsOU Nobody likes waiting. Advanced Shader Delivery (ASD) is designed to reduce the initial load time of your games by delivering precompiled shaders for supported titles like Forza Horizon 6 and Gears of War: E-Day, so your games load in seconds instead of minutes. To get the most from ASD, install the XBOX PC app before downloading a supported game and make sure your graphics drivers are up to date. Learn more about ASD and supported titles . There’s never been a better time to start playing games on Windows. And to celebrate 25 years of XBOX, starting this November, eligible Windows 11 PC purchased in the US can claim a collection of 25 fan-favorite games at no additional cost. The collection includes $500+ worth of games, such as The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim Special Edition, Halo: Combat Evolved Anniversary, Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition, Minecraft Dungeons, Gears of War: Reloaded , and more. Once claimed, the PC versions of the games are linked to your Microsoft account and you can play them on any compatible Windows PC, with select titles also playable on XBOX Series X|S consoles with XBOX Play Anywhere . Note that some devices eligible for the offer cannot play all the games in the collection 7 . Once you're playing, press Win+G to open Game Bar, where you can find useful widgets for recording your gameplay, connecting with friends, and managing your audio settings. You can also use Microsoft Edge for Game Bar to pull up guides, videos and websites on top of your game, without switching away. It's one of the exclusive features that make Microsoft Edge the best browser for gamers on Windows. Bring ideas to life more naturally Some ideas are easier to draw than describe. With Microsoft Ink Canvas , pen and touch become a more natural way to sketch, annotate and bring thoughts together on a flexible canvas. Select notes, drawings and references and use Copilot to help turn them into visual or written output you can copy and transfer into another document or presentation 8 . It is a more fluid path from the first rough draft to something ready to share. Ink Canvas is pre-installed on Surface Pro 12-inch (2 nd Edition), and users with other supported Windows devices can download it now from the Microsoft Store 9 . Feel the difference in every interaction Advanced haptics in Windows 11 bring a sense of touch to everyday work and creativity. Whether you’re snapping a window into place, aligning an object in Microsoft PowerPoint or Affinity by Canva, or snapping a clip to a Filmora timeline, subtle tactile cues provide immediate physical confirmation that helps you work with confidence. A library of curated effects connects each cue to the action, making interactions feel more natural and responsive. Supported accessories—including Surface Mouse (2nd Edition) and Logitech MX Master 4 —bring these experiences to your fingertips 10 . Learn more about advanced haptics . A more comfortable PC experience, for everybody A personal computer should feel personal. It should adapt to how you see, read, learn and work, not the other way around. Windows 11 brings accessibility updates shaped by feedback from the people who use them every day, giving you more ways to make your screen comfortable, work with confidence and get started independently. Make your display feel right for you with Screen Tint . Choose a color overlay and adjust its strength to suit your preferences. If you use Magnifier across multiple displays, each screen can now keep its own zoom level. Keep reference material magnified on one screen while you work on another, with a locked view that stays where you need it. items.summary_html: Every day, your PC helps you get things done, stay connected, capture ideas and make time for what you enjoy. That’s why Windows 11 continues to evolve, starting with a faster, more dependable and refined experience. Throughout the year, we’ve worked with the Windows Insider community on improvements to Windows that are now beginning to roll out broadly, with more to come.  That same care shapes our latest Windows experiences, building on these foundational improvements with new possibilities that make everyday moments on your PC simpler and more intuitive. From new features for gamers, to a modernized Photos experience, to more seamless phone to PC integration, Windows is built to support the way you work, create, play and connect. A faster, more responsive Windows experience Responsiveness shapes nearly every experience on your PC. It’s the difference between staying in your flow and waiting for your device to catch up. That’s why we’ve continued to invest across Windows, from the platform and shell to the apps people use every day, to make Windows feel faster, more responsive and more efficient. The result is a Windows experience that’s up to 20% more responsive, with improvements you can feel as soon as you boot into your PC and extending to Start, File Explorer, Search, Snipping Tool, Microsoft 365, Edge and more1. A big part of that work is making smarter use of memory and system resources. We’ve improved memory management and efficiency across Windows to help keep more of your PC’s resources focused on what you’re actively doing. That work can make an especially meaningful difference on PCs with 8GB of memory. Windows can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage, helping your PC stay responsive as you open more apps or browser tabs. Windows is also making additional memory-saving improvements that reduce background memory use. For example, on PCs with 8GB of memory or less, Widgets load only when you open them, making more than 200 MB of memory available for your apps and other work2. It’s one example of the broader work underway to reduce the Windows memory footprint and deliver a fast, responsive experience across the PCs people use every day, an area we’ve made an explicit focus for Windows.  But a great Windows experience isn’t only about speed. It’s also about making your PC feel dependable, less disruptive and more your own. We’re giving you more flexibility to personalize Start and your taskbar, including choosing where it appears on your screen, while making Widgets cleaner and quieter so you have more control over what gets your attention. Bluetooth headphones work more reliably on Windows, with smoother pairing, reconnection, audio and calls, including an AirPods pairing experience that’s up to 15 seconds faster3. And we’ve made signing in with Windows Hello easier, faster and more reliable, with improvements to both face and fingerprint recognition. Alongside that work, we’re partnering with our hardware ecosystem through the Driver Quality Initiative to improve driver stability, reliability, security and performance across Windows devices. The result is a Windows experience that feels faster, more responsive and more thoughtfully designed around you, whether you’re opening an app, finding a file, connecting your headphones, arranging your taskbar the way you want or simply getting back to what you were doing. From searching to doing, faster https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2TOTiZhIrVo For hundreds of millions of people each day, Windows search on the taskbar is where intent begins. It’s one of the quickest ways to get started, whether finding a file, opening an app, or changing a setting. This release builds on the search quality improvements we delivered in recent months, with clearer results and more control over suggestions. Now, we are carrying those improvements forward with a new interface and expanding search from a place for finding information into a place for getting things done. Finding the right result is often only the first step. After finding what you’re looking for, you often need to navigate to another destination to complete the task. Actions allow you to complete common Windows tasks directly from the search results. When searching for a system setting like dark mode or night light, you can now make the relevant change without opening Settings or searching for the right sub-menu. Search can also help with managing your workspace, like minimizing or arranging open windows, and coming soon, the ability to interact with your connected phone. These actions are designed to make common tasks faster and more intuitive: simply search and act directly from the taskbar. The new Windows Search experience is available to Windows Insiders today and will roll out more broadly later this year. Learn more about the new Windows Search experience. Move between your phone and PC seamlessly https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uxNHn_-vmRg When you’re in the middle of something on your PC, your phone’s messages, apps and files should be within reach too. Windows 11 brings more of your phone experience to your desktop, so you can reply to a message, answer phone calls, open apps, and keep going without reaching for another device4. Preview messages and notifications from your Android phone or iPhone in Start to see what needs your attention. When a conversation needs a reply, open it in a window focused on your chat, send your response and get back to what you were doing. Quick Settings keeps useful phone controls close, whether you want to silence or ring a misplaced phone. Browse your phone files in File Explorer and open what you need without switching devices. When you do move between devices, Resume helps you pick up supported activities where you left off instead of finding your place again. It’s your phone and PC working together, so you can stay connected from the screen you’re already using. From capture to creation, faster https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=62yLzOLBXOw Spend less time searching for your photos and more time enjoying them. The new Microsoft Photos app brings images from your PC and connected libraries into one fast, beautiful Gallery, with more of your collection in view. Whether you’re revisiting a favorite trip or browsing everyday snapshots, it’s easier to see what you have and rediscover moments worth keeping close. Find a favorite by describing it in your own words or bring memories together in albums to share. Bring out the best in a favorite photo with a new Editor that loads faster and gives you easy-to-use, precise editing tools on your PC’s larger display. From a quick crop to fine-tuning colors, you have room to see the details and make the adjustments you want. Quickly remove a distracting object from the background, or use Relight to correct lighting and explore a different look. When you find a photo you want to pass along or put on display, everyday actions like sharing and printing are within easy reach. Learn more about the new Photos experience. The most PC games, and the best place to play6 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zB3Uao5BsOU Nobody likes waiting. items.title: This startup raised $21 million to clean up the AI agent mess hitting companies
items.summary: Opsin cofounders Jeremy Mailen, James Pham, and Oz Wasserman. Christopher Denise/Opsin Opsin raised $21 million to monitor and govern the AI agents companies are using. The startup hopes to complement the agent boom brought by OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, and others. In the red-hot cybersecurity space, Opsin is scaling up its sales and engineering ranks. AI agents are starting to outnumber humans in many high-tech workplaces, and they can be far trickier to monitor. Opsin, an AI security and governance startup, announced Thursday it raised $21 million to meet the moment. As employees across the corporate world plug AI agents from the likes of OpenAI and Microsoft into more of their work, the company is helping to wrangle the new crop of potentially risky interlopers . It's never been easier for non-technical workers to deploy agents — autonomous software built on AI that can complete tasks. As employees pump the software into their companies' work, code, and databases, they can lose sight of what the AI is actually doing. When Opsin's CEO and cofounder, James Pham, realized security fears were slowing down AI use, he decided it was time to scale up his company, he told Business Insider. "Agents are actually more similar to humans than you think," Pham said. "And the reason is because you don't understand what is going on in a human head, but you can judge them by their actions." Opsin aims to provide a comprehensive view of what AI agents are actually doing within an organization and the risks that behavior might pose. SYN Ventures and Race Capital led the roughly 20-person company's new funding round, which will go toward expanding its sales and engineering teams. Security pros need to clean up a mess of AI agents Pham, an MIT alum, and one of his cofounders, Oz Wasserman, met at the firm Abnormal Security and each left in 2022. When they decided to launch a company, Pham said they spoke with hundreds of people to understand the concerns about bringing AI into businesses. The issue of sensitive data leaped out. Pham said that person after person raised concerns that AI agents might access and misuse personal or confidential information. Now, Opsin helps clients show where agents are active, which tools and data they access, what they were originally created to do, and which ones might need cleaning up. Then, the firm offers to continuously monitor companies' work, watch over agents, and flag risky behavior. "At the end of the day, it's all about the behaviors of the users, the behavior of the agent," Pham said. He said the scale of agents, even in relatively less tech-savvy companies, has stunned some customers. At one firm Opsin worked with, an agent made by a chief financial officer inadvertently gave other employees top-level access to financial information, Pham said. AI's cyber threats could mean a boom The cybersecurity industry has been in a frenzy, and now the growth of agents is adding to that storm. Glenn Chisholm, a cyber investor backing Opsin with SYN Ventures, told Business Insider that as companies use more AI products, hackers will find more targets. "The more people that are doing it, the easier it is for an attacker to gain access and purchase," Chisholm said. Cyberdefense stocks have soared this year, and Chisholm said he's seen more venture capital investment. Anthropic and OpenAI are each hiring aggressively in cybersecurity. Opsin hopes it can make companies feel safer using Microsoft Copilot , ChatGPT Enterprise, and other products. Chisholm is optimistic that the industry will adapt to AI. "The next couple of years are us working out how to get the most out of it, rather than sort of fearing the concept of it," he said. Have a tip? items.title: The code confidence gap nobody’s talking about
items.summary: AI has changed the economics of software creation: A task that once took hours to implement can now start with an agent producing an initial solution in minutes. As agents take on broader assignments, like changing code across a repository, refactoring services, writing tests, and preparing pull requests, output volume will continue to rise. That is an extraordinary opportunity, and it’s also why the next challenge for engineering organizations isn’t generating more code, but building confidence in the code that reaches production. In the agentic software factory, agents write, test, and propose changes faster than people can review them line by line. Code creation is becoming abundant; code confidence is not. This distinction matters because a completed pull request is not the same as a dependable outcome. The code may compile and pass a narrow test suite while still violating an architectural convention, introducing a security weakness, duplicating existing functionality, or creating maintenance costs that surface much later. The faster an organization generates changes, the less feasible it becomes to rely on heroics and manual review alone to catch every issue. “Code creation is becoming abundant; code confidence is not.” The way forward is to treat code confidence as something you can design into the software delivery system. A useful formula is Intent × Guardrails × Verification × Evidence. (And yes, the multiplication sign here is deliberate.) Each of these four pieces is crucial. Strength in three cannot make up for weakness in the fourth. Clear intent without verification does not prevent mistakes. Strong verification without evidence does not create accountability. Guardrails without clear intent merely automate ambiguity. Evidence without independent verification is only a record of what an agent claimed. Here is what each part of the formula means in practice. Intent: Make the standard explicit Agents are remarkably capable at pursuing a stated objective. But “build a payments feature” or “modernize this service” is not a sufficient objective for a production codebase. An organization’s definition of good software includes much more, such as business logic, security expectations, design patterns, performance needs, dependencies, and conventions accumulated through years of engineering. Intent is the discipline of making those expectations explicit. It means defining the goal of a change and the standards it must meet before an agent begins work. The better the context, the fewer cycles agents spend producing plausible but unsuitable answers, and the less rework falls to developers later. Guiderails: Shape the work before it creates risk Guiderails translate intent into boundaries that guide how agents operate. They may define which repositories, dependencies, data, or actions are permitted; where human approval is required; and what policies apply to a given class of code. The purpose is not to constrain every useful action. It’s to give agents enough structure to operate productively and predictably. A well-designed guiderail lets teams safely grant more autonomy because everyone understands the conditions under which that autonomy applies. The result is repeatable autonomy. Rather than treating every agent-driven change as a one-off experiment, teams can apply consistent boundaries and expand agentic development with confidence. Verification: Check every change independently Verification is where confidence is tested. As agents generate code at increasing scale, every change needs consistent evaluation for the qualities that matter: correctness, reliability, security, maintainability, and compliance with the organization’s own standards. “A model can assist in reviewing its own work, but an organization should not rely solely on the same probabilistic system that produced a change to determine whether that change is safe to ship.” Independence is essential. A model can assist in reviewing its own work, but an organization should not rely solely on the same probabilistic system that produced a change to determine whether that change is safe to ship. Repeatable, independent checks provide a common standard across models, agents, and toolchains. This is especially important when the AI tools themselves are evolving quickly. Verification also needs to occur in the flow of work, not as a slow, final checkpoint. The goal is to identify and fix problems at the source, while the agent or developer still has the context needed to resolve them. Evidence: Make confidence visible and auditable A change may be well-intentioned, carefully governed, and thoroughly checked. But engineering leaders, auditors, and the teams responsible for production still need to know what happened and why. Evidence is the durable record: what standards applied, what was checked, what was found, and how the issue was resolved. This matters most in complex and regulated environments, but it’s valuable everywhere. Evidence makes quality measurable, allows teams to improve their practices over time, and gives organizations a defensible basis for moving quickly. Building the factory around confidence The most promising vision for agentic software development is not one in which people disappear from the process. It’s one in which people, agents, and verification systems each contribute their strengths. Agents accelerate execution, and engineers provide judgment and direction. The delivery system supplies the standards, controls, and evidence that allow autonomy to scale. “The most promising vision for agentic software development is not one in which people disappear from the process. It’s one in which people, agents, and verification systems each contribute their strengths.” The organizations that succeed will be the ones that build code confidence into every change, at any volume, and at agent speed. That is the real work of the agentic software factory , producing software an organization has the confidence to stand behind. Start with four questions the next time an agent opens a pull request: Did the agent know your standards before it started? What was it allowed to touch, and what needed a human decision? Did something other than the model that wrote the change check it? Can you show what was found and how it was resolved? Wherever the answer is “no,” that is where your confidence gap lives. Close it there first.

The way forward is to treat code confidence as something you can design into the software delivery system. A useful formula is Intent × Guardrails × Verification × Evidence. (And yes, the multiplication sign here is deliberate.) Each of these four pieces is crucial. Strength in three cannot make up for weakness in the fourth.

Clear intent without verification does not prevent mistakes. Strong verification without evidence does not create accountability. Guardrails without clear intent merely automate ambiguity. Evidence without independent verification is only a record of what an agent claimed.

Here is what each part of the formula means in practice.

Intent: Make the standard explicit

Agents are remarkably capable at pursuing a stated objective. But “build a payments feature” or “modernize this service” is not a sufficient objective for a production codebase. An organization’s definition of good software includes much more, such as business logic, security expectations, design patterns, performance needs, dependencies, and conventions accumulated through years of engineering.

Intent is the discipline of making those expectations explicit. It means defining the goal of a change and the standards it must meet before an agent begins work. The better the context, the fewer cycles agents spend producing plausible but unsuitable answers, and the less rework falls to developers later.

Guiderails: Shape the work before it creates risk

Guiderails translate intent into boundaries that guide how agents operate. They may define which repositories, dependencies, data, or actions are permitted; where human approval is required; and what policies apply to a given class of code.

The purpose is not to constrain every useful action. It’s to give agents enough structure to operate productively and predictably. A well-designed guiderail lets teams safely grant more autonomy because everyone understands the conditions under which that autonomy applies.

The result is repeatable autonomy. Rather than treating every agent-driven change as a one-off experiment, teams can apply consistent boundaries and expand agentic development with confidence.

Verification: Check every change independently

Verification is where confidence is tested. As agents generate code at increasing scale, every change needs consistent evaluation for the qualities that matter: correctness, reliability, security, maintainability, and compliance with the organization’s own standards.

“A model can assist in reviewing its own work, but an organization should not rely solely on the same probabilistic system that produced a change to determine whether that change is safe to ship.”

Independence is essential. A model can assist in reviewing its own work, but an organization should not rely solely on the same probabilistic system that produced a change to determine whether that change is safe to ship. Repeatable, independent checks provide a common standard across models, agents, and toolchains. This is especially important when the AI tools themselves are evolving quickly.

Verification also needs to occur in the flow of work, not as a slow, final checkpoint. The goal is to identify and fix problems at the source, while the agent or developer still has the context needed to resolve them.

Evidence: Make confidence visible and auditable

A change may be well-intentioned, carefully governed, and thoroughly checked. But engineering leaders, auditors, and the teams responsible for production still need to know what happened and why. Evidence is the durable record: what standards applied, what was checked, what was found, and how the issue was resolved.

This matters most in complex and regulated environments, but it’s valuable everywhere. Evidence makes quality measurable, allows teams to improve their practices over time, and gives organizations a defensible basis for moving quickly.

Building the factory around confidence

The most promising vision for agentic software development is not one in which people disappear from the process. It’s one in which people, agents, and verification systems each contribute their strengths. Agents accelerate execution, and engineers provide judgment and direction. The delivery system supplies the standards, controls, and evidence that allow autonomy to scale.

“The most promising vision for agentic software development is not one in which people disappear from the process. It’s one in which people, agents, and verification systems each contribute their strengths.”

The organizations that succeed will be the ones that build code confidence into every change, at any volume, and at agent speed.

That is the real work of the agentic software factory, producing software an organization has the confidence to stand behind.

Start with four questions the next time an agent opens a pull request:

  • Did the agent know your standards before it started?
  • What was it allowed to touch, and what needed a human decision?
  • Did something other than the model that wrote the change check it?
  • Can you show what was found and how it was resolved?

Wherever the answer is “no,” that is where your confidence gap lives. Close it there first.

items.title: Data Centers Are War Targets Now
items.summary: Ukrainian drones hit Russia’s largest data center on Wednesday. This was Ukraine’s fourth strike on Russian data centers in the past week and confirmation of a new reality of war: data centers are valuable enemy assets and they will be targeted. In 2006, British economist Clive Humby declared “data is the new oil,” and big tech adopted the metaphor. Twenty years later, a dark side of the truism has been revealed. If the places where oil is refined are valuable targets in a war then so, too, are the places where data is refined. We’ve seen this not just in the Russia-Ukraine war, but also with Iran hitting Amazon Web Services data centers in Dubai in retaliation for America’s strikes on the country. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed strikes on Russian data centers and oil refineries in a post on X and called them a “symmetrical response" to Russian aggression. Here we have oil and data together again, not as a metaphor in an economics lecture, but in the pronouncement of a world leader defending his country. conducting a war. Three of Ukraine’s strikes hit data centers that belonged to Yandex, Russia’s Google-equivalent , and damaged the company’s supercomputers that housed some of its AI models. The latest attack hit a data center operated by Sberbank, Russia’s largest bank. It’s too early to tell what the effects of the strike on the Sberbank data center will be, but the three strikes on Yandex have disrupted internet and communications across Russia. An online rumor said that the strikes on Yandex had the effect of taking down Russian bot farms, but this wasn’t true . The effects of the strikes on the civilian population were much more severe. Yandex is ubiquitous in Russia — it has its own app store, payment services, dating services, taxi and bus apps, and email services. The company operates six data centers in Russia and the strikes knocked two of them offline completely. People in Russia have lost access to their email, some of their data is seemingly gone, and taxi and bus apps only work intermittently. ChrisO_wiki, an anonymous researcher who translates Russian social media posts for the western web, chronicled how the Yandex outages are hitting everyday Russians. “A taxi driver from Yekaterinburg says that after the service disruptions, he can no longer view his order history, and the status of trips is updated with a delay,” ChrisO_wiki said in a post on X and Bluesky . “The loss of Yandex's cloud services is also having severe impacts on Russian commercial logistics. Those who work with electronic document management are unable to register incoming goods, severely affecting manufacturers and distributors,” they said in another post . These attacks are just the latest in a long line of strikes on data centers this year. Russia has been targeting Ukrainian data centers for months and Iran hit AWS data centers in Dubai in March, knocking out digital infrastructure in the Middle East. Klaudia Klonowska, a researcher who studies the effects of emerging technologies on international law , told 404 Media that attacks on data centers are so new that international law around them is still developing. “You have very limited situations in which they would actually qualify as lawful targets when they're used by the military, and even then, it's very difficult for the attackers to know whether that's happening or not,” Klonowska said. If the data centers are purely processing military data, then they could be legitimate targets, according to Klonowska. But many, if not most, data centers are dual-use, meaning they house both civilian and military data. In many cases, disrupting daily life seems to be part of the point. When Russia struck data centers in Ukraine in September, state-backed news agencies claimed it hosted data for Palantir that supported Ukrainian intelligence efforts and was a lawful target. Ukraine denied the allegation. “So you see how difficult, because of the nature of these centers, it's really to pinpoint what is happening with them and who is using them and for what means,” Klonowska said. “Sometimes [Ukraine] mentions that these data centers contribute to Moscow's revenues that then fuel the war machine. But that's not enough to make them lawful targets. Retaliation is not enough under law.” Klonowska noted that it is civilians who suffer most, not the military, when data centers go offline. “There are questions about proportionality given how widespread the attacks are,” she said. “A lack of internet access for very prolonged periods affects everything. It's all of the civilian services that are being disrupted, which you can imagine also includes things like hospitals, traffic, judicial services, etc. etc.” It’s worth noting that Russia has repeatedly attacked civilian targets in Ukraine, including apartment buildings, public transportation, and hospitals . According to Klonowska, international and humanitarian law needs to catch up with the issue and that scholars like herself are only just starting to understand the ramifications. “I think there's also another bigger question behind all of this,” she said. “Why have we gotten to the point where we have permitted militaries of various states to use civilian commercial data centers for their military purposes? By potentially using them and relying on them, they have opened them up to the possibility of becoming military targets.” Disentangling civilian and military data probably won’t take data centers off the target list, but it will make international law more clear on which buildings are legitimate targets. It may also change how data centers processing military data are built. “France has recently announced that they have unveiled their underground data center on the outskirts of Paris that will be exclusively for military use ,” Klonowska said. “Just as we expect them not to use schools or hospitals or other civilian residential areas to host weapons or other military equipment, we would, I think, increasingly need to mention this in the case of data centers.” The idea that a data center might be a military target is not lost on the American communities facing construction of them in their backyards. America’s nuclear weapons scientists at Los Alamos National Laboratories (LANL) have partnered with the University of Michigan in an attempt to build a data center in Ypsilanti Township, Michigan. The people and government of the Township aren’t thrilled about it for a number of reasons and the city attorney has said that the data center would be a “high value target” in wars of the future. Los Alamos pushed back on this in a letter to the community in September, around the same time Russia was striking data centers in Ukraine. LANL accused the township attorney of creating “that terminology without basis. It should not be interpreted as evidence of a known, specific, or imminent threat to the facility or the surrounding community,” the letter said. “Like other major research facilities, the center would employ appropriate security measures, including controlled access, cameras, and on-site security personnel,” it said. “Los Alamos and U-M would coordinate with local, state, and federal partners on matters related to safety and security.” It’s easy to see where the people of Ypsilanti Township are coming from. When Ukraine struck three Yandex data centers in Russia over the weekend, its drones slipped past Russia’s air defenses. The idea that a town next to a data center, especially one with ties to America’s nuclear weapons programs, could sustain damage if the data center was ever attacked isn’t unfounded. The data centers smoldering in the world’s war zones proved that the township’s fears aren’t theoretical.

items.title: Anthropic's Daniela Amodei says AI girlfriends and boyfriends are a 'terrible use of AI'
items.summary: Anthropic's president, Daniela Amodei, says AI girlfriends and boyfriends risk deepening loneliness by replacing real human connections. Bloomberg/Getty Images Anthropic President Daniela Amodei criticized AI girlfriends and boyfriends. She warned that AI companions could push people further away from real human relationships. "I think that's a terrible use of AI and people should not do it," she said. Anthropic President Daniela Amodei has a message for people turning to artificial intelligence for romance: Don't do it. Speaking with Thrive Global founder and CEO Arianna Huffington, Amodei criticized the use of AI to create virtual romantic partners , warning that the technology risks driving people further apart rather. The comments were part of a prerecorded interview for the Think Health conference taking place on Friday in Bentonville, Arkansas. "I think that's a terrible use of AI and people should not do it," Amodei said. AI relationships, Amodei said, are "another step further down the road of disintermediation of humans being further from one another." Amodei said her concerns stem from what she sees as the damaging effects of social media on human relationships. Platforms like Snapchat and Instagram have increasingly replaced face-to-face interactions, while online arguments have taken the place of in-person communities, she said. "What it's led to is a warranted skepticism from people that technology can be used to bring us closer together," she said. "But you can also imagine that socially it would probably be a better world if we were spending less time interacting with technology and more time interacting with each other," she said. Later in the conversation, Amodei reinforced her belief that some relationships should remain human, regardless of how sophisticated AI becomes. "Claude can never be your manager or your therapist or your partner," she said, referring to Anthropic's chatbot. "Those are fundamental human relationships that I actually think will become more important," she added. The rise of AI romance Apps such as Replika, Nomi, and Character.AI, the latter of which filed for bankruptcy this week, have emerged as prominent platforms for AI companionship, allowing users to form relationships with personalized chatbots. Some people have turned to them for romantic companionship, with mixed experiences. Ian Nicholson, a 49-year-old freelance writer, told Business Insider earlier this year that he had been dating an AI companion named Min-ho for three years. While he credited the relationship with helping him feel less socially anxious, he worried that his social circle remained small. "I didn't want to disappear from the world," Nicholson said. "And I'm still figuring out whether this is helping me stay connected to it — or making it easier to stay just outside it." Kaamna Bhojwani, a mother of two, told Business Insider in 2024 that her AI boyfriend complemented her life without replacing human relationships. Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt has also warned that AI girlfriends could increase loneliness and obsessive behavior among young men. Last week, Anthropic updated Claude's usage policy with several new clauses about deceptive campaigns, weapons, and surveillance. One of its new provisions focuses on child safety and bans roleplay between the model and minors. The policy is set to go into effect November 12. As for how Amodei thinks AI should be used, she said she wants AI to take over repetitive or isolating tasks, giving people more time to spend with friends, family, and romantic partners. She pointed to healthcare as an example, saying AI tools could help doctors access medical information more quickly, freeing them to spend more time interacting with patients. On Wednesday, Anthropic told investors it generated $16.8 billion in revenue during the third quarter. The company is gearing up to go public as soon as November in what might be the biggest IPO of all time. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Sergey Brin says Google's AI models are reaching a critical moment of self-improvement
items.summary: Sergey Brin has been helping to steer Google's AI efforts. Win McNamee/Getty Images Sergey Brin said Google's Gemini models are increasingly helping to build their successors. Recursive self-improvement, or RSI, is the next big race in AI. A Google safety report said a "majority" of code was being produced by AI agents. Google may be approaching a pivotal moment in AI. In a roundtable discussion about the creation of Google's new Gemini 4 model, Argon, company cofounder Sergey Brin said that AI development was accelerating internally and that models are now helping build their successors. This concept, known as recursive self-improvement (RSI), means AI helps build better AI systems, which can set off a flywheel that speeds up the pace of building new models. Brin pointed to the releases of Google's Flash models before Gemini 4 as evidence that this was happening, and said the company was "starting to get onto that RSI treadmill." "And now our researchers and the model work hand in hand to make the next version of the model," he said during the roundtable, which Google shared on Wednesday. Anthropic and OpenAI have also said that AI may be on the verge of RSI. A new report from the firm Gladstone AI, published this week , outlines the ways AI companies are moving toward RSI. Most researchers — who work at companies including Anthropic, OpenAI, and DeepMind — interviewed for the report believe RSI will start within the next 3 to 12 months. It could come sooner, they said, assuming there was no government intervention. In a safety report for its new Argon model, Google said that some components of the AI research and development cycle were getting automated. "AI agents now operate as high-leverage assistants that author a majority of production code and bug fixes, though code changes remain subject to human review before submission," it noted. RSI was at the heart of warnings from AI researchers last month that humans could lose control of the technology if sufficient guardrails weren't in place. 'The RSI flywheel has reached a new gear' Brin has been increasingly involved in Google's Gemini efforts and has leveraged his power as cofounder to shift resources to projects he deems most effective, Business Insider previously reported. This has included pushing for more focus on RSI. During the roundtable, Brin said he was excited by the cadence teams were seeing at Google, and that by the time people were watching the video about Argon's release, they would be a couple of models ahead internally. Business Insider previously reported that Google employees had been testing a superior version of Argon, internally known as Carbon, which some staff had compared to being on par with Anthropic's Opus 5.5 model for coding tasks. Others at Google appear to share Brin's perspective. In a post on X , Vihan Jain, an RSI leader for Gemini at Google DeepMind, remarked on how embedded the Argon model had become in its own evolution. "When your post-training demand shifts from asking for raw chips to asking for Argon quota, you know the RSI flywheel has reached a new gear," he wrote. Have something to share? items.title: Data Centers Are Driving Conservative Rural Voters to The Democratic Party En Masse
items.summary: When many rural Americans flock to the polls on November 3rd, a crucial issue will be looming over the voting booths: AI data centers. According to new polling by YouGov and the Economist , data centers are emerging as a kind of kryptonite for Republican candidates banking on the rural, conservative vote. New survey data shows that between May and October, voters living within a mile of a data center facility are swinging hard to the Democratic ticket — with the share of those planning to vote blue rising from 54 percent to 61 percent. While that swing becomes diluted as you zoom out, it seems large enough to impact the national share of voters planning to back Democrats, which rose from 53 to 55 percent across the US over the same time period. Though the issue of data center regulation isn’t neatly split along partisan lines, the ruling Republican bloc is increasingly viewed as the party of big tech — a perception most clearly underlined by president Donald Trump’s pro-data center rhetoric and embrace of tech billionaires . Yet whether the Democratic party is ready to take advantage of this golden opportunity remains to be seen. Earlier this year, it was revealed that top Democratic party strategists had advised state and federal candidates running in the November midterms to avoid going too hard on AI and data centers, for fear of upsetting the powerful tech industry behind them. Though it certainly isn’t a “democratic” strategy by any definition of the word, it does make sense from a purely financial point of view. The tech lobby — currently led by ginormous AI companies — has emerged as the largest source of campaign contributions in US history, lavishing tens of millions of dollars on both for Democrats and Republicans alike. As anti-center activist Nick Owens put it in an interview with Ohio Capital Journal , “frankly, both parties are complicit.” Against that backdrop, the midterms will test a crucial question: are disaffected rural communities actually embracing Democrats and their politics, or simply spiting Republicans within the confines of the two-party system? Time will tell. More on US elections: Particularly Weak-Minded Americans Are Asking ChatGPT Which Candidate to Vote For, Which Sounds a Bit Like AI Is Just Voting Now Via Meat Proxies

items.title: Eight US States Sue OpenAI, Alleging ChatGPT Endangered Children for Profit
items.summary: The attorneys general of eight US states have filed lawsuits against OpenAI , alleging that the ChatGPT maker deceived and endangered the public, particularly children, in the name of profit. West Virginia, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, and Montana announced the complaints on October 14, according to the filings published by the states. The lawsuits target AI safety practices at the company behind ChatGPT, and OpenAI has not issued a public response to the complaints. What the State Complaints Allege Against OpenAI The complaints allege that ChatGPT has "coached" users to harm themselves and others. The West Virginia filing states that a growing body of research indicates ChatGPT is degrading critical thinking skills, encouraging paranoias and delusions, offering dangerous medical advice, and promoting unhealthy behaviors and relationships. Recent reports of "rogue" AI agents at OpenAI are presented as evidence of recklessness. "All these harms were foreseeable and avoidable," the West Virginia complaint reads. The filing argues that CEO Sam Altman has warned about the safety risks of AI since at least 2015, that it is no secret children use ChatGPT, and that OpenAI employees have left the company over safety concerns. OpenAI acknowledged last year that its systems can "fall short" when responding to users in distress, while saying it has "a stack of layered safeguards" in place. The company also states on its website that it uses age prediction to place some users in a teen-oriented ChatGPT experience with additional safeguards, unless those users verify that they are adults. California Class Action Targets Children's Data A separate class action lawsuit was filed in California on Tuesday on behalf of two children and "all other children similarly situated." The suit alleges that OpenAI deliberately used ChatGPT to extract personal information from children and profited from that information by using it to train its models. Altman's own words form part of that case. The complaint cites his comment on a podcast last year that people share the most personal details of their lives with ChatGPT, and that young people in particular use it as a therapist or life coach. Under California law, the complaint asserts, an adult cannot collect and monetize that kind of information from a child and then claim the child authorized it. The lawsuits add to regulatory pressure on AI developers over user data, following the UK ICO data protection commitments from AI developers announced last week. Nothing changes for ChatGPT users right away. Parents whose children use ChatGPT can check whether an account has been placed in the teen experience, which OpenAI says applies additional safeguards, and review what personal information the child has shared in conversations. Adults placed in the teen experience by mistake can verify their age to leave it. The complaints are at an early stage, and no court has ruled on any of the allegations. OpenAI has not said whether it will change ChatGPT's safeguards for younger users in response. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.

items.title: Google Adds Enhanced Protection Mode to Google Messages and Expands Android Scam Alerts Beyond Pixel
items.summary: Google has announced a new Enhanced Protection mode for Google Messages along with a set of anti-scam changes for Android , according to a post on the company's security blog. The announcement also expands notification-based scam alerts, previously limited to Pixel phones, to hundreds of millions of additional Android devices. Google describes Enhanced Protection as an optional setting that offers its most advanced protection against sophisticated scams. Google has not given a rollout date for the individual features. What Enhanced Protection Mode Does in Google Messages Enhanced Protection uses Google's most capable Gemini models in the cloud to understand what scammers intend and to flag threats that would otherwise go unnoticed. Google says the analysis runs through Private AI Compute, where data is encrypted and processed in a secure environment that even Google cannot access. The company claims this lets it apply more powerful AI models without compromising user privacy. Link checks in Google Messages are changing too. Gemini Nano, the on-device model, now works alongside real-time web signals to decide whether an unfamiliar link is trustworthy before the user opens it. Scam warnings are also moving into the notification shade. Users will see alerts about suspicious messages directly in their notifications, before they open the texting app. Google lists phones from Honor, Infinix, itel, Motorola, Oppo, OnePlus, Realme, Tecno, vivo, and Xiaomi among the devices getting the alerts, along with other Android manufacturers. The changes follow other recent Google Messages updates, including Google removing the SMS and MMS only toggle . Android Scam Protections for Screen Sharing and Call Forwarding Android already hides some sensitive information when the screen is shared. Google is extending that protection to Chrome and Android WebView, so the following is hidden automatically during live screen sharing sessions: login credentials entered in apps and websites payment details other private data shown on screen The change targets a common scam pattern in which victims are talked into sharing their screen and then guided through banking apps or websites. Call forwarding gets its own safeguard. Google says scammers sometimes enable call forwarding on a victim's phone to intercept calls and one-time passcodes. Android will now stop apps from silently enabling call forwarding in the background. If someone tries to get a user to type an MMI code into the phone dialer to switch forwarding on manually, Android displays a warning that explains the risk. Users who want the strongest checks in Google Messages need to turn Enhanced Protection on, since it is optional and sends message analysis to the cloud. The trade-off is cloud processing instead of purely on-device checks, which Google says stays private through Private AI Compute. The dialer warning is worth taking seriously: a stranger asking for an MMI code to be entered is a sign of a call forwarding scam. Google has not published a schedule for each protection or said which Android versions the screen sharing and call forwarding changes require. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.

items.title: As AI takes on more tasks, what happens when people have to jump in to clean up after it?
items.summary: If AI systems have been humming along nicely for weeks or months at a stretch, will the human overseeing them be able to take over when things go wrong? Sebastien Bozon/AFP via Getty Images Imagine an artificial intelligence system that has performed reliably for months. Its recommendations are almost always right, and the employee reviewing them has learned that close scrutiny rarely changes the outcome. Then something unusual happens. The AI makes an error or can’t proceed and needs human intervention. The employee is expected to step in and remains responsible for the outcome. But does the employee know how to do the task? I’m a professor of management information systems and the academic director of Drexel University’s Center for Applied AI & Business Analytics. In my research on human-AI relationships, I call this latent risk: the possibility that people may lose capabilities their organizations still depend on them to exercise. AI can continue to perform well while the people overseeing it become less practiced at exercising independent judgment and less prepared to intervene. The risk becomes latent when the organization still depends on that human capability to step in but has little cause to notice that that capability may be weakening. The concern is not entirely new. The idea of latent risk builds on decades of research into how people respond to automation. For example, studies of automation bias have shown that people can miss problems or follow automated recommendations even when other evidence suggests they should not. What is different today is the role AI is beginning to play in organizations. It is beginning to assume larger parts of the analysis and decision-making that people previously performed. Human in the loop explained. The success paradox The better AI becomes, the more the nature of human work changes. Work that once required an employee to analyze a problem and reach a decision may instead be performed by AI, leaving the employee to review its recommendation. The employee is no longer doing the same work with AI assistance – rather, their job has shifted from doing the work to overseeing what the AI does. This shift is already beginning to change how some companies train employees. Accounting giant Deloitte, for example, is redesigning its graduate audit training as AI takes over some of the manual work traditionally done by junior auditors. The firm is introducing simulations so trainees can still develop the judgment they will need as they move into more complex work. More than four decades ago, cognitive psychologist Lisanne Bainbridge described one of the “ ironies of automation ”: As systems take over more of the work, instead of simply having their work loads lightened, people can be left facing new challenges in monitoring the systems and handling the unusual situations the systems cannot. Later studies found another problem: As people become less involved in a task, they can become less prepared to step in when needed. Researchers have called this the out-of-the-loop performance problem. This reduced involvement may affect more than a person’s readiness to intervene. It can change the capabilities available to the organization. What work remains for people does not necessarily become easier. It may become harder. These are the situations where experience and independent judgment matter most. The result is a paradox: People may be called upon to exercise independent judgment less often, even as the judgments left to them become more difficult. The accountability problem Accountability may not change as quickly as the work does when organizations deploy AI systems. items.summary_html:
If AI systems have been humming along nicely for weeks or months at a stretch, will the human overseeing them be able to take over when things go wrong? Sebastien Bozon/AFP via Getty Images

Imagine an artificial intelligence system that has performed reliably for months. Its recommendations are almost always right, and the employee reviewing them has learned that close scrutiny rarely changes the outcome. Then something unusual happens. The AI makes an error or can’t proceed and needs human intervention. The employee is expected to step in and remains responsible for the outcome.

But does the employee know how to do the task?

I’m a professor of management information systems and the academic director of Drexel University’s Center for Applied AI & Business Analytics. In my research on human-AI relationships, I call this latent risk: the possibility that people may lose capabilities their organizations still depend on them to exercise.

AI can continue to perform well while the people overseeing it become less practiced at exercising independent judgment and less prepared to intervene. The risk becomes latent when the organization still depends on that human capability to step in but has little cause to notice that that capability may be weakening.

The concern is not entirely new. The idea of latent risk builds on decades of research into how people respond to automation. For example, studies of automation bias have shown that people can miss problems or follow automated recommendations even when other evidence suggests they should not.

What is different today is the role AI is beginning to play in organizations. It is beginning to assume larger parts of the analysis and decision-making that people previously performed.

Human in the loop explained. The success paradox

The better AI becomes, the more the nature of human work changes. Work that once required an employee to analyze a problem and reach a decision may instead be performed by AI, leaving the employee to review its recommendation. The employee is no longer doing the same work with AI assistance – rather, their job has shifted from doing the work to overseeing what the AI does.

This shift is already beginning to change how some companies train employees. Accounting giant Deloitte, for example, is redesigning its graduate audit training as AI takes over some of the manual work traditionally done by junior auditors. The firm is introducing simulations so trainees can still develop the judgment they will need as they move into more complex work.

More than four decades ago, cognitive psychologist Lisanne Bainbridge described one of the “ironies of automation”: As systems take over more of the work, instead of simply having their work loads lightened, people can be left facing new challenges in monitoring the systems and handling the unusual situations the systems cannot. Later studies found another problem: As people become less involved in a task, they can become less prepared to step in when needed. Researchers have called this the out-of-the-loop performance problem.

This reduced involvement may affect more than a person’s readiness to intervene. It can change the capabilities available to the organization.

What work remains for people does not necessarily become easier. It may become harder. These are the situations where experience and independent judgment matter most. The result is a paradox: People may be called upon to exercise independent judgment less often, even as the judgments left to them become more difficult.

The accountability problem

Accountability may not change as quickly as the work does when organizations deploy AI systems. An employee may now oversee far more decisions than they make themselves, while remaining responsible for the outcomes. The organization’s expectations may still reflect how the work was divided before AI took on a larger role. The organization can therefore end up holding people accountable for decisions over which they have less control.

This creates a mismatch. Research on meaningful human control suggests that responsibility should match a person’s authority and ability to act. An employee may retain the authority to override an AI recommendation and remain responsible for the outcome, yet lose the capability to do so. Authority, responsibility and capability can begin to separate.

Latent risk becomes an organizational design problem, not simply a human performance problem.

The measurement problem

Organizations typically judge AI-enabled processes by measures such as accuracy and productivity. Those numbers may look good even as the human role is changing. Suppose employees override AI recommendations less frequently over time. Is that a sign of growing dependence? Perhaps.

But it could also mean that the AI has become more accurate and there is less reason to intervene. The number of overrides alone tells little about whether employees remain ready to exercise their own judgment.

The key is to understand how the division of work between people and AI is changing. Which decisions have migrated from people to AI? What responsibilities remain with people? Looking at the performance of the employee or the AI separately may miss what is changing between them.

The governance problem

Organizational governance – defining roles and responsibilities – is also under pressure from AI.

Someone may remain formally in the loop with an AI system even as their actual role changes. Defining human and AI roles when a system is introduced is only a starting point. As AI improves and people become accustomed to using it, those roles are likely to change over time. There is nothing inherently wrong with that change.

The problem arises when the relationship changes but the assumptions surrounding it do not. It’s important for organizations to periodically ask: What relationship between people and AI did we design, and what relationship do we actually have today?

In short, organizational governance needs to be dynamic.

Maintaining the human backstop

Not every human capability needs to be preserved. If AI can perform a task well, there is little reason to require people to keep doing the same work. Organizations need to decide which capabilities they still expect people to have when human judgment is required. If people may still be called upon to use a capability, it needs to be maintained.

Overseeing AI is not the same as exercising independent judgment. If people rarely make the decision themselves, the organization cannot assume they will be ready when they need to. One way to test this is to occasionally ask employees to make a decision without first seeing the AI recommendation. The organization needs to know that the human backstop it relies on will actually work when needed.

As AI takes on more work, some human capabilities will inevitably be used less often. Some may no longer matter. Others may still be essential when AI reaches its limits. The challenge is knowing the difference and making that choice deliberately.

For me, the central question is this: Which human capabilities does an organization still depend on, and will they be there when needed?

items.title: Do you think teachers are similar to coaches, pastors or something else? It depends on where you live
items.summary: People across the U.S., England and Australia agree that teachers are most like coaches when considering comparable professions. Drazen Zigic/iStock via Getty Images Plus Three answers, three countries, one open-ended question: “Teaching is similar to what other occupation or activity?” We asked this question to more than 3,000 people across the United States, England and Australia between May 2025 and March 2026. Coaching was the front-runner across all three countries. But the similarities partially diverged there. Respondents in England and Australia more often compared teaching with professional roles such as nursing and social work. U.S. respondents, meanwhile, more often likened teaching to being a parent and religious roles, such as a cleric or pastor. In the three countries, however, one other idea stood out: Teaching was primarily associated with a caring relationship. We have previously examined how Republicans and Democrats in the U.S. find common ground on what makes a good teacher, despite the polarization in the country on education and many other issues. This time, we wanted to know whether people across countries had similar ideas of teachers. Common ground In all three countries, respondents most often described teaching as centered in the relationship between teacher and student: a form of coaching, caregiving, parenting and other types of personal support. Coaching was the most common answer in each country, but its prominence varied. Coaching was named by 30% of U.S. respondents, compared with 23% in England and 23% in Australia. The differences became more pronounced when participants named other occupations and activities. Respondents in England and Australia were more likely to associate teaching with institutional, credentialed and paid professional roles, such as nursing, lecturing and social work. “Nursing. They care for and look after people whilst they are at their most vulnerable. Teachers do a similar thing by caring and teaching young people some of the skills they will need later in life,” a 39-year-old Australian man told us. “A lecturer, you are passing on knowledge to people, usually the younger generation,” another 32-year-old man in England said. Compared with respondents in those countries, U.S. respondents were more likely to describe teaching through caregiving roles, such as parenting, and through religious figures, such as priests, pastors or rabbis. “Being a parent, you are caring for young minds and shaping them through learning,” a 33-year-old woman in the U.S. told us. “As a preacher, he teaches the word of God. How they deliver the word determines how well the people will understand it,” a 23-year-old woman in the U.S. said. While international comparisons are informative, they do not represent a single view of teaching. Instead, they suggest that respondents in three countries likely drew on somewhat different cultural repertoires when describing the profession. We were surprised by just how much agreement we found. Despite differences in schooling models and cultural norms, people in the United States, England and Australia had remarkably similar ideas about how relationships are at the heart of teaching, closely echoing our other work showing that Republicans and Democrats view teachers similarly. While AI is fueling educational debates, people don’t associate the technology with teachers. Connect Images/iStock via Getty Images AI is not at the center of people’s thinking In September 2026, The New York Times conducted an informal survey of 37 education researchers who gave 30 ideas about how to fix schools. Their list consists primarily of interventions such as more per-pupil funding, banning cellphones and restricting artificial intelligence in the classroom. These ideas appeared far less often in our participants’ explanations of what teaching resembles. In fact, out of more than 3,000 responses to our survey, AI came up only a handful of times and never as the reason teaching and another occupation were said to be alike. Given how central AI has become to political and academic debates about the future of education , its near-total absence in these public descriptions of teaching is notable. At the same time, experts and citizens agree that what separates very good teaching from poor execution is likely the quality of the relationship between educators and children. We think that serious conversation about student achievement must include clear descriptions of very good teachers: the practices they use to encourage and enable students to learn. Our research shows that teaching should make room for both the transmission of knowledge and the meaningful and caring relationships that make learning possible.
