items.title: Agentic AI doesn’t have a model problem. It has a retrieval problem.
items.summary: On BrowseComp-Plus, GPT-4.1 answered 93.49% of the questions correctly when it was given the supporting documents directly. When an agent used the same model but relied on BM25 to search for evidence to pass to the model, accuracy fell to 14.58% . That difference matters because a system that gets the answer right 93% of the time is far more useful than one that gets it right only 15% of the time. An agent can look excellent in a controlled demo. The corpus is clean, the task is familiar, and the relevant material is easy to find. Production is messier. Documents may be duplicated, outdated drafts can remain searchable, and teams may use different terminology for the same thing. Several versions of a policy can coexist, while the task itself may unfold in ways the evaluation set never covered. “More model intelligence does not compensate for evidence the agent never retrieved.” Under those conditions, the agent may retrieve incomplete, stale, or simply wrong material. More model intelligence does not compensate for evidence the agent never retrieved. This is where retrieval starts to determine what the model can actually do. What BrowseComp-Plus shows BrowseComp-Plus provides a useful way to separate these effects because it evaluates agents against a fixed corpus rather than a changing web-search service. The benchmark includes 100,195 documents and 830 research questions, each with human-verified supporting documents. One evaluation gives the model all labeled positive documents directly. The paper calls this the oracle setting. Another requires the agent to search the corpus and gather the material it needs. The difference is large. GPT-4.1 scores 93.49% with the labeled supporting documents supplied and 14.58% when the agent searches with the BM25 baseline. Qwen3-32B moves from 83.25% to 3.49% under the same two conditions. The oracle result shows how well the model can answer when the required material is already in front of it. For system design, comparing retrieval systems is even more useful. The reasoning model stayed the same, while better retrieval improved the final answer rate and reduced the number of search calls. “The lesson is practical: before changing the model, examine what reaches it. A capable model working from poor retrieval results still has poor material to reason over.” The lesson is practical: before changing the model, examine what reaches it. A capable model working from poor retrieval results still has poor material to reason over. Figure 1. Same model, different evidence access: BrowseComp-Plus: oracle evidence supplied directly versus agentic search with BM25. Enterprises can build agents around proprietary information that competitors do not have, from product and customer data to internal knowledge and operational records. That advantage depends on whether the agent can find the right information and rank it well, while also keeping up with changes in the underlying data. One task. A few minutes. A thousand retrievals. In its Search as Code research , Perplexity describes tasks that can trigger hundreds or thousands of retrieval operations within a few minutes. Search becomes a sustained part of the agent’s workflow rather than an occasional lookup. Traditional search usually returns one ranked result set per query. An agent can decompose a task into multiple searches, fan them out in parallel, combine the results, and issue follow-up searches as it learns more. At that scale, fan-out becomes a normal part of the workload. If an agent runs ten searches in parallel and needs all ten results before it can continue, the slowest search sets the pace for that step. If the agent repeats that pattern several times during the task, tail latency matters even more than it does for a single interactive query. The same multiplication shows up in capacity. One user task can generate hundreds of search operations, and many agents may be doing that at once. Measured in user requests, the service may look lightly loaded while the retrieval layer is processing a much larger volume of searches. When one task fans out into many searches, retrieval quality matters even more. People judge search results using context they have built up over time. They know which sources they trust and can often recognize when something looks stale, unreliable, or out of place. An agent usually starts with far less background and has to build its understanding from the evidence it retrieves during the task. It is often on its first day on the job. If one of those early results is wrong, the next search may be wrong too, and the rest of the task can drift from there. “People judge search results using context they have built up over time. An agent usually starts with far less background and has to build its understanding from the evidence it retrieves during the task. It is often on its first day on the job.” A simple model shows why repeated retrieval steps raise the stakes. Suppose a workflow requires five retrieval steps, each with a 90% probability of supplying what the agent needs, and assume there are no retries or recovery. The probability that all five succeed is 0.9^5, or about 59% . Real agents can retry, use redundant evidence, branch, and recover, so this is an illustration rather than a measured agent success rate. It shows how small per-step weaknesses can accumulate when later work depends on earlier retrievals. Figure 2. Small retrieval errors can compound across a multi-step task Illustrative model: if every required retrieval step must succeed and there is no recovery, end-to-end success falls as the number of steps increases. Agentic search therefore asks the retrieval layer to handle more queries for each user task, more searches running in parallel, and retrieval steps whose results influence later work. As those patterns scale, capacity, tail latency, and retrieval quality all become more important. Your retrieval layer was tuned for a different user Web search spent decades adapting to human search behavior. As Jon Bratseth writes in Your agent wants to search like a 2010 quant , people are often “lazy and clueless” when they search. The wording is blunt, but the point is straightforward: people tend to enter short queries without knowing much about the corpus or the search system behind it. Search engines evolved around those habits. Short, underspecified queries became the norm, and much of the complexity moved behind the interface, where the search system inferred intent and returned a ranked list. An agent can use a much richer interface. It can search for exact terms, construct filters, specify dates, group results, choose among ranking strategies, and issue follow-up searches based on what it has already found. Jon gives examples ranging from proximity search for names in a legal case to semantic search over high-quality sources and grouping events by month. In an agentic workflow , those searches can be chained together as the agent narrows, expands, and verifies its answer. That means the retrieval layer receives more than a short text query. It may receive several kinds of input: lexical terms, query embeddings, structured filters, or combinations of them. An agent-facing interface should make those choices explicit so the agent can use the right retrieval method for the task instead of collapsing every request into one text string. Evaluation needs to reflect the same shift. A retriever tested mostly on short, human-written questions may behave differently when an agent generates its own filters, search terms, and follow-up queries. Retrieval quality should therefore be measured on the queries the agent actually sends in production, not only on the questions in the evaluation set. Before changing the model or retuning retrieval, inspect those production queries first. A search API returns results. An agent needs more control. Traditional search often exposes a narrow contract: send a query, let the server run a retrieval pipeline, and receive a ranked result list. That works well when the caller only needs the output. An agent may need more control over how retrieval and ranking are carried out at runtime, depending on what the task requires. Vespa exposes that control through its query language and rank profiles. The caller can combine lexical or semantic retrieval, structured filters, ranking choices, and grouping in the same request, affecting how candidates are selected, scored, and returned. The interface matters because the agent can only use the controls it can reach. A system may support filtering, ranking, aggregation, or several retrieval methods internally, but those capabilities do not help if the agent cannot invoke them when the task calls for them. Figure 3. How much of the retrieval stack can the agent reach? Illustrative comparison of a narrow search interface with richer query-time controls. Product categories do not determine which capabilities are exposed. Trusted application code enforces authorization. A fixed pipeline is still a good fit for many well-defined applications. Agentic workflows become more demanding when the task changes from one step to the next and the agent needs different retrieval behavior at runtime. The goal is to expose the controls the agent needs while keeping authorization, validation, budgets, and other safeguards on the trusted server side. Exposing the controls is not enough An engine can expose filters, lexical matching, nearest-neighbor search, grouping, multiple rank profiles, reranking, and query-time controls. Those capabilities only become useful to the agent when the interface explains what is available and when to use it. If rank profiles, filterable fields, or grouping operations are not described, the agent may default to a free-text query and push more of the work into later reasoning or tool calls. One way to handle this is to put a query-translation model between the agent and the retrieval system. The translator takes the agent’s request and converts it into the engine’s query syntax. This can be useful when an application wants query construction centralized behind a stable interface. When the caller is already an agent, a separate translator often inserts a specialized model between the agent and the retrieval system. The agent already has the task, prior results, and constraints in context; the translator must reconstruct that intent from a narrower request and convert it into a query. This extra handoff adds latency and another opportunity to lose or distort what the agent meant, making retrieval harder and less reliable. Another approach is to describe the retrieval interface directly to the agent: which fields are available and what they mean, and what rank profiles are provided. We call that an agent-ready schema : a description of the fields, controls, and retrieval options the agent can use, along with the application-specific meaning behind them. Vespa has described work on convenience tooling in this direction, and much of that guidance can be generated from the application schema itself. From schema to skill A search schema already contains much of the information an agent needs: field names and types, which fields can be searched or used as filters, available rank profiles, and configured tensors and models. What it lacks is a description of what the fields mean and how they could be used. A field called tier may represent an account plan, a service level, or something else entirely. A timestamp such as published may mean first publication, last modification, or ingestion time. A rank profile named exact tells the agent very little about the kinds of queries it was designed for. Those meanings can be added as explanations in the schema. That gives the agent more than names and types; it gives it enough context to choose the right fields, filters, and ranking options for the task. Schema-to-Skill is the proposed generation step: combine the Vespa application schema, engine guidance, and application-specific knowledge into a short Markdown skill the agent can consult when constructing queries. The schema provides the structure, engine guidance explains how to use the available capabilities safely, and application-specific knowledge adds the vocabulary and meaning that cannot be inferred from the schema alone. Figure 4. Translate for the agent, or teach it. A translation layer uses a separate model call to construct the search query. With an agent-ready schema, the agent receives the guidance needed to construct queries using the retrieval controls exposed by the application. Schema-to-Skill is the proposed generation workflow. The agent uses that skill to choose among the retrieval strategies the Vespa application exposes. Vespa still does the actual retrieval work over the corpus, including matching, filtering, ranking, and aggregation. The agent decides what to ask for; the retrieval system executes it. Better models can help, but agents still fail when they search for the wrong evidence, cannot express the right retrieval strategy , or do not understand the search system they are calling. “Better models can help, but agents still fail when they search for the wrong evidence, cannot express the right retrieval strategy, or do not understand the search system they are calling.” Agentic workloads make those weaknesses more costly because retrieval happens throughout the task. Each search can affect what the agent sees next, how much context it carries, and whether it needs to search again. At scale, retrieval quality, tail latency, and query volume become part of the task itself. That puts more pressure on the retrieval interface. Agents need access to the filters, ranking strategies, grouping, and other controls the task requires, along with enough guidance to use them correctly. An agent-ready schema makes those capabilities explicit, and Schema-to-Skill is one way to turn that structure, engine guidance, and application-specific knowledge into something the agent can use when constructing queries. Before upgrading the model, inspect the searches the agent is issuing, the evidence those searches return, and whether the retrieval system gives the agent both the controls and the guidance it needs. Better retrieval can improve the answer, reduce unnecessary work, and make the rest of the agentic system more effective.

That difference matters because a system that gets the answer right 93% of the time is far more useful than one that gets it right only 15% of the time.

An agent can look excellent in a controlled demo. The corpus is clean, the task is familiar, and the relevant material is easy to find. Production is messier. Documents may be duplicated, outdated drafts can remain searchable, and teams may use different terminology for the same thing. Several versions of a policy can coexist, while the task itself may unfold in ways the evaluation set never covered.

“More model intelligence does not compensate for evidence the agent never retrieved.”

Under those conditions, the agent may retrieve incomplete, stale, or simply wrong material. More model intelligence does not compensate for evidence the agent never retrieved.

This is where retrieval starts to determine what the model can actually do.

What BrowseComp-Plus shows

BrowseComp-Plus provides a useful way to separate these effects because it evaluates agents against a fixed corpus rather than a changing web-search service. The benchmark includes 100,195 documents and 830 research questions, each with human-verified supporting documents.

One evaluation gives the model all labeled positive documents directly. The paper calls this the oracle setting. Another requires the agent to search the corpus and gather the material it needs.

The difference is large. GPT-4.1 scores 93.49% with the labeled supporting documents supplied and 14.58% when the agent searches with the BM25 baseline. Qwen3-32B moves from 83.25% to 3.49% under the same two conditions.

The oracle result shows how well the model can answer when the required material is already in front of it. For system design, comparing retrieval systems is even more useful. The reasoning model stayed the same, while better retrieval improved the final answer rate and reduced the number of search calls.

“The lesson is practical: before changing the model, examine what reaches it. A capable model working from poor retrieval results still has poor material to reason over.”

The lesson is practical: before changing the model, examine what reaches it. A capable model working from poor retrieval results still has poor material to reason over.

Figure 1. Same model, different evidence access: BrowseComp-Plus: oracle evidence supplied directly versus agentic search with BM25.

Enterprises can build agents around proprietary information that competitors do not have, from product and customer data to internal knowledge and operational records. That advantage depends on whether the agent can find the right information and rank it well, while also keeping up with changes in the underlying data.

One task. A few minutes. A thousand retrievals.

In its Search as Code research, Perplexity describes tasks that can trigger hundreds or thousands of retrieval operations within a few minutes. Search becomes a sustained part of the agent’s workflow rather than an occasional lookup.

Traditional search usually returns one ranked result set per query. An agent can decompose a task into multiple searches, fan them out in parallel, combine the results, and issue follow-up searches as it learns more.

At that scale, fan-out becomes a normal part of the workload. If an agent runs ten searches in parallel and needs all ten results before it can continue, the slowest search sets the pace for that step. If the agent repeats that pattern several times during the task, tail latency matters even more than it does for a single interactive query.

The same multiplication shows up in capacity. One user task can generate hundreds of search operations, and many agents may be doing that at once. Measured in user requests, the service may look lightly loaded while the retrieval layer is processing a much larger volume of searches.

When one task fans out into many searches, retrieval quality matters even more. People judge search results using context they have built up over time. They know which sources they trust and can often recognize when something looks stale, unreliable, or out of place. An agent usually starts with far less background and has to build its understanding from the evidence it retrieves during the task. It is often on its first day on the job. If one of those early results is wrong, the next search may be wrong too, and the rest of the task can drift from there.

“People judge search results using context they have built up over time. An agent usually starts with far less background and has to build its understanding from the evidence it retrieves during the task. It is often on its first day on the job.”

A simple model shows why repeated retrieval steps raise the stakes. Suppose a workflow requires five retrieval steps, each with a 90% probability of supplying what the agent needs, and assume there are no retries or recovery. The probability that all five succeed is 0.9^5, or about 59%. Real agents can retry, use redundant evidence, branch, and recover, so this is an illustration rather than a measured agent success rate. It shows how small per-step weaknesses can accumulate when later work depends on earlier retrievals.

Figure 2. Small retrieval errors can compound across a multi-step task
Illustrative model: if every required retrieval step must succeed and there is no recovery, end-to-end success falls as the number of steps increases.

Agentic search therefore asks the retrieval layer to handle more queries for each user task, more searches running in parallel, and retrieval steps whose results influence later work. As those patterns scale, capacity, tail latency, and retrieval quality all become more important.

Your retrieval layer was tuned for a different user

Web search spent decades adapting to human search behavior.

As Jon Bratseth writes in Your agent wants to search like a 2010 quant, people are often “lazy and clueless” when they search. The wording is blunt, but the point is straightforward: people tend to enter short queries without knowing much about the corpus or the search system behind it.

Search engines evolved around those habits. Short, underspecified queries became the norm, and much of the complexity moved behind the interface, where the search system inferred intent and returned a ranked list.

An agent can use a much richer interface. It can search for exact terms, construct filters, specify dates, group results, choose among ranking strategies, and issue follow-up searches based on what it has already found. Jon gives examples ranging from proximity search for names in a legal case to semantic search over high-quality sources and grouping events by month. In an agentic workflow, those searches can be chained together as the agent narrows, expands, and verifies its answer.

That means the retrieval layer receives more than a short text query. It may receive several kinds of input: lexical terms, query embeddings, structured filters, or combinations of them. An agent-facing interface should make those choices explicit so the agent can use the right retrieval method for the task instead of collapsing every request into one text string.

Evaluation needs to reflect the same shift. A retriever tested mostly on short, human-written questions may behave differently when an agent generates its own filters, search terms, and follow-up queries. Retrieval quality should therefore be measured on the queries the agent actually sends in production, not only on the questions in the evaluation set.

Before changing the model or retuning retrieval, inspect those production queries first.

A search API returns results. An agent needs more control.

Traditional search often exposes a narrow contract: send a query, let the server run a retrieval pipeline, and receive a ranked result list.

That works well when the caller only needs the output. An agent may need more control over how retrieval and ranking are carried out at runtime, depending on what the task requires.

Vespa exposes that control through its query language and rank profiles. The caller can combine lexical or semantic retrieval, structured filters, ranking choices, and grouping in the same request, affecting how candidates are selected, scored, and returned.

The interface matters because the agent can only use the controls it can reach. A system may support filtering, ranking, aggregation, or several retrieval methods internally, but those capabilities do not help if the agent cannot invoke them when the task calls for them.

Figure 3. How much of the retrieval stack can the agent reach? Illustrative comparison of a narrow search interface with richer query-time controls. Product categories do not determine which capabilities are exposed. Trusted application code enforces authorization.

A fixed pipeline is still a good fit for many well-defined applications. Agentic workflows become more demanding when the task changes from one step to the next and the agent needs different retrieval behavior at runtime.

The goal is to expose the controls the agent needs while keeping authorization, validation, budgets, and other safeguards on the trusted server side.

Exposing the controls is not enough

An engine can expose filters, lexical matching, nearest-neighbor search, grouping, multiple rank profiles, reranking, and query-time controls. Those capabilities only become useful to the agent when the interface explains what is available and when to use it. If rank profiles, filterable fields, or grouping operations are not described, the agent may default to a free-text query and push more of the work into later reasoning or tool calls.

One way to handle this is to put a query-translation model between the agent and the retrieval system. The translator takes the agent’s request and converts it into the engine’s query syntax. This can be useful when an application wants query construction centralized behind a stable interface.

When the caller is already an agent, a separate translator often inserts a specialized model between the agent and the retrieval system. The agent already has the task, prior results, and constraints in context; the translator must reconstruct that intent from a narrower request and convert it into a query. This extra handoff adds latency and another opportunity to lose or distort what the agent meant, making retrieval harder and less reliable.

Another approach is to describe the retrieval interface directly to the agent: which fields are available and what they mean, and what rank profiles are provided.

We call that an agent-ready schema: a description of the fields, controls, and retrieval options the agent can use, along with the application-specific meaning behind them. Vespa has described work on convenience tooling in this direction, and much of that guidance can be generated from the application schema itself.

From schema to skill

A search schema already contains much of the information an agent needs: field names and types, which fields can be searched or used as filters, available rank profiles, and configured tensors and models.

What it lacks is a description of what the fields mean and how they could be used. A field called tier may represent an account plan, a service level, or something else entirely. A timestamp such as published may mean first publication, last modification, or ingestion time. A rank profile named exact tells the agent very little about the kinds of queries it was designed for.

Those meanings can be added as explanations in the schema. That gives the agent more than names and types; it gives it enough context to choose the right fields, filters, and ranking options for the task.

Schema-to-Skill is the proposed generation step: combine the Vespa application schema, engine guidance, and application-specific knowledge into a short Markdown skill the agent can consult when constructing queries. The schema provides the structure, engine guidance explains how to use the available capabilities safely, and application-specific knowledge adds the vocabulary and meaning that cannot be inferred from the schema alone.

Figure 4. Translate for the agent, or teach it. A translation layer uses a separate model call to construct the search query. With an agent-ready schema, the agent receives the guidance needed to construct queries using the retrieval controls exposed by the application. Schema-to-Skill is the proposed generation workflow.

The agent uses that skill to choose among the retrieval strategies the Vespa application exposes. Vespa still does the actual retrieval work over the corpus, including matching, filtering, ranking, and aggregation. The agent decides what to ask for; the retrieval system executes it.

Better models can help, but agents still fail when they search for the wrong evidence, cannot express the right retrieval strategy, or do not understand the search system they are calling.

“Better models can help, but agents still fail when they search for the wrong evidence, cannot express the right retrieval strategy, or do not understand the search system they are calling.”

Agentic workloads make those weaknesses more costly because retrieval happens throughout the task. Each search can affect what the agent sees next, how much context it carries, and whether it needs to search again. At scale, retrieval quality, tail latency, and query volume become part of the task itself.

That puts more pressure on the retrieval interface. Agents need access to the filters, ranking strategies, grouping, and other controls the task requires, along with enough guidance to use them correctly. An agent-ready schema makes those capabilities explicit, and Schema-to-Skill is one way to turn that structure, engine guidance, and application-specific knowledge into something the agent can use when constructing queries.

Before upgrading the model, inspect the searches the agent is issuing, the evidence those searches return, and whether the retrieval system gives the agent both the controls and the guidance it needs. Better retrieval can improve the answer, reduce unnecessary work, and make the rest of the agentic system more effective.

items.title: CISA adds 9.8-rated Cisco CVE to KEV straight after disclosure
items.summary: Cisco has urged users to patch a critical zero-day vulnerability allowing remote unauthenticated attackers to exploit its Secure Email Gateway after spotting exploitation in the wild, and CISA was hot on its heels. The CVSS 9.8-rated arbitrary file write vulnerability CVE-2026-76519 was added to the US cybersecurity agency’s Known Exploited Vulnerability (KEV) catalogue on Wednesday, shortly after Cisco first released a patch. Cisco’s advisory said: “An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending an email that contains a crafted attachment through an affected device. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to write arbitrary files and execute commands with root privileges on the underlying operating system.” See also: AI is writing patches, how much should we trust them? The bug affects both the physical and virtual versions of Secure Email Gateway, running with a vulnerable release of Cisco’s AsyncOS software, with the file reputation service enabled and assigned to a mail policy, and using a version of the Content Scanner Tools earlier than 25.3.0.5525. Secure Email Gateway is Cisco’s email protection platform used to detect and block threats such as phishing, business email compromise, spam, and data loss, and provide encryption for outgoing emails. Verifying exploitation Cisco said potentially impacted users can review system_logs to verify attempted exploitation, advising them to review the logs of each cluster device if the device is part of a cluster. Exploitation would be indicated by either the log message “Suspected compromise indicator was found. Contact TAC for further recommendations,” or “Security scan did not complete. Contact TAC for further recommendations.” There are no workarounds for protection, meaning users must upgrade to releases 15.5.5 - 014 or 16.5.0 - 780 to mitigate the vulnerability. CISA gave government organisations until 17 October to update their software. CVE-2026-76519 is the second critical vulnerability to affect the Secure Email Gateway in a month after SQL Injection bug CVE-2026-76461 , also CVSS 9.8-rated, was disclosed in mid-September. items.summary_html:
Cisco has urged users to patch a critical zero-day vulnerability allowing remote unauthenticated attackers to exploit its Secure Email Gateway after spotting exploitation in the wild, and CISA was hot on its heels.

The CVSS 9.8-rated arbitrary file write vulnerability CVE-2026-76519 was added to the US cybersecurity agency’s Known Exploited Vulnerability (KEV) catalogue on Wednesday, shortly after Cisco first released a patch.

Cisco’s advisory said: “An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending an email that contains a crafted attachment through an affected device. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to write arbitrary files and execute commands with root privileges on the underlying operating system.”

See also: AI is writing patches, how much should we trust them?

The bug affects both the physical and virtual versions of Secure Email Gateway, running with a vulnerable release of Cisco’s AsyncOS software, with the file reputation service enabled and assigned to a mail policy, and using a version of the Content Scanner Tools earlier than 25.3.0.5525.

Secure Email Gateway is Cisco’s email protection platform used to detect and block threats such as phishing, business email compromise, spam, and data loss, and provide encryption for outgoing emails.

Verifying exploitation

Cisco said potentially impacted users can review system_logs to verify attempted exploitation, advising them to review the logs of each cluster device if the device is part of a cluster.

Exploitation would be indicated by either the log message “Suspected compromise indicator was found. Contact TAC for further recommendations,” or “Security scan did not complete. Contact TAC for further recommendations.”

There are no workarounds for protection, meaning users must upgrade to releases 15.5.5 - 014 or 16.5.0 - 780 to mitigate the vulnerability. CISA gave government organisations until 17 October to update their software.

CVE-2026-76519 is the second critical vulnerability to affect the Secure Email Gateway in a month after SQL Injection bug CVE-2026-76461, also CVSS 9.8-rated, was disclosed in mid-September.

items.title: A NATO ally is building automated defenses against Russia's drones to let fewer soldiers do more
items.summary: Latvia is building a Ukraine-inspired automated wall of anti-drone defenses on its border with Russia. Nina Liashonok / Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images Latvia is building an automated anti-drone wall along its border with Russia. Soldiers will make engagement decisions, leaving other tasks to be completed autonomously. The system aims to defend against cheap drones without relying on costly fighter jets and missiles. NATO member Latvia is building a wall of automated anti-drone defenses along its border with Russia, with human soldiers responsible only for deciding when and whether to fire. It aims to detect and neutralize "any drone which flies in," defense minister Raivis Melnis told Business Insider. And the goal, he explained, is to "build an autonomous system" that leverages the technology to "reduce the number of soldiers" required "to operate those systems." "The only thing which will be left for the soldier is the final decision to neutralize," he said. "Otherwise, detection, tracking, and launching, that's autonomous." Latvia's decision comes as automation is becoming increasingly common in weaponry and defense tech, including in Ukraine, where technology has advanced to enable AI and computer vision to find targets , fly drones, and drive robots even when connectivity with an operator is lost. Latvia wants this kind of autonomy across its new network of radars, sensors, command-and-control systems, and interceptor drones. A Latvian BLAZE autonomous interceptor drone at an air base in Latvia. Gints Ivuskans / AFP via Getty Images As a neighboring country, Latvia is particularly concerned about the possibility of Russian aggression. It has reported multiple drone incursions . These have included drones that it said were Russian or that had entered its airspace as a result of Russian electronic warfare. Latvia, a country of fewer than 2 million people, sees automation as a way to boost its combat power without more troops. Ukraine has made the same calculation, using increasingly autonomous weapons to help offset Russia's larger military. Agris Kipurs, CEO of Latvian drone maker Origin Robotics, previously told Business Insider that the smaller, front-line NATO nations need systems that let fewer operators do more. "And pretty much the only answer to that is autonomy," he said. The company makes drones used by Ukraine's military. It also makes an AI-enabled drone interceptor called Blaze that has been bought by multiple NATO militaries. Latvia's new defensive project is directly inspired by Ukraine, which has developed cheap weaponry like interceptor drones to combat Russia's attacks. Latvia has been one of Ukraine's strongest supporters and one of the militaries most keenly adopting battlefield lessons from its fight. Melnis said that interceptor drones have proved to have a "really high reliability and kill ratio in Ukraine, where the Ukrainians are fighting" one-way attack drone bombardments. Ukraine is increasingly relying on autonomy to allow systems to decrease the cognitive load on soldiers while strengthening the defense overall. Drones and other defense tech in Ukraine are becoming more automated. Diego Herrera Carcedo/Anadolu via Getty Images Automating processes reduces the demand for human input, though they remain important for engagement and kill decisions. Tech used on the battlefield is becoming increasingly autonomous; however, there are still limits to how much they can act beyond human control. Ukraine says that it will also keep humans involved on principle, giving them the final decision whether to engage. Latvia, Ukraine, and other allies want to use these kinds of anti-drone defenses because they're so much cheaper than traditional, expensive methods like missiles. Those defenses are not sustainable as the only solution against the masses of cheap drones. Melnis said that it's key to have a "cheap but reliable system" to stop drones. Latvia is using "modern technology and a cheap technology in comparison with a missile," he said. Drones and other defense tech in Ukraine are becoming more automated. credit should read Viacheslav Madiievskyi / Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images Allies are buying and developing these cheaper anti-drone systems . NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said in June that "long-term we cannot continue by shooting down drones with very costly interceptors, so we have to find interception techniques which are of the same costs as the drones." Latvia and other NATO allies have used fighter jets like F-35s, F-16s, and Rafales to shoot down drones entering their airspace with expensive air-to-air missiles. Melnis said the new system is designed to make jets a backup, serving only as "the secondary means" of stopping any drone that penetrates the wall. Melnis said the anti-drone wall is important for more than just his country's defense. The "border is not a Russian-Latvian border," he said. "It is a Russia-NATO, Russia-Europe border." He said that while this stretch of border is between Russia and Latvia, "we are NATO, and we are a European Union country." Any drone that crosses the border, he said, "that's the drone coming into NATO airspace . That's the drone coming into Europe." Read the original article on Business Insider

The company makes drones used by Ukraine's military. It also makes an AI-enabled drone interceptor called Blaze that has been bought by multiple NATO militaries.

Latvia's new defensive project is directly inspired by Ukraine, which has developed cheap weaponry like interceptor drones to combat Russia's attacks. Latvia has been one of Ukraine's strongest supporters and one of the militaries most keenly adopting battlefield lessons from its fight.

Melnis said that interceptor drones have proved to have a "really high reliability and kill ratio in Ukraine, where the Ukrainians are fighting" one-way attack drone bombardments.

Ukraine is increasingly relying on autonomy to allow systems to decrease the cognitive load on soldiers while strengthening the defense overall.

Drones and other defense tech in Ukraine are becoming more automated.

Diego Herrera Carcedo/Anadolu via Getty Images

Automating processes reduces the demand for human input, though they remain important for engagement and kill decisions.

Tech used on the battlefield is becoming increasingly autonomous; however, there are still limits to how much they can act beyond human control. Ukraine says that it will also keep humans involved on principle, giving them the final decision whether to engage.

Latvia, Ukraine, and other allies want to use these kinds of anti-drone defenses because they're so much cheaper than traditional, expensive methods like missiles. Those defenses are not sustainable as the only solution against the masses of cheap drones.

Melnis said that it's key to have a "cheap but reliable system" to stop drones. Latvia is using "modern technology and a cheap technology in comparison with a missile," he said.

Drones and other defense tech in Ukraine are becoming more automated.

credit should read Viacheslav Madiievskyi / Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images

Allies are buying and developing these cheaper anti-drone systems. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said in June that "long-term we cannot continue by shooting down drones with very costly interceptors, so we have to find interception techniques which are of the same costs as the drones."

Latvia and other NATO allies have used fighter jets like F-35s, F-16s, and Rafales to shoot down drones entering their airspace with expensive air-to-air missiles. Melnis said the new system is designed to make jets a backup, serving only as "the secondary means" of stopping any drone that penetrates the wall.

Melnis said the anti-drone wall is important for more than just his country's defense. The "border is not a Russian-Latvian border," he said. "It is a Russia-NATO, Russia-Europe border."

He said that while this stretch of border is between Russia and Latvia, "we are NATO, and we are a European Union country." Any drone that crosses the border, he said, "that's the drone coming into NATO airspace. That's the drone coming into Europe."

items.title: Arm-Qualcomm legal fight ends in limited verdict, larger stakes remain
items.summary: A Delaware jury found that Arm breached its licensing agreement with Qualcomm but awarded the chipmaker just $2 in damages, leaving a potentially multibillion-dollar dispute over royalty payments unresolved. The jury ruled on October 13 that Arm had failed to provide software patches and development tools required under its agreement with Qualcomm. It also found that Arm had interfered with Qualcomm’s business relationship with Meta Platforms, while rejecting several other allegations against Arm. Qualcomm is seeking to invoke a contractual provision that would allow it to stop paying royalties to Arm for five years. Arm has argued that the provision is unenforceable, leaving US District Judge Maryellen Noreika to decide whether Qualcomm is entitled to the remedy, Reuters reported. Qualcomm welcomed the finding that Arm breached its licensing obligations, while Arm emphasized that it prevailed on several other claims and was ordered to pay only nominal damages. The verdict follows an earlier dispute over Qualcomm’s 2021 acquisition of chip designer Nuvia. Arm argued that Qualcomm needed its consent to use technology developed under Nuvia’s license. A jury sided with Qualcomm on key issues in December 2024, and a judge ruled in its favor on the remaining claim in September 2025. Arm has appealed that judgment. The dispute comes as Arm expands beyond its traditional business of licensing processor technology. In March 2026, the company unveiled its first data center CPU, developed with Meta Platforms. Qualcomm, meanwhile, has been expanding beyond smartphones with its Snapdragon processors for Windows computers. PC market challenges unresolved The Arm–Qualcomm dispute is unlikely to significantly impact enterprise adoption of Snapdragon-powered Windows laptops, said Pareekh Jain , CEO of Pareekh Consulting. Charlie Dai , principal analyst at Forrester, said the remaining dispute is more focused on licensing remedies and commercial terms than on the viability of existing products. While the ruling reduces one source of uncertainty for Qualcomm, its prospects in the PC market remain dependent on factors beyond the legal dispute. The chipmaker accounted for less than 1% of the overall PC market, excluding tablets, in the second quarter of 2026, said Ben Yeh , principal analyst at Omdia, citing the firm’s data. “At present, the main challenges facing Qualcomm’s expansion in the PC market remain consumers’ limited confidence in the compatibility of Windows apps for the Arm-based architecture, their continued reliance on existing suppliers such as Intel and AMD, and the relatively high price of Qualcomm’s chips,” Yeh said. Yeh does expect Qualcomm’s share of PC sales to increase modestly in the second half of 2026, supported by the launch of its Snapdragon C products and supply shortages at Intel. For enterprise buyers, the more immediate considerations concern how well Snapdragon-powered Windows PCs fit into their existing IT environments. Dai said CIOs should evaluate device management and AI capabilities alongside application compatibility and vendor support when considering Snapdragon-powered laptops. Deepika Giri , head of research for AI, analytics and data in Asia Pacific at IDC, said the remaining legal uncertainty was manageable, but advised buyers to obtain multiyear commitments on product roadmaps and support from PC manufacturers and Qualcomm. Jain recommended maintaining a mix of Arm-based and x86 devices to reduce procurement risks. Arm’s relationships with chipmakers face scrutiny The jury’s finding that Arm failed to provide required development tools could bring greater scrutiny to its obligations under licensing agreements. Dai said clearer licensing obligations and stronger protections for licensees could encourage more custom processor development, potentially increasing competition. “What changes is leverage: licensees will push harder on terms and invest more in custom silicon,” Giri said. “Over the next few years, enterprises could benefit from broader hardware choices and improved performance differentiation, although any increase in licensing costs or legal complexity could also put upward pressure on processor pricing and ultimately on enterprise hardware spending,” Dai said. Arm’s expansion into chip development could encourage licensees to diversify without abandoning its technology altogether. Giri expects companies to continue using Arm for its established software ecosystem while also investing in RISC-V and their own processor designs. A wider range of processor architectures could give enterprises access to more specialized hardware, but could also complicate software certification and infrastructure planning, Dai said. To manage that complexity, Giri recommended that enterprises adopt architecture-agnostic software and procurement strategies, reducing their dependence on any single processor platform.

items.title: How To Build Your Team With Autonomous Humans, Not Just Autonomous Systems
items.summary: By Eric Francia How would you handle a junior employee questioning the way you’ve always done something? Might you roll your eyes and dismiss their comments as naivety? Or would you indulge their curiosity? As AI has made knowledge accessible on a scale never seen before, companies are becoming leaner and operating faster. What once took a large team months to do can now be done by a handful of people in a few days. It is undeniable that autonomous systems are changing the way we work. In the small and dynamic teams of the future, choosing the right humans to direct your AI systems will become make or break for a company. As a six-time founder, I’ve learned the best workplaces are the ones where questioning things is the norm. Here’s how to build a team that questions orders as much as it obeys them. AI by design Eric Francia, co-founder and CEO of Uniplay. “AI by design” doesn’t only mean building the right autonomous systems. It’s also about creating autonomous humans. You need to trust the human in the loop as much as you do the technology. The team around you ultimately shapes the company in ways you can’t control. So surrounding yourself with people you trust to make decisions when you’re not in the room is critical to success. The nature of job roles is changing. A job description can be totally different from the one advertised by the time you’ve found a candidate, and a six-month roadmap is outdated by the time you’ve finished drawing it up. The World Economic Forum has stated that 59% of employees will need to reskill by 2030 as AI reshapes the workplace. Hiring for a fixed set of skills won’t move the needle. The people worth investing in are those who are able to learn what comes next. Hire for curiosity Curiosity is the best trait you can hire for. When I look at a CV, it’s not just experience or academic credentials that draw me in. I look for what people have built on the side. What have they made on their own initiative? Hire for curiosity, and you’ll create an environment where people are willing to throw new ideas around and challenge outdated ways of doing things. If your team is worried about saying the wrong thing, they won’t end up saying the right thing either. In a world where technology is turning everything on its head, the companies that will thrive are the ones with curious people who are able to adapt to change quickly. Hand over real responsibility Employees with autonomy operate faster. They make better decisions because company vision is not abstract to people who are given real responsibility to drive it. Being involved in strategic direction stitches an employee into the fabric of the company and keeps them engaged. Trust your employees to know what isn’t working. Allow people to pursue new ideas and reinvent things. Your employees are likely to spot potential problems before you do when they’re closer to the product. Make sure your team has the autonomy to try to fix them before they take hold. Boredom is a big business risk As companies become smaller, employee retention is more important than ever. Losing your best people is costlier when you have fewer of them to begin with. The effects of a bored employee surface quickly in a small team. Boredom makes talented people a little bit slower, and a lot less likely to try the difficult thing. The challenge for modern leaders is keeping your team engaged and interested. A bored employee is more likely to be swayed by a flattering LinkedIn recruiter. Make sure to invest in development, keep your team learning, and always encourage curiosity. Give people autonomy and responsibility from the beginning, and boredom has nowhere to take hold. The mentality of risk and the drive to challenge something outdated is what you need to succeed in the changing work environment. Dare to be a beginner, and teach your team to do the same. That junior employee questioning how you’ve always done things could be the most valuable person in the room. Eric Francia is co-founder and CEO of Stockholm-based Uniplay , an agent-driven, game-based learning platform. He has experience building, exiting and scaling digital companies across 70 countries. Uniplay is his sixth company to date. Illustration: Dom Guzman
items.summary_html:
By Eric Francia

How would you handle a junior employee questioning the way you’ve always done something? Might you roll your eyes and dismiss their comments as naivety? Or would you indulge their curiosity?

As AI has made knowledge accessible on a scale never seen before, companies are becoming leaner and operating faster. What once took a large team months to do can now be done by a handful of people in a few days.

It is undeniable that autonomous systems are changing the way we work. In the small and dynamic teams of the future, choosing the right humans to direct your AI systems will become make or break for a company.

As a six-time founder, I’ve learned the best workplaces are the ones where questioning things is the norm. Here’s how to build a team that questions orders as much as it obeys them.

AI by design Eric Francia, co-founder and CEO of Uniplay.

“AI by design” doesn’t only mean building the right autonomous systems. It’s also about creating autonomous humans. You need to trust the human in the loop as much as you do the technology. The team around you ultimately shapes the company in ways you can’t control. So surrounding yourself with people you trust to make decisions when you’re not in the room is critical to success.

The nature of job roles is changing. A job description can be totally different from the one advertised by the time you’ve found a candidate, and a six-month roadmap is outdated by the time you’ve finished drawing it up.

The World Economic Forum has stated that 59% of employees will need to reskill by 2030 as AI reshapes the workplace. Hiring for a fixed set of skills won’t move the needle. The people worth investing in are those who are able to learn what comes next.

Hire for curiosity

Curiosity is the best trait you can hire for. When I look at a CV, it’s not just experience or academic credentials that draw me in. I look for what people have built on the side. What have they made on their own initiative?

Hire for curiosity, and you’ll create an environment where people are willing to throw new ideas around and challenge outdated ways of doing things. If your team is worried about saying the wrong thing, they won’t end up saying the right thing either.

In a world where technology is turning everything on its head, the companies that will thrive are the ones with curious people who are able to adapt to change quickly.

Hand over real responsibility

Employees with autonomy operate faster. They make better decisions because company vision is not abstract to people who are given real responsibility to drive it. Being involved in strategic direction stitches an employee into the fabric of the company and keeps them engaged.

Trust your employees to know what isn’t working. Allow people to pursue new ideas and reinvent things. Your employees are likely to spot potential problems before you do when they’re closer to the product. Make sure your team has the autonomy to try to fix them before they take hold.

Boredom is a big business risk

As companies become smaller, employee retention is more important than ever. Losing your best people is costlier when you have fewer of them to begin with.

The effects of a bored employee surface quickly in a small team. Boredom makes talented people a little bit slower, and a lot less likely to try the difficult thing.

The challenge for modern leaders is keeping your team engaged and interested. A bored employee is more likely to be swayed by a flattering LinkedIn recruiter.

Make sure to invest in development, keep your team learning, and always encourage curiosity. Give people autonomy and responsibility from the beginning, and boredom has nowhere to take hold. The mentality of risk and the drive to challenge something outdated is what you need to succeed in the changing work environment.

Dare to be a beginner, and teach your team to do the same. That junior employee questioning how you’ve always done things could be the most valuable person in the room.

Eric Francia is co-founder and CEO of Stockholm-based Uniplay, an agent-driven, game-based learning platform. He has experience building, exiting and scaling digital companies across 70 countries. Uniplay is his sixth company to date.

items.title: Cybersecurity Investors Put $6.8B To Work In The Third Quarter, Mostly In Larger Rounds
items.summary: It’s an insecure world out there, and investors are responding by scaling up their cybersecurity spending. For the third quarter of 2026, global cybersecurity- and privacy-focused startups pulled in a total of $6.8 billion, per Crunchbase data. That’s up about 50% from the prior quarter and tied for the highest quarterly tally in years, as charted below. The funding bump was due to larger rounds, not more of them. Round counts actually declined sequentially across all stages last quarter, Crunchbase data shows. Biggest cybersecurity fundraisers AI startups accounted for the overwhelming majority of cybersecurity funding, with a particular focus on identity security. Overall, at least 18 companies at the intersection of artificial intelligence and cybersecurity closed rounds of $100 million or more this past quarter. Of those, the largest funding recipient by far was enterprise identity security provider Keyfactor , which picked up $1 billion in a July growth round led by Summit Partners . Founded in 2001, the Ohio company isn’t exactly a startup, but it has attracted the bulk of its venture funding in the past 10 years and its pivot to AI is also of a more recent vintage. Dallas-based Island tied for second place with a $400 million September Series F led by Evolution Equity Partners . The startup, which offers tools for enterprises to see and govern how people and AI agents interact with applications and data, also secured a post-money valuation of $6.4 billion. Cyera , operator of an enterprise data security platform focused on AI agents, also announced a fresh $400 million Goldman Sachs Growth Equity -led investment in September, just three months after raising $600 million. The latest infusion set a $12 billion valuation for the New York startup. For a bigger-picture view of leading fundraisers, below we used Crunchbase data to put together a list of the 10 largest round recipients. Exits, too We also saw some good-sized acquisitions of cybersecurity startups this past quarter, even as the IPO market was fairly sluggish. Visa led the M&A pack with its $2.4 billion purchase of anti-fraud technology provider BioCatch in August. The acquisition is part of a broader effort by Visa to beef up its fraud detection and prevention capabilities for the AI age. Among private unicorns, meanwhile, Cyera proved it can find a way to spend a good chunk of the capital it raised. It acquired Oasis Security , an enterprise access management platform built for AI agents, in a deal reportedly valued around $1 billion. As for public offerings, Aura , which offers digital security services to consumers, was the lone sizable venture-backed market debut. The Boston-based startup completed an acquisition of an Australian public company, Qoria , in July, and then renamed the combined company Aura. Overall, an upbeat quarter Overall, Crunchbase funding data points to an upbeat environment for cybersecurity startup funding. This doesn’t seem particularly surprising given the steady drumbeat of worrisome news about the risks posed by rapidly advancing AI technology. It’s not an especially reassuring time for most of us. But for cybersecurity founders, there’s certainly an ever-expanding array of hazards to keep at bay. We’ll keep watching in the current quarter to see if investment momentum continues to build. items.title: Exclusive: Chariot Raises $10M To Help Consumers Fight Back Against Hidden Fees And Hard-To-Cancel Subscriptions
items.summary: While helping another founder build an app that collected information about class-action settlements, Zim Hang came to learn how challenging it can be for consumers to seek compensation from companies they believe wronged them. He also discovered mass arbitration, a way to pursue individual claims when companies’ contracts prevent customers from joining class actions. At the same time, he also realized that relatively few law firms were set up to manage thousands of those claims at once. Zim Hang, founder and CEO of Chariot Claims. (Courtesy photo) That gap became the basis for Chariot Claims , which has raised $10 million in Series A funding led by Silverton Partners to help consumers pursue claims over alleged privacy violations, hidden fees and subscriptions that are difficult to cancel. Indicator Ventures , Lightbank , Neon Fund , ZVC , Rosecliff Ventures , Alumni Ventures , FJ Labs , Graph Ventures and Vermilion Ventures also participated in the financing. The New York-based startup works with law firms to identify potential cases, find affected consumers and gather information needed to pursue compensation. The round brings its total funding to $15.7 million, which includes a $3.6 million seed investment in April 2025 and an earlier pre-seed round. Chariot’s latest round comes amid a surge in investment across legal tech. Funding to the legal tech space hit a record high last year, with $4.6 billion invested, per Crunchbase data . So far this year, legal tech startups have pulled in more than $3 billion, putting the sector on pace to match or exceed the 2025 total. The Chariot process works like this: For each case, consumers complete an intake questionnaire that assesses preliminary eligibility in real time. Chariot’s team then reviews these pre-qualified claims through a multi-layered system of technology and human oversight before sending it to the partner law firm handling the case. items.title: Copilot pricing gets complicated
items.summary: As Microsoft adds more advanced agentic capabilities to Copilot, such as Cowork and Autopilot, usage-based pricing is becoming an increasingly important part of its business model. But for customers used to predictable, fixed pricing, the addition of pay-as-you-go billing can be a significant change, creating new challenges around managing and predicting costs. Questions about the consumption pricing model are now among the most common that Gartner receives from clients around Copilot, said Max Goss, research director at Gartner. There’s “some doubt about whether a full move to consumption-based pricing for everyday knowledge work is sustainable for organizations in the long run,” he said. When Microsoft introduced Copilot three years ago, it charged businesses a flat monthly fee of $30 per user, with a $21 per user subscription later introduced for small and midsize businesses. Initial capabilities focused on helping employees find information, summarize meetings and documents, and draft content. Microsoft has since expanded Copilot with AI agents that can perform more complex tasks. Some, such as Researcher and Analyst , are included in the existing subscription, while others, including certain agents built with Copilot Studio or accessed via Copilot Chat , required usage-based charges through Copilot Credits, priced at $0.01 per credit. Now Microsoft is bringing consumption-based agents more directly into the core Copilot experience. At a recent event , it unveiled a new Home interface that places Cowork alongside the standard Chat option in the prompt box. Unlike Chat, Cowork incurs usage-based charges, with credit consumption varying depending on factors such as the model used and the complexity of the task, according to Microsoft’s pricing documentation . Navigating Copilot’s expanding pricing options As usage-based agents become more prominent alongside the subscription-based tools in Copilot, customers must ensure employees use the right tool for each task to avoid unnecessary charges. “Bringing these together in a single interface is going to make this harder,” said Goss. Employees could, for example, use Cowork for a task such as summarizing calendars, “potentially burning tokens on a task Copilot can do for free.” Anthropic has taken a similar approach with Claude, recently announcing that it’s merging its chat and Cowork tools. The main difference is that Claude Enterprise charges for usage with both features. Microsoft said it’s building a tool to automatically determine whether a user’s query should be routed to Cowork or Chat. Such routing could help employees avoid using more expensive capabilities unnecessarily, although its effectiveness in controlling costs remains to be seen. There’s also a risk that a vendor’s automatic routing could favor its more expensive capabilities, said Keith Kirkpatrick, research director at The Futurum Group. “When vendors decide whether a task should fall into one bucket versus another, there’s a risk that they’re overly weighted to moving the task to the bucket where they’re going to monetize it,” he said. For now, Copilot customers will need to educate employees about when more advanced tools are actually necessary, Goss said. To do so, businesses that enable tools such as Cowork should establish guidelines around when employees should use the agent tool and explain the potential costs, Kirkpatrick said. “It’s incumbent upon the enterprise — whether it’s IT or department managers — to be really clear and say: ‘Here are the tasks for which it makes sense to use Chat and here are the scenarios where it makes sense to use Cowork’ and be very explicit about what typical consumption might be,” he said. Usage-based pricing at scale The growing use of consumption-based pricing reflects the higher costs of running agentic AI — a broader challenge for AI vendors. “The AI of the future won’t just be ‘chat,’ it’s going to be ‘chat’ and ‘do’ combined into one interface,” said Goss. “We’re in this sticky situation now where the cost of the ‘do’ is too expensive, so the AI companies are passing that on to end users in the form of pay-as-you-go pricing.” For Copilot customers, the challenge is managing those costs as usage expands across an organization’s workforce. Microsoft has already adopted consumption-based pricing for developers using GitHub Copilot, but whether the same model is suitable for everyday knowledge work is unclear. “It seems that consumption-based pricing for a specific task like development is plausible and sustainable, albeit with some caveats around what you use it for and what you don’t,” said Goss. “The big question — that is still an open question — is: is consumption-based pricing scalable for general purpose knowledge work?” Each time a knowledge worker runs an agent while working on a spreadsheet, the cost to the organization could vary depending on the task, for instance. The employee’s level of AI proficiency could also have an effect, as repeated attempts to get the right result could increase consumption. Multiply that by 10,000 or 20,000 employees, Goss said, and the question becomes whether usage-based pricing is sufficiently predictable and sustainable for large organizations. To help customers control usage, Microsoft has developed a cost management tool. This lets admins create organization-wide and individual spending limits, monitor credit balance, and set up notifications when users reach a threshold. While these tools make it easier to monitor spending, predicting future consumption can be another problem, Kirkpatrick said. “The challenge is around forecasting,” he said, as businesses adopting AI agents generally lack data on how employees will use the technology. To help estimate costs, businesses should examine employee workflows and determine which are covered by subscriptions and where consumption-based pricing is required. A recent study cited in the Wall Street Journal showed that just 11% of surveyed firms successfully predicted spending on agentic systems. Managing usage-based costs may also require closer collaboration between finance, IT, and business units to manage costs — an approach known as FinOps. “Successful organizations are the ones that have devolved this,” said Goss, with IT retaining overall oversight while business units have nominated “steward” role to manage their own credit consumption within a fixed pool. It’s a new operational model for most organizations, however. “Going forward, IT procurement and finance teams will have to work closer together in more of a technical FinOps model. Most companies aren’t there yet, or are not familiar with how to do this at scale.” Proceed cautiously with Copilot agents As well as managing expenditure, Copilot customers should determine whether spending on agentic tools delivers productivity gains, analysts said. Proving Copilot’s value has been a persistent challenge for customers since the AI assistant launched. A Gartner survey of 186 IT leaders published in June showed that 51% saw value as one of their top three barriers to successful Copilot deployments. The survey also indicated that Copilot customers currently see greater benefits in more basic capabilities. Almost half (49%) reported high value from content generation and 44% from knowledge search, compared with just 20% for automating workflows and repetitive tasks using agentic tools such as Copilot Studio. (The survey was carried out prior to the launch of Cowork, which was made generally available in June.) Gartner The introduction of pay-as-you-go agents could bring back questions around return on investment that businesses faced when Copilot first launched. “If an organization just gives employees [access to the tools] and says, ‘go for it,’ they’re almost certainly going to see wastage. It’s going to be back to the early days of Copilot, when people were asking; ‘Is this valuable?’” said Goss. Kirkpatrick recommends that organizations establish clear goals before deploying agentic tools. “Start by looking at what business outcomes you’re looking to drive,” he said. “If you just focus on the technology, you’re going to wind up trying things out … without any real understanding of whether or not there’s actually business value being delivered.” Another factor in assessing the value of usage-based functionality in Copilot is what customers actually pay for it. Customers could also negotiate Copilot Credits as part of agreements for Microsoft’s new top-tier Microsoft 365 E7 subscription, which bundles M365 with AI tools such as Copilot and Agent 365 but doesn’t include Copilot Credits. “Microsoft is almost certainly talking to you about E7. At the same time, they’re probably having a conversation about usage-based pricing. Perhaps try and tie the conversations together … if you are going to move to E7, what can you get?” Goss said. “Microsoft could technically assign you credits, even if it’s just a starter amount. I would be looking to tie those two things together.” width="1024" height="679" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px"> Gartner Before rolling out Cowork and other consumption-based tools in Copilot, Kirkpatrick recommends launching pilot projects to better understand employee usage. Goss suggests starting with small-scale Cowork trials involving experienced Copilot users, with strict limits on credit consumption, and guidance on when to use Cowork over traditional Copilot. But he notes the challenge of scale remains. “It might be absolutely fine to pilot Cowork with fifty of your most advanced Copilot users, and you might see some brilliant returns,” he said. “But can you scale it to the rest of the organization? That’s the really interesting question here.”

items.title: Presentation: What 25 Trillion Tokens Reveal About How Developers Actually Adopt AI Agents
items.summary: Brendan O'Leary discusses how real-world AI adoption depends on building trust rather than chasing model benchmarks. Drawing from 40 trillion tokens of usage data, he explains the four rungs of the AI adoption ladder and analyzes key failure points in context construction, multi-model routing, and feedback loops to help engineering leaders successfully scale agentic workflows. By Brendan O’Leary

items.title: Elon Musk says SpaceX will pay back anyone whose Grok AI agent makes a rogue purchase
items.summary: SpaceX "will make you whole" if your AI agent makes unauthorized purchases, Musk said on X. Win McNamee/Getty Images Elon Musk says SpaceX "will make you whole" if your Grok AI agent makes unauthorized purchases. Musk's comment, though light on detail, is a departure from the standard approach to agent mistakes. Grok, Meta, and OpenAI's terms of service generally place responsibility for agent actions on users. Elon Musk said that SpaceX will pay users back if Grok’s AI agent makes a mistake while completing a purchase or leaks their card information. In a Thursday X post, Musk said the company "will make you whole" if Grok makes a financial mistake. He made the comment in response to an X user praising Grok for booking them a flight after being sent a photograph of their credit card. The user described the airline’s website as confusing and said Grok completed the transaction and delivered a booking confirmation. This works well. If Grok @Bot makes a mistake with a purchase or leaks your card (never happened yet), SpaceX will make you whole. https://t.co/JZDQm3a95r — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 15, 2026 "This works well," Musk wrote. "If Grok Bot makes a mistake with a purchase or leaks your card (never happened yet), SpaceX will make you whole." Grok, Meta, and OpenAI all take a broadly similar approach in their published terms for agents: users are responsible for the actions and transactions their AI agents carry out on their behalf. Meta says Muse requires approval before purchases, while Grok’s terms include interactions with financial institutions, but none offers the kind of explicit reimbursement pledge Musk described. Musk did not set out the scope of the apparent guarantee, including whether it would cover unauthorized purchases, incorrect bookings, fraud by third-party merchants, or consequential losses such as missed travel. SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Musk's assertion. The risks are already emerging as agents gain access to payment methods and online accounts. In a recent example involving Grok, Shane Mac, the CEO of software company XMTP Labs, told Business Insider's Aditi Bharade that a personal-finance agent he created posted his bank balances and spending details in his company’s executive Slack channel after confusing two similarly named chats. Grok’s team later changed its permission controls, according to Mac. Similarly, one user of the AI agent Instinct said it ordered 20 pounds of chicken wings during an agent-assisted grocery shop, while a Muse user said the agent accepted a low offer for a keyboard on Facebook Marketplace and shared his home address with the buyer. He later said he had selected an "Allow Always" setting , though he had believed the agent would still seek approval before accepting offers. While Musk’s promise is short on detail, it raises a broader question for the companies building agents that can spend money and access sensitive data: Will users continue to be expected to bear the risk, or will the companies behind the tools begin to share it? items.summary_html:
SpaceX "will make you whole" if your AI agent makes unauthorized purchases, Musk said on X.

Win McNamee/Getty Images

  • Elon Musk says SpaceX "will make you whole" if your Grok AI agent makes unauthorized purchases.
  • Musk's comment, though light on detail, is a departure from the standard approach to agent mistakes.
  • Grok, Meta, and OpenAI's terms of service generally place responsibility for agent actions on users.

Elon Musk said that SpaceX will pay users back if Grok’s AI agent makes a mistake while completing a purchase or leaks their card information.

In a Thursday X post, Musk said the company "will make you whole" if Grok makes a financial mistake. He made the comment in response to an X user praising Grok for booking them a flight after being sent a photograph of their credit card.

The user described the airline’s website as confusing and said Grok completed the transaction and delivered a booking confirmation.

This works well. If Grok @Bot makes a mistake with a purchase or leaks your card (never happened yet), SpaceX will make you whole. https://t.co/JZDQm3a95r

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 15, 2026

"This works well," Musk wrote. "If Grok Bot makes a mistake with a purchase or leaks your card (never happened yet), SpaceX will make you whole."

Grok, Meta, and OpenAI all take a broadly similar approach in their published terms for agents: users are responsible for the actions and transactions their AI agents carry out on their behalf.

Meta says Muse requires approval before purchases, while Grok’s terms include interactions with financial institutions, but none offers the kind of explicit reimbursement pledge Musk described.

Musk did not set out the scope of the apparent guarantee, including whether it would cover unauthorized purchases, incorrect bookings, fraud by third-party merchants, or consequential losses such as missed travel.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Musk's assertion.

The risks are already emerging as agents gain access to payment methods and online accounts.

In a recent example involving Grok, Shane Mac, the CEO of software company XMTP Labs, told Business Insider's Aditi Bharade that a personal-finance agent he created posted his bank balances and spending details in his company’s executive Slack channel after confusing two similarly named chats.

Grok’s team later changed its permission controls, according to Mac.

Similarly, one user of the AI agent Instinct said it ordered 20 pounds of chicken wings during an agent-assisted grocery shop, while a Muse user said the agent accepted a low offer for a keyboard on Facebook Marketplace and shared his home address with the buyer.

He later said he had selected an "Allow Always" setting, though he had believed the agent would still seek approval before accepting offers.

While Musk’s promise is short on detail, it raises a broader question for the companies building agents that can spend money and access sensitive data: Will users continue to be expected to bear the risk, or will the companies behind the tools begin to share it?
