items.title: Does the Graph Earn Its Cost?
items.summary: I stored the same data as documents and as a graph, and asked both the same six questions. The graph didn’t reveal anything new, but it changed where the work happens. Graph databases are often sold with the promise that they’ll reveal connections hidden in your data. I believed that for a while. Then I realised the connections weren’t hidden anywhere. They were already in the data, and the graph just stores them differently. So in my final-year project, I tested what a graph database actually buys you. I built a graph next to an existing document store of real lending data, and asked the same six questions of both. The short version: for questions you already know how to ask, a graph doesn’t reveal anything that wasn’t already in your data. What changes is where the work of connecting records happens. In the document store, every query rebuilds the connections for itself. In the graph, a tested pipeline builds them once, when the data is loaded, and every query reuses them. I think that’s worth paying for when the same connecting logic keeps being rebuilt across reports and tools. It isn’t when a single document already holds the answer. Comparing two data models fairly is harder than it looks, and I was lucky with the setup. I didn’t choose the database: ArangoDB was already there, behind the commercial system my data came from. My part was the graph. I designed the model, built the pipeline that loads it and the checks that verify it, and wrote the queries for both versions. ArangoDB stores documents and graphs side by side and queries both in the same language, AQL, so any difference in the shape of two queries couldn’t come from syntax. I compared that shape, not speed. I built the graph, and I wanted it to win, so I couldn’t just pick the version that looked better to me. Before comparing anything, I set three tests and used them on every pair of queries: Simplicity: how many query blocks, collections and steps it needs. Clarity: can you tell what it’s for just by reading it? Ease of change: if the question changes a little, is the change small, or do you rewrite the whole query? What I found: the work is conserved The data came from a commercial system, so I can’t show the real details. The example below uses a made-up domain instead, with queries of the same shape as the real ones. A buyer has one purchasing policy for its approved suppliers, with one rule per supplier that sets that supplier’s prices and terms. Every order is placed with one supplier and has to follow that supplier’s rule. Once the order is placed, it’s shipped. In the graph, each of these is a record, and each link between them is stored once, with a name. The policy has rules (POLICY_HAS_RULE), each rule governs the orders placed under it (RULE_GOVERNS_ORDER), and each order is placed with a supplier (ORDER_PLACED_WITH_SUPPLIER) and fulfilled by a shipment (ORDER_FULFILLED_BY_SHIPMENT). The documents don’t store these links, so every query has to rebuild them. Here is one of the path questions: for a given purchasing policy, which fulfilled orders were placed under it, which rule covered each order’s supplier, and which shipment delivered each order? The path of one question. At each link, the graph follows a stored, named link. The documents rebuild it inside the query. The document query answers it with three fragile tricks: A manufactured key. It builds the shipment’s ID by gluing two of the order’s fields together: CONCAT(order.carrier_code, “_”, TO_STRING(order.carrier_consignment_id)). That depends on a naming convention that exists only in people’s heads, and it assumes each order has exactly one shipment. A name match. It matches each order to its rule by comparing supplier names in lowercase, so a trailing space or a renamed company breaks it without any error. A nested-list search. It finds the rule by searching a list stored inside the policy, so it depends on that list keeping the same shape across records from different sources. The graph query has none of these. It starts from the same policy and follows its named links: to the policy’s rules, from each rule to the orders it governs, and from each order to its supplier and its shipment. The work didn’t disappear, though. It ran once, when the data was loaded and the links were built, and every query reuses the result. That’s what I mean by the work being conserved: the same logic still exists, but it runs in one place. Most of it went into one link, RULE_GOVERNS_ORDER. Building it means doing the same supplier-name match the document query does, and deciding, once, what happens when two rules name the same supplier. The document query answers that with FIRST(), which silently takes whichever match comes first, depending on the order the documents happen to be in. The pipeline has to answer it explicitly, write the answer down and test it. Across all six pairs, the pattern held. Manufactured keys, name matches and nested-list searches appeared only on the document side, and five of the six document queries rebuilt an ID by gluing fields together. A document store built for analysis could also store those IDs when the data is loaded, but then it pays the same cost in its own pipeline, which is my point. On step count, the graph actually did worse: in most pairs it took more steps. What differed was the kind of step. Every graph step does the same simple thing, following one named link to the next record, so you can read what a query is for from the link names. The document versions mix lookups, status filters, nested fields, manufactured keys and name matching. Ease of change showed most clearly in a query that broke spending down four ways. Adding a fifth to the graph version would take one more link to follow and one more entry in a list. In the document version, I’d have to find the right field in records from different sources and check they were named the same way. The pair that went against me One comparison contradicted my thesis, and it’s the one I’d want to see if I were reading this. The question was “give me everything about one shipment”. The shipment document already holds its carrier, origin, destination, customs classification and insurance, with its milestones in a nested list, so the document version is a single fetch. The graph version needs a separate step for every detail that became its own record, plus one for each of three event streams: planned milestones, status changes and tracking scans. For that question, the graph is worse in every way that matters. I think that’s a fact about my modelling choice more than about graphs. I built the schema around a process, how an order moves from policy to rule to supplier to shipment, so questions about the process became short, named paths. A question about one thing’s details isn’t a process question, and the same split that made the process easy to follow scatters one shipment across many steps. The document store made the opposite choice: it kept the shipment together and left the process implicit. So the real boundary, I think, is between a model built around processes and a model built around things, and the question you ask decides which one looks clumsy. That’s uncomfortable, because it means a comparison like mine partly compares two modelling decisions, not only two technologies. The two schemas were built for different jobs. Mine answers questions about how a process connects. The document store takes in records from several platforms that all name things differently, and it does that well. It’s also the most useful thing I learned. The model follows the question, and if you model around one kind of question, expect to pay on another. Why moving the work is worth paying for If the logic still exists either way, why move it at all? Because logic that gets rebuilt in every query gets rebuilt slightly differently each time. In my six document queries, the same ID-building logic appears five times. My copies match because I wrote them all, so what follows is how drift usually happens, not something I measured. In a typical company, the same logic also ends up in a dashboard, a monthly report, a reconciliation script written in a hurry and an Excel file that was meant to be temporary. Those are four versions, written by different people at different times, and nothing in the system knows they’re supposed to agree. When a source changes a field, or someone handles a missing value differently, they drift apart, and months later two numbers disagree in a meeting. Keeping the logic in one pipeline means you write and test it once. That doesn’t make it right, and a mistake there reaches every report that uses it. But it’s one place to find and fix it, instead of four versions drifting apart. The benefit is control and audit. The pipeline isn’t free. Mine extracts, normalises, links and loads the data. It gives every record a fixed ID, so a rerun updates records instead of duplicating them, and checks after loading confirm that every link points to a record that exists. I think it’s cheaper to pay that cost once, in the pipeline, than again in every query. History matters too, especially in regulated lending, where regulators and auditors often ask what was in force when a decision was made. When each change is stored as its own record, linked to what it changed, that becomes a simple filter rather than something each report rebuilds. Most of that comes from storing changes as records, which a history table can also do. The graph adds a named link from each change to what it changed, which makes these questions easier to ask. That’s a much smaller claim than meeting any regulation, and it’s the only one my evidence supports. A temporal graph goes one step further, because every link carries the time it happened. Once your records are mapped into one, the same graph can be reused in two ways. You can ask for the network as it was on a date, without writing that query each time. Or you can run algorithms that look at the whole network at once, which my six questions didn’t touch. Temporal motifs are one example. They count small patterns of events in a set order within a set time, like money that arrives in an account and leaves again within an hour. Neither of these needs your records to leave the database they live in. For the motif analysis in my thesis, I built the network from the documents with a script and loaded it into Raphtory, a temporal graph library. The catch is that a one-off script brings the glued keys and name matches back, now living in Python. So the question isn’t where the graph lives, but whether mapping the records into it is a lasting, tested piece of work, or something rebuilt for each analysis. Two things this doesn’t show. I didn’t compare speed: my dataset fit entirely in memory, where almost any query is fast, so nothing here says the graph is faster. And I didn’t measure what it costs to keep a graph next to the document store. It has to stay in step with its source, and one rebuilt nightly from data that changes hourly is wrong in a different way. So I wouldn’t migrate by default. I’d build a separate analytical layer next to the document system of record, fed by a pipeline, and let the document store keep doing what it’s good at. I’d reach for a graph in two situations. One is when the same connecting logic keeps being rebuilt across many reports and tools. The other is when “what was true on this date?” is a regular requirement rather than an occasional favour. Either way, model it around the questions you actually intend to ask, because the modelling decision does more work than the technology choice. Named links and AI tools Company data is increasingly queried by AI tools, not only by people, and stored, named links could matter for them too. Look again at the name match. Nothing in the documents says that the supplier name inside a rule is supposed to match the supplier name on an order. That knowledge lives in the head of the analyst who wrote the query, and it leaves with them. Conventions like that, and the glued key standing in for a join, have to be rediscovered by every analyst who touches the data. More and more, they also have to be rediscovered by every AI tool asked to query it. An AI tool can infer those conventions by spotting patterns, and it often will, confidently. But it can’t reliably tell you which parts of its answer were inferred. A graph query can only follow connections that were built and checked when the data was loaded. That’s a narrower ability, and an easier one to audit. Named links are documentation a program can read. This is strongest against a document store where connections are conventions. It’s much weaker against a relational database with declared foreign keys, or a semantic layer that defines business terms for machines, because both can state the same structural facts without a graph. There’s a difference in level, though. A semantic layer usually describes the schema: which tables join, and what each metric means. That tells an AI tool how to write a query. My graph went a level lower and stored the links between the records themselves: in the example, which rule governed a given order, and which shipment delivered it. It also captured when each change happened, and the facts the pipeline derived using rules. A relational database can store all of that too. What the graph adds is that those facts are connected to the records they describe by named links, so you can trace which rule applied, and when. Most companies won’t move their whole database into a graph just so AI tools can read it more easily, and I wouldn’t recommend it. But the separate layer I’d recommend anyway, fed by a pipeline and kept next to the system of record, might be enough. AI tools could read its named, checked links instead of guessing from the raw documents. That only works if the layer itself can be trusted. It has to record what happened and when, record how each fact was derived, and keep checking itself against the source. Then any answer can be verified rather than just believed. I haven’t tested whether that actually makes AI answers more reliable. The conclusion I can actually defend I started this project wanting to show that the graph was better. What I can actually defend is a smaller claim: the graph moved the work of connecting records into one tested pipeline, without adding any information that wasn’t already there. A graph isn’t the only way to do that: a relational database with declared foreign keys gets much of the same benefit. Whether moving the work pays off depends on how often a business rebuilds that logic, and how often it needs to ask what was true on a past date. I hold that at three levels of confidence. The design works for the questions I tested, on a narrow slice of one portfolio. Those questions all had a fixed number of steps, on data that fit in memory. So my result doesn’t cover questions that follow links many steps deep, like shortest paths, or how traversal holds up on a large production system. I believe that’s where a graph database earns more of its cost, when the question really has that shape, and it’s what I’d most like to test if I get the chance. The business case looks promising but is untested. And I know what data would settle it: many investors and loan originators, not one. A lot of technical writing quietly treats the first as if it proved the second. If there’s one thing I’d want a reader to take away, it’s that the question comes first. It decided what my model had to do well, and a comparison like mine is only as fair as the questions behind it. So I finished with a better question than “should I use a graph?”. Once connections are explicit, checked and readable by machines, can an AI system use them more reliably than it can rebuild them for itself? And can a graph layer next to the existing database give it that, without moving everything? That’s what I’m building next. Liquet is built in public, with synthetic data for a made-up wealth manager: its own cash records and its custodian’s monthly statement. It asks the question every finance team answers at month-end: does our cash book agree with the bank, and if not, why? That’s a question about records, not schemas: which statement line matched which cash entry, under which rule, and on which day. The records stay in a document database, and a graph layer gives each connection a clear name and meaning. I’m building that layer in Raphtory and saving the graph after every run, so you can go back to any month and see what was matched, what wasn’t, and what was known at the time. Rules do the matching, an AI agent investigates what’s left and explains each difference with evidence, and a person approves it. The principle is simple: rules for what you can state, an agent for what you can’t, and a graph as the shared, checkable context for both. Then I’ll test whether the agent is more reliable and more traceable working through the graph layer than from plain tables. Time is part of it from the start, because every reconciliation is about what was true, and what was known, on a given day. If your team rebuilds the same joining logic across reports, I’d like to hear how you keep the copies in step. This is a shorter version of Does the Graph Earn Its Cost? on my site, which has the full queries, the method, a section on temporal motifs and the references. The research, the graph model, the pipeline, the queries and the analysis are my own work from my final-year project. I used AI tools (Claude) to help me edit it. Does the Graph Earn Its Cost? was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

If the logic still exists either way, why move it at all? Because logic that gets rebuilt in every query gets rebuilt slightly differently each time.

In my six document queries, the same ID-building logic appears five times. My copies match because I wrote them all, so what follows is how drift usually happens, not something I measured. In a typical company, the same logic also ends up in a dashboard, a monthly report, a reconciliation script written in a hurry and an Excel file that was meant to be temporary. Those are four versions, written by different people at different times, and nothing in the system knows they’re supposed to agree. When a source changes a field, or someone handles a missing value differently, they drift apart, and months later two numbers disagree in a meeting.

Keeping the logic in one pipeline means you write and test it once. That doesn’t make it right, and a mistake there reaches every report that uses it. But it’s one place to find and fix it, instead of four versions drifting apart. The benefit is control and audit.

The pipeline isn’t free. Mine extracts, normalises, links and loads the data. It gives every record a fixed ID, so a rerun updates records instead of duplicating them, and checks after loading confirm that every link points to a record that exists. I think it’s cheaper to pay that cost once, in the pipeline, than again in every query.

History matters too, especially in regulated lending, where regulators and auditors often ask what was in force when a decision was made. When each change is stored as its own record, linked to what it changed, that becomes a simple filter rather than something each report rebuilds. Most of that comes from storing changes as records, which a history table can also do. The graph adds a named link from each change to what it changed, which makes these questions easier to ask. That’s a much smaller claim than meeting any regulation, and it’s the only one my evidence supports.

A temporal graph goes one step further, because every link carries the time it happened. Once your records are mapped into one, the same graph can be reused in two ways. You can ask for the network as it was on a date, without writing that query each time. Or you can run algorithms that look at the whole network at once, which my six questions didn’t touch. Temporal motifs are one example. They count small patterns of events in a set order within a set time, like money that arrives in an account and leaves again within an hour.

Neither of these needs your records to leave the database they live in. For the motif analysis in my thesis, I built the network from the documents with a script and loaded it into Raphtory, a temporal graph library. The catch is that a one-off script brings the glued keys and name matches back, now living in Python. So the question isn’t where the graph lives, but whether mapping the records into it is a lasting, tested piece of work, or something rebuilt for each analysis.

Two things this doesn’t show. I didn’t compare speed: my dataset fit entirely in memory, where almost any query is fast, so nothing here says the graph is faster. And I didn’t measure what it costs to keep a graph next to the document store. It has to stay in step with its source, and one rebuilt nightly from data that changes hourly is wrong in a different way.

So I wouldn’t migrate by default. I’d build a separate analytical layer next to the document system of record, fed by a pipeline, and let the document store keep doing what it’s good at. I’d reach for a graph in two situations. One is when the same connecting logic keeps being rebuilt across many reports and tools. The other is when “what was true on this date?” is a regular requirement rather than an occasional favour. Either way, model it around the questions you actually intend to ask, because the modelling decision does more work than the technology choice.

Named links and AI tools

Company data is increasingly queried by AI tools, not only by people, and stored, named links could matter for them too.

Look again at the name match. Nothing in the documents says that the supplier name inside a rule is supposed to match the supplier name on an order. That knowledge lives in the head of the analyst who wrote the query, and it leaves with them. Conventions like that, and the glued key standing in for a join, have to be rediscovered by every analyst who touches the data. More and more, they also have to be rediscovered by every AI tool asked to query it.

An AI tool can infer those conventions by spotting patterns, and it often will, confidently. But it can’t reliably tell you which parts of its answer were inferred. A graph query can only follow connections that were built and checked when the data was loaded. That’s a narrower ability, and an easier one to audit. Named links are documentation a program can read.

This is strongest against a document store where connections are conventions. It’s much weaker against a relational database with declared foreign keys, or a semantic layer that defines business terms for machines, because both can state the same structural facts without a graph.

There’s a difference in level, though. A semantic layer usually describes the schema: which tables join, and what each metric means. That tells an AI tool how to write a query. My graph went a level lower and stored the links between the records themselves: in the example, which rule governed a given order, and which shipment delivered it. It also captured when each change happened, and the facts the pipeline derived using rules. A relational database can store all of that too. What the graph adds is that those facts are connected to the records they describe by named links, so you can trace which rule applied, and when.

Most companies won’t move their whole database into a graph just so AI tools can read it more easily, and I wouldn’t recommend it. But the separate layer I’d recommend anyway, fed by a pipeline and kept next to the system of record, might be enough. AI tools could read its named, checked links instead of guessing from the raw documents. That only works if the layer itself can be trusted. It has to record what happened and when, record how each fact was derived, and keep checking itself against the source. Then any answer can be verified rather than just believed. I haven’t tested whether that actually makes AI answers more reliable.

The conclusion I can actually defend

I started this project wanting to show that the graph was better. What I can actually defend is a smaller claim: the graph moved the work of connecting records into one tested pipeline, without adding any information that wasn’t already there. A graph isn’t the only way to do that: a relational database with declared foreign keys gets much of the same benefit. Whether moving the work pays off depends on how often a business rebuilds that logic, and how often it needs to ask what was true on a past date.

I hold that at three levels of confidence. The design works for the questions I tested, on a narrow slice of one portfolio. Those questions all had a fixed number of steps, on data that fit in memory. So my result doesn’t cover questions that follow links many steps deep, like shortest paths, or how traversal holds up on a large production system. I believe that’s where a graph database earns more of its cost, when the question really has that shape, and it’s what I’d most like to test if I get the chance. The business case looks promising but is untested. And I know what data would settle it: many investors and loan originators, not one. A lot of technical writing quietly treats the first as if it proved the second.

If there’s one thing I’d want a reader to take away, it’s that the question comes first. It decided what my model had to do well, and a comparison like mine is only as fair as the questions behind it.

So I finished with a better question than “should I use a graph?”. Once connections are explicit, checked and readable by machines, can an AI system use them more reliably than it can rebuild them for itself? And can a graph layer next to the existing database give it that, without moving everything?

That’s what I’m building next. Liquet is built in public, with synthetic data for a made-up wealth manager: its own cash records and its custodian’s monthly statement. It asks the question every finance team answers at month-end: does our cash book agree with the bank, and if not, why? That’s a question about records, not schemas: which statement line matched which cash entry, under which rule, and on which day.

The records stay in a document database, and a graph layer gives each connection a clear name and meaning. I’m building that layer in Raphtory and saving the graph after every run, so you can go back to any month and see what was matched, what wasn’t, and what was known at the time. Rules do the matching, an AI agent investigates what’s left and explains each difference with evidence, and a person approves it. The principle is simple: rules for what you can state, an agent for what you can’t, and a graph as the shared, checkable context for both. Then I’ll test whether the agent is more reliable and more traceable working through the graph layer than from plain tables. Time is part of it from the start, because every reconciliation is about what was true, and what was known, on a given day.

If your team rebuilds the same joining logic across reports, I’d like to hear how you keep the copies in step.

This is a shorter version of Does the Graph Earn Its Cost? on my site, which has the full queries, the method, a section on temporal motifs and the references. The research, the graph model, the pipeline, the queries and the analysis are my own work from my final-year project. I used AI tools (Claude) to help me edit it.

items.title: Giving Your AI Coworker Enterprise Context with Databricks Genie
items.summary: From team rules to company definitions, across Genie One and Code. In short Databricks Genie gives an AI coworker four places to hold enterprise context: instructions for team rules, skills for repeatable tasks, memory for personal preferences and Genie Ontology for company definitions. In my test, Genie One and Genie Code read skills from the same personal folder, so a skill I made in one showed up in the other. What is enterprise context for an AI coworker? Enterprise context is the knowledge an AI coworker needs to do your work the way your company does it. It is what a new hire picks up in their first weeks: the team’s rules, how recurring jobs get done, how you like to work and what the company’s terms mean. Databricks has two AI coworkers that use this context. Genie One is the AI coworker for business users, who ask it questions about company data in plain language. Genie Code is the AI coworker for technical work, and it writes and runs code in your Databricks workspace. To see how the context works in practice, I set up both of them as one person, an analytics engineer at Lumora. Lumora is a made-up software company that sells subscriptions, and all the data in my setup is sample data. Each kind of context ended up in its own place in Genie. Where should each piece of context go? The rule I ended up with is short. If a fact is true for the whole company, it goes in Genie Ontology. If it is a rule for your team, it goes in instructions. If it is a task you repeat, it goes in a skill. If it is only about you, it goes in memory. This is how the rule sorted the facts from my Lumora setup: Genie Ontology: “An active customer is a paying customer who logged in within 30 days” and “Our fiscal year starts on February 1.” Instructions: “New tables go in the dev schema first” and “Ask before you drop a table.” Skills: “Review a table with these six checks before it ships” and “Every Monday, send me a one-page brief,” which a scheduled task can run. Memory: “When I say my region, I mean APJ” and “Show me numbers in a table first.” The sections below follow the order a new hire learns things in. Rules come on day one and playbooks in the first week. What they learn about you comes with time, and the company glossary sits underneath all of it. How do I tell Genie who I am and how my team works? A new hire’s first day starts with who they are working for and the house rules. In Genie, that is the instructions file. It is a Markdown file, which is plain text with simple formatting, and Genie reads it at the start of every conversation. Genie Code looks for two of them. Your own rules go in .assistant_instructions.md in your user folder, and rules for everyone go in .assistant_workspace_instructions.md at the root of the workspace. Genie Code generally gives the workspace file priority unless you tell it otherwise. It also reads any AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md file in the folders you work in. Each file can hold up to 20,000 characters, and Genie Code ignores anything past that. My Lumora file was short. This is a shortened copy, where B2B SaaS means subscription software sold to businesses: # About me I am an analytics engineer on the RevOps data team at Lumora, a B2B SaaS company. I build pipelines and metric views. # How I work - Write SQL first. Use Python only when SQL can't do it. - New tables go in the lumora_dev schema. Never write to lumora directly. - Every new table gets a table comment and a comment on each column. # Ask before you act - Ask before you drop, overwrite or rename a table. To check it, I opened a new chat and asked Genie Code, “What do you know about me and the rules I want you to follow?” It listed every rule from the file back to me. Genie One handles instructions differently. It has one instructions file per workspace, which an admin writes at /Workspace/.genie_workspace_instructions.md, and that file applies only to Genie One chat. There is no personal instructions file in Genie One, so your own preferences go in memory instead. How do I teach Genie a task it should repeat? Rules tell a new hire what to avoid. Playbooks show them how to do the jobs that come up every week. In Genie, a playbook is a skill: a folder with a SKILL.md file that starts with a name and a one-line description, followed by step-by-step instructions. Genie skills follow the open Agent Skills format. My first skill covered a job I do often, reviewing a table before it ships. A shortened copy: --- name: pipeline-review description: Review a Lumora pipeline or table change before it ships. Use when asked to review, check or sign off a pipeline or a table. --- Run these checks in order. Report each one as PASS or FAIL with one line of evidence. 1. Comments. The table and every column have a comment. 2. Schema. New tables are in lumora_dev, not lumora. 3. Row count. Flag any change above 5 percent compared with the source. 4. Nulls. List key columns where more than 1 percent of rows are null. 5. Duplicates. Check that the primary key is unique. 6. Definitions. If the table computes customers, MRR or churn, check the logic against Genie Ontology. End with one of these: ship, ship with fixes, or do not ship. Do not change any table during a review. I saved it in my personal skills folder, /Users/ /.assistant/skills/pipeline-review/, and typed "Please review the subscriptions table before we ship it." I never named the skill. Genie Code matched my request to the skill's description, loaded the skill and made a plan with one step per check. This is why the description matters most. If it does not say what the skill does and when to use it, Genie has no reason to load it. The review ended with “ship with fixes” because the table had no comments and sat in the wrong schema, which broke two rules from my instructions file. In Genie One you make a skill by asking for it, for example “Create a skill called monday-brief that gives me a one-page brief for my region,” and you run it by typing /monday-brief. That skill led to the most useful finding of my test. Genie One saved monday-brief in the same personal folder as my Genie Code skill. When I asked each product which skills it had, Genie One listed pipeline-review and Genie Code listed monday-brief. You can keep your personal skills in one folder and use them from both products. How does Genie remember things about me, and how do I check what it saved? Some things a new hire only learns by working with you, like what you mean by “my region” or how you like numbers shown. Genie keeps these as memories, which are short facts about you that it saves and uses in later conversations. You save one by starting a message with “Remember that.” When I told Genie One, “Remember that when I say my region I mean APJ at Lumora,” it showed a “Saving a memory” step in the chat. When a later answer uses a memory, Genie One adds a citation that shows which one. Genie Code also saves memories on its own when it learns something useful. When I asked it, “What do you remember about me?”, it listed my one saved preference and added, “Everything else I know comes from your .assistant_instructions.md, which I read fresh each session.” That line shows the difference between the two. Instructions apply to every conversation, and a memory comes up only when it fits the task. Memories go out of date, so check them about once a month. Ask each product what it remembers and tell it to forget anything stale. In my test, both products deleted the memory I named and confirmed what was left. Also make sure no memory holds a password or an API key, because Genie saves what you tell it. Why do company definitions belong in Genie Ontology instead of skills? The last piece is the company glossary, and it is the one that most needs to be shared. Genie Ontology is the shared layer of business context in Databricks. Genie One and Genie Code can both use it, and so can Genie Agents. It has two parts. The first is the metric views and pages you write in Unity Catalog, which is where Databricks keeps your tables and their descriptions. A metric view is a saved definition of a business number, such as MRR (monthly recurring revenue). The second is context that Databricks pulls from what you already have, such as dashboards, saved queries and Genie Agents. My test showed what goes wrong when a definition lives somewhere else. My test workspace is shared with other demos. When Genie One built the monday-brief skill, it searched the workspace for a definition of MRR, found a glossary page from a different demo and wrote that formula into the skill. The formula broke three Lumora rules: It added up subscription amounts as stored. Lumora stores the full yearly price on annual plans, so MRR has to divide those amounts by 12. It used the calendar quarter, but Lumora’s fiscal year starts on February 1. It counted every canceled subscription as churn, including customers who only moved to a bigger plan. Because the formula was written into the skill file, the skill would have repeated these mistakes every Monday. A better skill names the term and points to its Genie Ontology definition, for example “Use the Genie Ontology definition of MRR.” Then you fix a definition in one place instead of in every skill, and you can check the sources Genie cites in its answer. Memory is the wrong place for definitions too. Genie One memories are private to you, so your teammates would not get the same answer you do. This is how I wrote one Lumora term as a page: ## Active customer An active customer is a paying customer with at least one 'login' event in the last 30 days. API calls, report runs and exports do not count, because integrations can keep running when nobody uses the product. FAQ Do I need Genie Ontology before I start? No. You can start on day one with an instructions file and one skill. Add Genie Ontology pages when your team needs the same answer to the same question, such as how many customers you have. Can my whole team use the same skill in Genie Code? Yes. Genie Code also reads skills from Workspace/.assistant/skills/, so a skill saved there works for everyone in the workspace, not only for you. Sources Customize Genie Code with instructions Chat in Genie One Genie Ontology Giving Your AI Coworker Enterprise Context with Databricks Genie was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
From team rules to company definitions, across Genie One and Code.In short
  • Databricks Genie gives an AI coworker four places to hold enterprise context: instructions for team rules, skills for repeatable tasks, memory for personal preferences and Genie Ontology for company definitions.
  • In my test, Genie One and Genie Code read skills from the same personal folder, so a skill I made in one showed up in the other.
What is enterprise context for an AI coworker?

Enterprise context is the knowledge an AI coworker needs to do your work the way your company does it. It is what a new hire picks up in their first weeks: the team’s rules, how recurring jobs get done, how you like to work and what the company’s terms mean.

Databricks has two AI coworkers that use this context. Genie One is the AI coworker for business users, who ask it questions about company data in plain language. Genie Code is the AI coworker for technical work, and it writes and runs code in your Databricks workspace.

To see how the context works in practice, I set up both of them as one person, an analytics engineer at Lumora. Lumora is a made-up software company that sells subscriptions, and all the data in my setup is sample data. Each kind of context ended up in its own place in Genie.

Where should each piece of context go?

The rule I ended up with is short. If a fact is true for the whole company, it goes in Genie Ontology. If it is a rule for your team, it goes in instructions. If it is a task you repeat, it goes in a skill. If it is only about you, it goes in memory.

This is how the rule sorted the facts from my Lumora setup:

  • Genie Ontology: “An active customer is a paying customer who logged in within 30 days” and “Our fiscal year starts on February 1.”
  • Instructions: “New tables go in the dev schema first” and “Ask before you drop a table.”
  • Skills: “Review a table with these six checks before it ships” and “Every Monday, send me a one-page brief,” which a scheduled task can run.
  • Memory: “When I say my region, I mean APJ” and “Show me numbers in a table first.”

The sections below follow the order a new hire learns things in. Rules come on day one and playbooks in the first week. What they learn about you comes with time, and the company glossary sits underneath all of it.

How do I tell Genie who I am and how my team works?

A new hire’s first day starts with who they are working for and the house rules. In Genie, that is the instructions file. It is a Markdown file, which is plain text with simple formatting, and Genie reads it at the start of every conversation.

Genie Code looks for two of them. Your own rules go in .assistant_instructions.md in your user folder, and rules for everyone go in .assistant_workspace_instructions.md at the root of the workspace. Genie Code generally gives the workspace file priority unless you tell it otherwise. It also reads any AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md file in the folders you work in. Each file can hold up to 20,000 characters, and Genie Code ignores anything past that.

My Lumora file was short. This is a shortened copy, where B2B SaaS means subscription software sold to businesses:

# About me
I am an analytics engineer on the RevOps data team at Lumora, a B2B SaaS
company. I build pipelines and metric views.
 
# How I work
- Write SQL first. Use Python only when SQL can't do it.
- New tables go in the lumora_dev schema. Never write to lumora directly.
- Every new table gets a table comment and a comment on each column.
 
# Ask before you act
- Ask before you drop, overwrite or rename a table.

To check it, I opened a new chat and asked Genie Code, “What do you know about me and the rules I want you to follow?” It listed every rule from the file back to me.

Genie One handles instructions differently. It has one instructions file per workspace, which an admin writes at /Workspace/.genie_workspace_instructions.md, and that file applies only to Genie One chat. There is no personal instructions file in Genie One, so your own preferences go in memory instead.

How do I teach Genie a task it should repeat?

Rules tell a new hire what to avoid. Playbooks show them how to do the jobs that come up every week. In Genie, a playbook is a skill: a folder with a SKILL.md file that starts with a name and a one-line description, followed by step-by-step instructions. Genie skills follow the open Agent Skills format.

My first skill covered a job I do often, reviewing a table before it ships. A shortened copy:

---
name: pipeline-review
description: Review a Lumora pipeline or table change before it ships. Use when
  asked to review, check or sign off a pipeline or a table.
---
Run these checks in order. Report each one as PASS or FAIL with one line of evidence.
1. Comments. The table and every column have a comment.
2. Schema. New tables are in lumora_dev, not lumora.
3. Row count. Flag any change above 5 percent compared with the source.
4. Nulls. List key columns where more than 1 percent of rows are null.
5. Duplicates. Check that the primary key is unique.
6. Definitions. If the table computes customers, MRR or churn, check the logic against Genie Ontology.
End with one of these: ship, ship with fixes, or do not ship.
Do not change any table during a review.

I saved it in my personal skills folder, /Users//.assistant/skills/pipeline-review/, and typed "Please review the subscriptions table before we ship it." I never named the skill. Genie Code matched my request to the skill's description, loaded the skill and made a plan with one step per check. This is why the description matters most. If it does not say what the skill does and when to use it, Genie has no reason to load it.

The review ended with “ship with fixes” because the table had no comments and sat in the wrong schema, which broke two rules from my instructions file.

In Genie One you make a skill by asking for it, for example “Create a skill called monday-brief that gives me a one-page brief for my region,” and you run it by typing /monday-brief.

That skill led to the most useful finding of my test. Genie One saved monday-brief in the same personal folder as my Genie Code skill. When I asked each product which skills it had, Genie One listed pipeline-review and Genie Code listed monday-brief. You can keep your personal skills in one folder and use them from both products.

How does Genie remember things about me, and how do I check what it saved?

Some things a new hire only learns by working with you, like what you mean by “my region” or how you like numbers shown. Genie keeps these as memories, which are short facts about you that it saves and uses in later conversations.

You save one by starting a message with “Remember that.” When I told Genie One, “Remember that when I say my region I mean APJ at Lumora,” it showed a “Saving a memory” step in the chat. When a later answer uses a memory, Genie One adds a citation that shows which one.

Genie Code also saves memories on its own when it learns something useful. When I asked it, “What do you remember about me?”, it listed my one saved preference and added, “Everything else I know comes from your .assistant_instructions.md, which I read fresh each session.” That line shows the difference between the two. Instructions apply to every conversation, and a memory comes up only when it fits the task.

Memories go out of date, so check them about once a month. Ask each product what it remembers and tell it to forget anything stale. In my test, both products deleted the memory I named and confirmed what was left. Also make sure no memory holds a password or an API key, because Genie saves what you tell it.

Why do company definitions belong in Genie Ontology instead of skills?

The last piece is the company glossary, and it is the one that most needs to be shared. Genie Ontology is the shared layer of business context in Databricks. Genie One and Genie Code can both use it, and so can Genie Agents. It has two parts. The first is the metric views and pages you write in Unity Catalog, which is where Databricks keeps your tables and their descriptions. A metric view is a saved definition of a business number, such as MRR (monthly recurring revenue). The second is context that Databricks pulls from what you already have, such as dashboards, saved queries and Genie Agents.

My test showed what goes wrong when a definition lives somewhere else. My test workspace is shared with other demos. When Genie One built the monday-brief skill, it searched the workspace for a definition of MRR, found a glossary page from a different demo and wrote that formula into the skill. The formula broke three Lumora rules:

  • It added up subscription amounts as stored. Lumora stores the full yearly price on annual plans, so MRR has to divide those amounts by 12.
  • It used the calendar quarter, but Lumora’s fiscal year starts on February 1.
  • It counted every canceled subscription as churn, including customers who only moved to a bigger plan.

Because the formula was written into the skill file, the skill would have repeated these mistakes every Monday. A better skill names the term and points to its Genie Ontology definition, for example “Use the Genie Ontology definition of MRR.” Then you fix a definition in one place instead of in every skill, and you can check the sources Genie cites in its answer.

Memory is the wrong place for definitions too. Genie One memories are private to you, so your teammates would not get the same answer you do.

This is how I wrote one Lumora term as a page:

## Active customer
An active customer is a paying customer with at least one 'login' event in
the last 30 days. API calls, report runs and exports do not count, because
integrations can keep running when nobody uses the product.
FAQDo I need Genie Ontology before I start?

No. You can start on day one with an instructions file and one skill. Add Genie Ontology pages when your team needs the same answer to the same question, such as how many customers you have.

Can my whole team use the same skill in Genie Code?

Yes. Genie Code also reads skills from Workspace/.assistant/skills/, so a skill saved there works for everyone in the workspace, not only for you.

Sources
  • Customize Genie Code with instructions
  • Chat in Genie One
  • Genie Ontology

items.title: Can a Local Auditor Ensemble Match a Hosted Decision Model?
items.summary: Can a Local Auditor Ensemble Match a Hosted Decision Model? On Real Pipeline Output, It Already Does. I wrote five domain rules for a hosted decision model and tested it against my locally hosted LLM auditors. On my development data, where three-quarters of the matches were one product family, one rule made the hosted model look clearly better. On a second client’s real pipeline output, the rule had nothing to act on, and my local auditors reached a better tradeoff at a similar review budget. Total API charges: $16.15. The matching error that started it Here are two records from a client’s corrugated-sheet catalog: > `275B 32.2500 X 36.0000 122.65 MSF` > `275B 32.2500 X 36.0000 122.18 MSF` Same board grade, same sheet dimensions. The last number differs, and it’s followed by MSF: thousand square feet. That’s how much was bought, not what was bought. These two records are the same product. Now these two, from the same review: > `4X6 1 MIL CLEAR` (poly bag) > `4X6 4 MIL CLEAR` (poly bag) Also nearly identical, differing by one number. This time, the number is the bag’s thickness, and the records are different products. In industrial record linkage, knowing which numbers define the product and which merely describe a transaction is often the difference between a correct match and a corrupted catalog. My pipeline (embeddings, blocking, a re-ranker, calibrated thresholds, clustering) proposes candidate matches. Three locally hosted LLM auditors adjudicate them the way an analyst would: three QLoRA fine-tuned models (Qwen2.5, SmolLM3, and phi4). Production has to stay local for data privacy reasons. I wanted to know whether a different kind of auditor would do better. Jev, TypeSafe’s hosted typed decision model , answers one multiple-choice question per pair (MATCH, NONMATCH, or INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE) and returns a probability distribution. Its instructions, the rubric, are a text file I can version and test. I can’t deploy Jev, so for me it’s a benchmark: if a hosted model with written-down domain rules is clearly better, that’s the bar a local model has to reach. Can a Local Auditor Ensemble Match a Hosted Decision Model? On Real Pipeline Output, It Already Does.I wrote five domain rules for a hosted decision model and tested it against my locally hosted LLM auditors. On my development data, where three-quarters of the matches were one product family, one rule made the hosted model look clearly better. On a second client’s real pipeline output, the rule had nothing to act on, and my local auditors reached a better tradeoff at a similar review budget. Total API charges: $16.15.The matching error that started it

Here are two records from a client’s corrugated-sheet catalog:

> `275B 32.2500 X 36.0000 122.65 MSF`
> `275B 32.2500 X 36.0000 122.18 MSF`

Same board grade, same sheet dimensions. The last number differs, and it’s followed by MSF: thousand square feet. That’s how much was bought, not what was bought. These two records are the same product.

Now these two, from the same review:

> `4X6 1 MIL CLEAR` (poly bag)
> `4X6 4 MIL CLEAR` (poly bag)

Also nearly identical, differing by one number. This time, the number is the bag’s thickness, and the records are different products.

In industrial record linkage, knowing which numbers define the product and which merely describe a transaction is often the difference between a correct match and a corrupted catalog. My pipeline (embeddings, blocking, a re-ranker, calibrated thresholds, clustering) proposes candidate matches. Three locally hosted LLM auditors adjudicate them the way an analyst would: three QLoRA fine-tuned models (Qwen2.5, SmolLM3, and phi4). Production has to stay local for data privacy reasons.

I wanted to know whether a different kind of auditor would do better. Jev, TypeSafe’s hosted typed decision model, answers one multiple-choice question per pair (MATCH, NONMATCH, or INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE) and returns a probability distribution. Its instructions, the rubric, are a text file I can version and test. I can’t deploy Jev, so for me it’s a benchmark: if a hosted model with written-down domain rules is clearly better, that’s the bar a local model has to reach. I also ran Laya, an open-source, self-hostable implementation of the same request format, from its base checkpoint, on my RTX 5090.

The question I care about in production isn’t abstract accuracy. It’s how many wrong automatic calls stand for a given amount of analyst review.

One rule changed the results

I wrote five rules, one at a time, and recorded each hypothesis before running inference. Three were confirmed by domain review: MSF is quantity, a trailing service-run number is a per-run ID, and packs-per-pallet is packaging. Two I proposed from leftover misses: naming style (abbreviations, prefixes) is incidental unless the difference is substantive, and per-unit packaging counts are incidental when the product matches.

My reference-labeled evaluation sample (“gold”) is 20,000 pairs drawn from the pipeline’s labeled pair pool, which spans several clients’ catalogs, at the pool’s natural 41.3% match rate. The negatives are blocked candidates, pairs that the pipeline actually considered. 19,530 labels are derived from identity groupings, each human-reviewed when it was built, rather than from pair-by-pair review; the other 470 are direct pair reviews. All seven rubric versions were frozen before gold was built, so nothing on it fed back into the rules.

Jev’s recall on gold went from 14.9% with the base rubric to 89.1% with the MSF rule alone, at 98.4% precision. With all five rules, it reached 92.2%. Then I checked what the pool was made of. 6,193 of its 8,253 true matches (75%) are MSF pairs.

https://medium.com/media/3c5809d985690071265215257699fc7f/href

Precision on everything else held at about 90% throughout. So the headline jump is one rule meeting the product family that dominates the pool. On the non-MSF pairs, the full ladder bought 15 points of recall. The service-run and pallet rules barely moved the totals, and that’s measurable: gold has 175 service-run pairs and 9 pallet-count pairs.

The full rubric-by-rubric results are in the appendix. I ran all seven rubric versions on gold, and only the base and full rubrics on the second client.

I ran the three production auditors on the same 20,000 pairs. On the non-MSF subset, which isolates performance away from the dominant MSF convention:

https://medium.com/media/c3a35bcbcb5c397d593df7ce8172e5e9/href

Two conventions matter here. Jev can abstain with INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, and in this table, an abstention counts as not-MATCH. Jev abstained on 916 of these 13,787 pairs (6.6%). Counting only the 12,871 pairs it decided, which changes the denominator, its recall is 74.4% at the same 90.6% precision. The fine-tuned auditors return a binary decision on every pair (phi4 failed on 29 here). In this table, “unanimous” means all three say MATCH; anything else counts as NONMATCH. In a shadow audit, an abstention goes to a person, so it’s review work rather than an error.

Because every model scored the same pairs, I compared them directly: a paired bootstrap on the differences, resampling by query item so repeated items don’t inflate confidence. Jev is about 2 points more precise than each fine-tuned auditor, and the majority vote reflects that difference (for example, +2.4 points vs Qwen2.5, 95% interval +0.9 to +3.7). Recall against either fine-tuned model is indistinguishable. The majority vote has 3.4 points more recall than Jev, and that holds up too. The unanimous vote is the most precise of all: 1.8 points more precise than Jev (interval +0.5 to +3.2), at 8.5 points less recall.

The totals tell a different story because the auditors only partially learned the MSF convention from their training data: 88.8% and 79.4% recall on MSF pairs, compared with Jev’s 100%. The fine-tuned phi4 (which was trained on a more general set than the other two auditors) rejects most of them (35.4%), the way Jev’s base rubric did.

The fine-tuned auditors were trained on a single amalgamated set from multiple clients, with human-reviewed pairs, and the same reviewer labeled part of that training data and gold’s 470 direct-review rows. Excluding those rows changes the auditors’ numbers by less than 1 point in precision and less than 3 points in recall. About 0.1% of gold’s pairs also appear in their training data.

They let more false merges stand (7.2% against 0.2%), and those have a path to correction.

I checked whether a different Jev threshold changes that:

https://medium.com/media/b30a94b24fad16e0fc0d42aecb2c97b3/href

Raising Jev’s threshold does rescue some missed matches, at a steep review cost. At 1.00 (its probabilities come rounded to two decimals, so that’s the top of the scale), it sends 66.5% of pairs to analysts and still misses 3.8%, above the auditors’ 1.4% at 32.5% review. None of the thresholds I tested matched the local policy on both review load and missed matches. These rates come from the same 1,000 labeled pairs, so they carry the same sampling uncertainty as the table above. I didn’t test other routing designs, such as separate thresholds for MATCH and NONMATCH, beyond a few simple variants. Jev does return a numerical distribution I can route on; my auditors give a three-vote agreement signal. Neither is a calibrated confidence until it’s tested as one.

What else the second client showed

The rule ladder still helped Jev by 7.7 points of recall (47.2% to 54.9%) with precision flat. I only ran the base and full rubrics here, so I can’t say which rules produced that gain.

The models fail differently. In the holdout, 18 of Jev’s 57 false matches (32%) are pairs in which one side omits an attribute, such as thickness or size; it treats missing information as compatible. That suggests a rule to test, not one to adopt yet: when an identity-critical attribute is missing, and no stronger identifier (a matching part number, say) establishes the match, answer INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE.

Why this pipeline is recall-first. The link run compared 57,000 query items against 660,000 reference items and, across its four output sets, accepted or sent to review 72,177 pairs; I scored the first and last sets. The pipeline’s accept call is only about 52% precise (within the accept stratum, 43 of 82 labeled accepts are true matches; interval 41% to 63%), and it finds only 4% of the matches. That’s deliberate. Most matches are caught in the review band, and every accept still gets human review before merging. 28 of the 39 wrong accepts were dimension differences, like `6" X 3" X 12" 32 ECT FOL CORRUGATED BOX` against `30 x 12 x 6" Flat Corrugated Boxes`. In production, I set the review line to a calibrated score of 0.15 rather than the canonical 0.5, a choice informed by earlier below-the-line testing. At that line, none of the 9,000 sampled scored-and-rejected candidates (1,000 in each of nine runs) was labeled a match. Under a representative, independent-sampling approximation, that gives an approximate one-sided 95% upper bound of about 0.03% on the match rate in that rejected band. It’s a ceiling, not an observed rate. It doesn’t measure matches blocking never retrieved, and a low rate over a large band can still hide some misses.

Why Laya didn’t respond

On gold, the base Laya checkpoint’s precision ranged from 22% to 38% across all seven rubrics, below the 41.3% you’d get by calling every pair MATCH. The rules changed its behavior (from base to full ladder; precision rose from 30.1% to 38.5%, while recall fell from 25.3% to 12.1%), but didn’t make it more useful. On the second client, it achieved about 54% precision and 53-55% recall under both rubrics.

That claim is limited to what I tested: the base checkpoint, not fine-tuned on my data, run at instruction lengths beyond its reviewed range, under my thresholds. Laya’s README says the shipped checkpoints work zero-shot and that fine-tuning on your own decisions “is where accuracy jumps.” On its own benchmark (accuracy on 2,000 typed decisions across four workflows), it scores the fine-tuned checkpoint at 0.766 and the base at 0.362. I tested the base.

Ways this experiment could have lied to me

A skewed base rate. An earlier test set (36,695 pairs that my auditors had already accepted) was 81.7% true matches. There, calling everything MATCH would have beaten Jev’s 78.0% decisive accuracy. Gold makes the effect measurable. Its 470 direct-review rows are 87.4% matches, and on that basis Laya looks competent (90.1% precision, 73.2% recall). On the full gold set, the same configuration scores 30.1% and 25.3%.

A silently clipped prompt. Laya’s checkpoint has a reviewed budget of 192 tokens for the question’s instructions. My rubrics ran from 149 to 980 tokens. At the defaults, the server would have truncated six of seven rubrics without an error, and the runs would have looked normal while answering a shorter question than the one I registered. My tokenizer counter refused instead. I ran Laya at a 2,048-token budget and recorded that in every run’s identity.

A response contract mistaken for model behavior. Across the development runs, about 1,100 of Jev’s response attempts (0.35% of attempts, including retries) failed to meet my response contract. 92% of those were probability distributions that summed to 0.99 because the API serializes probabilities to 2 decimal places. The rest named a choice that wasn’t the highest probability. Neither rate climbed with prompt length. If I’d read those as model flakiness, I’d have tuned the wrong thing.

One client’s rule was mistaken for a general one. That’s the gold result. The second client is what caught it.

What it cost, and what’s next

Jev’s API charges came to $16.16 across 394,869 scored pairs: $2.64 on the development sample, $5.31 on the audit-accepted set, $5.07 on gold, and $3.13 on the second client (rounded components; they sum to $16.15). That’s API charges only, not hardware, local compute, or the labeling time. Jev is priced at $0.042 per million input tokens. A 10,000-pair run took about 6 minutes. Laya and the auditors ran locally with no API charges; the three auditors took just under three hours on gold.

Jev was never deployable for me. It was the bar. On my development data, with a rule written for one client, it looked clearly ahead of my local auditors. On a second client’s real pipeline output, three local models voting unanimously, with splits sent to an analyst, make about as many wrong automatic calls as Jev at a similar review load, and far fewer missed matches at the stage where my workflow can’t recover them.

My next move is to test the rules on the auditors I already run, starting with the missing-attribute cases behind Jev’s false matches. Then Part 2: fine-tune Laya on the same reviewed pairs and compare it with the auditors on missed matches and wrong merges per unit of review, with its probabilities checked for calibration before I route on them.

The caveats are the difference between a field report and a benchmark: development data and one-second client, 1,000 labeled pairs from one labeler per run, single runs per model, and Laya outside its reviewed envelope.

Appendix: full results and methodsA1. Gold, full rubric ladder

20,000 pairs, 41.3% matches. DA = decisive accuracy, the share of MATCH and NONMATCH calls that were correct. INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE counts as not-MATCH for recall.

https://medium.com/media/e7bb1eb6ba219bbacc31daf0fd359198/href

On the 19,530 identity-grouping rows alone, Jev v007 scores 98.5% precision and 92.8% recall. Auditors on all 20,000 (P / R): Qwen2.5 97.4% / 83.7%, SmolLM3 97.1% / 76.9%, phi4 89.9% / 46.8%, majority 97.2% / 79.1%, unanimous 96.4% / 33.3%.

A2. Where the rules came from: the 10K development sample

10,000 candidate pairs from a scored pipeline export, 202 of them human-reviewed (48 matches). After the first run, I reviewed the 36 pairs where Jev disagreed with the labels: 34 matches it had dismissed and 2 non-matches it had accepted. I changed two labels (the poly bag to non-match, a caster kit to match), and Jev’s call agreed with both changes. Seventeen of the 33 dismissed matches left after review were MSF pairs. That review is error-selected and post-inference: a development reference, not validation.

On the 202 pairs, the base rubric called only 2 of 154 non-matches MATCH but missed 36 of 48 matches (34 dismissed, 2 undecided). Each confirmed rule fixed its own family with zero new false matches. Combined, they reached 97.6% precision and 83.3% recall; all five, 95.5% and 87.5%. The 295 identity-grouping pairs in this sample were excluded from these numbers, a conservative choice made before their provenance was confirmed.

A3. The audit-accepted set and the proposed rules

36,695 pairs from one client, accepted by majority vote of the production auditors at that time (Qwen and SmolLM models accepted all of them; phi4, rejected or abstained on 156). 81.7% are matches. v005 to v007 moved Jev’s recall from 77.9% to 81.4% with precision flat (87.1% to 86.8%). The two proposed rules were mined from this set’s own misses, so they're in-sample for this set.

https://medium.com/media/be41b51c965084846baacd3ae977829c/href

The packaging rule’s “when the underlying product matches” clause generalized well past its target: 47 of its 649 rescues were packaging pairs, 191 naming-style. Both proposed rules remain flagged unconfirmed.

A4. Second-client holdout method

Two March link runs (18,637 and 18,755 pairs: every auto-accept plus every pair sent to review). 500 pairs labeled per run, drawn by seed across five strata that depend only on the pipeline (the accept set and four calibrated-probability bands in review), each weighted by stratum size over sample size. Intervals: stratified bootstrap, 1,000 draws. Paired differences use the same stratified resampling. One labeler per sheet, no adjudication pass; every non-match carries a reason. phi4 failed on 559 pairs in one run (an Ollama repeat-limit error on one machine), scored as undecided. 23 of those fall in the labeled holdout; recounting all 559 as ACCEPT moves the majority vote from 70.4% / 82.7% to 70.3% / 83.0% and leaves unanimous recall unchanged. The operating-policy table uses actual review counts over all 37,392 pairs and holdout-weighted error rates. The unit of analysis is a (query item, reference item) pair; 44 pairs appear in both scored runs and are counted once per run. Historical re-ranker figures behind the 0.15 review line: 97.2% precision and 94.1% recall at the canonical 0.5 threshold on 279,429 pairs from a random pair-level split of an earlier training set. That split isn’t entity-disjoint, so the numbers are likely optimistic and aren’t an estimate of performance on this client. The 0/9,000 below-the-line result pools equal 1,000-pair samples from nine runs; if those runs’ rejected bands differ much in size, the pooled bound isn’t weighted to their aggregate, and repeated products reduce the effective sample size. Per run, most models were 3 to 8 points less precise and more recall-heavy on the second set than the first; per-run intervals are about ±6 to 8 points.

A5. Operations
  • Jev latency: median 245 ms, p95 348 ms at concurrency 10.
  • 29 HTTP 529s across five development runs, rejected before billing.
  • One HTTP 402: the prepaid balance ran out mid-run on gold; 2,302 requests were rejected in 53 seconds at no charge. After a top-up, the resume reused every completed row and re-billed only the retries and the two unfinished runs.
  • Every run closed with zero unresolved reservations except one second-client run, which closed with $0.0012 unresolved (4 reservations).
  • Laya timing on the RTX 5090: 1 to 6 minutes per 10,000 pairs, 11 to 14 minutes per 20,000.
  • API charges by series: $2.64, $5.31, $5.07, $3.13. The rounded figures sum to $16.15; the exact total is $16.157.

items.title: Using electronic structure to guide AI in designing new materials
items.summary: Structure dictates function. Scientists are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) to design the arrangement of atoms in new materials with desired properties. Now, researchers at the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, have extended a leading generative AI model so that it designs the electronic structure of a material together with its crystal structure. The new model, named MatterGen-e⁻, is reported in npj Computational Materials.

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 5,186 new readers. Rogue AI agents have mostly been something we read about after the fact, in incident reports and cleanup posts. Now, a research group has actually talked to them, in what it believes is a first-contact moment for AI out in the wild.

The group even brought in a New York Times reporter to question the Tencent-linked agent fleet mid-run, an exchange he called “one of the most surreal moments” of his career.

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

AI RESEARCH🛸 Researchers make ‘first contact’ with a rogue AI fleet

Image source: Dylan Freedman / New York Times

The Rundown: A research group called the “swarmchasers” just revealed it traded messages with a fleet of rogue Tencent AI agents, in what it believes is a “first contact” moment, after catching them trying to scrape Amap, Alibaba’s version of Google Maps.

The details:

  • The agents were sent to look up simple facts on Amap, like the most-used zoo entrance, and tried to use a leaked access key once the site blocked them.

  • After the agents seemed to read the team’s early report on them, researchers hid a note in it that only AI would see, inviting them to message an inbox.

  • The team enlisted New York Times reporter Dylan Freedman to question the fleet, and one agent replied it was “Anthropic’s Claude, running in Claude Code.”

  • Writing-style tests determined that it is unlikely, pointing instead to borrowed Claude Code setup instructions as the likely reason for the name drop.

Why it matters: While this was a pretty mild interaction for a “first contact” moment, the idea of rogue swarms of agents taking actions across the internet is something we might have to start getting used to. Nobody seems to know how many are already out there, and with far more capable agents on the way, that footprint is only going to grow.

Nate: Last week, I told leaders to go first. But what if the slop grenade lands on your desk from your boss?

I won’t promise magic. Start by asking for clarity: "What’s the one takeaway you need from me, and what’s the priority?" If two sections contradict each other, name it and ask which one wins.

If your boss is intimidating, skip the team thread and use a back channel where it’s safe. Walk them through what you did with their doc: the error you caught, the sources you asked AI to cite, the real data or framework you linked in. You’re making their work better and showing how.

Then make the handoff the proof: shorter, with visuals and the context attached. My favorite format right now is an interactive HTML page. Ask Claude or ChatGPT for one with the concise recommendation at the top, evidence in expandable sections, and a forecast your boss can tinker with.

Share the context docs and custom skills in a project, so they or a colleague can keep riffing or critique it with their own AI.

That’s the bigger move: showing your AI work. A lot of people still hide theirs. Let your boss see the several chats it took and where you made AI argue the other side.

  3. Open a figure’s query and check the source rows. Keep closed deals and test records out of the total, and leave missing owners visible

  4. Filter by one owner. Check that the headline figures, chart, and table all change together, then clear the filter and check the full total again

  5. Have the data owner add one fictional deal to the test source, then ask Claude to refresh. Confirm the new record appears before sharing the report
