items.title: Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind
items.summary: Have you ever thought about what makes you you ? Science assures us it has everything to do with the three-pound organ between our ears, with its billions of neurons and trillions of delicate connections. But it’s a lot trickier to explain why we have a sense of self-awareness or to pin down precisely where that first memory of Mommy actually resides. As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you. To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are working on ways to keep your brain going—even beyond death. Let’s call them the “mind savers.” They’re exploring everything from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones to uploading our memories to the cloud. Here, we look at six possible paths for keeping your mind going, how feasible they’d be, and what benefits the ­present-day research might bring—even if cognitive immortality doesn’t pan out. EDDIE GUY Head transplant White’s experiments have been a source of grim fascination ever since. But to a few neuroscientists they’re inspiration, suggesting that one day a human head transplant—or, as some call it, a body transplant—could succeed. The idea’s main proponent is Sergio Canavero, a controversial Italian surgeon who, 10 years ago, even claimed he’d found a volunteer in Valery Spiridinov, a computer programmer suffering from a degenerative muscle disease. Spiridinov initially agreed to have his head transferred to the body of a brain-dead donor in China, but he later bowed out of the plan and instead got married. And that might be just as well. Critics say the procedure would be more like murder than medicine. Or, best-case scenario: Volunteers would be left paralyzed and in need of a ventilator for life. Canavero says that’s not necessarily true. He claims people’s views on the operation will change once they accept that reconnecting severed spinal cords is already possible. He pointed MIT Technology Review to a research article from this past summer that he coauthored with surgeons at Moscow’s Sklifosovsky Research and Clinical Institute for Emergency Medicine. The team cut through the spinal cords of three pigs at a point midway along their backs and then tested whether the severed nerve bodies could be fused back together using a surgical sealant. According to that paper, which appeared in the journal PLOS One , all the pigs regained the ability to stand and even walk unsteadily. Does that mean a head could be attached to a new body and then actually control it? Mainstream researchers aren’t convinced. Grégoire Courtine, a spinal rehabilitation specialist at the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne in Switzerland, says he’s been following Canavero’s claims “with little respect” and thinks that we should “pay zero attention.” “There is no technology … capable of such a crazy idea,” Courtine wrote in an email. Mindclones Just 12 years after the book came out, artificial-intelligence technology has already brought some of her predictions to “life,” so to speak. Services such as StoryFile, Afterlife AI, and Synthesia allow users to upload their personal information and likeness in order to produce either conversational bots that share their memories or video talking heads that sound (and look) exactly like them. Influencers now let their “AI clones” do their work on TikTok, and some people are even building avatars of their aging parents in order to preserve their personalities. While this mimicry can produce comical results, unhealthy attachments, or uncanny vibes, the increasing realism of generative AI invites people to emotionally accept the avatars as real beings. That was the case when Rothblatt appeared as a digital avatar during a 2025 event held by the UCLA Department of Communication called “The Bridge to Humanizing AI.” Her copy, named Marvatar, was projected on a screen, led the discussions, and talked with the meatspace Rothblatt as an equal, at one point saying, “The dance isn’t about who leads, but how we move together.” According to the university, attendees were “visibly moved” and wept “with wonder” at Rothblatt’s vision of digital equality. What’s still missing from Rothblatt’s mindclone prediction is evidence that these avatars have—or ever will have—any kind of true self-awareness. (We asked ChatGPT if it’s conscious, and it answered , “Probably not.”) But all that remains a gray zone. Neuroscientists don’t have a clear definition of consciousness, much less a diagnostic test they could apply to an avatar. Instead, what if the final determination is in the eye of the beholder? Your digital clone might not be you. But at some point it might be good enough for me. Brain in a jar So, campy sci-fi film lovers that we are, it got our attention last year when a company called Bexorg started showing journalists actual human brains in vats, which it has been acquiring from organ donors soon after death and then “rebooting” by infusing them with oxygen-rich artificial blood. The company claims these “physiologically intact human brains” will be more useful than animals for drug testing and safer than trying experiments on living volunteers. Add an Alzheimer’s compound to one of these disembodied brains and researchers can then measure exactly what the drug does inside the organ. Bexorg’s CEO, Zvonimir Vrselja, is “sure” that some people would like to restore consciousness to out-of-body brains, but he’s tried to douse such speculation. While they are metabolically active, the company says, the brains have lost all coordinated electrical activity. That means they aren’t conscious—although, just to make sure, the neuroscientists running the experiments add the strong anesthetic propofol to the tissues. What’s more, right now a brain can be kept “alive” outside the body for only about 24 hours. That wouldn’t be much of a second life. Still, efforts are underway to improve the life-support systems. Bexorg says it hopes to eventually keep its brains going for two weeks. EDDIE GUY Gradual brain replacement On paper, the goal is to manufacture tissue to graft into the brains of stroke victims, reversing damage and restoring function. Less officially, the project’s existence is a surprise coup for an extreme plan to defeat aging advanced by Jean Hébert, the neuroscientist leading the program, who argued in his 2020 book, Replacing Aging , that we can live longer by replacing our aging brain cells with young ones. We don’t want to lose our identities. That’s why—according to Hébert—it would have to happen gradually, in small chunks, so our brains would have time to adapt to the new tissue. Scientists who applied for the program say Hébert insisted on a very specific technological approach. While most researchers engineer individual cell types, ARPA-H asked for complex chunks of young, functional cortex—more or less like what you’d find in a developing fetus. “He wanted to create essentially an embryonic form of cortex that he thought you could somehow graft into an adult brain,” says Marius Wernig, a Stanford University stem-cell researcher who applied. Skeptics say it’s unknown whether replacement brain chunks will ever properly function as part of your brain—say, by taking over memories. What’s more, it’s still unclear how to manufacture youthful cortex, or what ARPA-H calls “neocortical precursor tissue,” in the lab. One idea is to employ the latest advances in brain organoids. Imagine, if you will, a human cortex grown in a lab dish without a body. We know that the agency has an aggressive timeline: Over the course of five years, it wants researchers to lay the foundation for the first human tests of replacement cortex. The aim, it says, is to “take the ‘permanent’ out of brain damage.” And maybe out of old age, too. Brain upload Scientists are already mapping this wiring in simpler animals. Two years ago, Seung took part in analyzing a fly brain that had been cut into paper-thin sheets and imaged with an electron microscope. Then he and his colleagues used image-analysis software to trace 139,255 neurons and about 55 million synapses. The fly map could lead to energy-efficient software that computes the way real brains do, Seung says. Others believe the ultimate outcome of “connectomics” research will be what’s called “whole-brain emulation,” or sometimes just “uploading.” It’s the idea, popular in some quarters of Silicon Valley, that a simulation created from a sliced-up brain could become so detailed that it would reproduce not only a generic intelligence but a particular one, like yours—complete with memories and opinions, and able to live again in a data server somewhere. Setting aside the question of whether a simulation would really be you, everyone agrees that this technology isn’t coming in time for those of us alive today. A survey of 312 neuroscientists, published in 2025 in PLOS One , estimated that human whole-brain emulation wouldn’t happen before 2125. That long and unpredictable tech horizon helps explain why two US companies, Nectome and Sparks Brain Preservation, are offering to preserve human brains (or bodies) today by infusing them with the same potent chemicals used to “fix” the brains of fruit flies for connectome mapping. The idea: If the fine details of a brain’s structure can be preserved, one day in the far future it might be reanimated. But there’s a startling twist. Because brain tissue needs to be preserved quickly after a person’s death, both companies say they want to work with people taking advantage of medical aid in dying, now legal in 13 states and Washington, DC. In that procedure, doctors supply a lethal dose of drugs, but it’s the patient—someone with a terminal prognosis—who pushes the plunger. For a fee, the companies say, they can have a preservation team at the ready. So far, the service is not popular. The companies each say they are still awaiting their first aid-in-dying customer. EDDIE GUY Synthetic neocortex That’s right: an extra brain. Recently, we’ve seen inklings of how this might come to pass. In 2024, Science Corporation, in California, unveiled a “biohybrid” brain-computer interface featuring nerve cells grown on a digital chip. Placed on an animal’s brain, these cells sent out long, thin axons that integrated with the animal’s own neurons. The result: two-way communication from computer to brain, in the brain’s language. The technology could permit new types of medicine, like an implant that directs brain cells to produce dopamine and thereby treat Parkinson’s. But Max Hodak, the company’s CEO, says it also might count as a new brain part, which he likens to a “big, externalized cranial nerve.” Such a device could serve as the connector to Kurzweil’s computerized neocortex in the cloud, giving a living person unlimited extra processing power. Still other entrepreneurs believe if you kept adding biohybrid components to a brain, eventually you could morph it into an immortal machine. Daniel Burger, founder of the venture-­funded stealth startup Eightsix Science (its name refers to the 86 billion neurons in a human brain), says this dream could require mixing several of the brain-saving techniques on this list. He thinks we might need brains in vats, affording neuro-­engineers easy access, so they can gradually replace brain parts with biohybrid neural grafts. The ultimate goal is to migrate your mind into your extra, engineered brain, without ever breaking the continuity of self. “It’s not the typical ‘scan, store, simulate,’” says Burger. “I don’t think simulations will be conscious.” He adds, “We’re saying it’s going to be way more complicated, and it’s probably going to look like gradual brain replacement into a hardware brain.” Once your mind is hardware, you won’t need a biological body. Instead, you could take up residence in a data center somewhere and perhaps even have backups distributed around the globe. “From that point on,” Burger acknowledges, “stuff becomes really crazy.”

items.title: I Built an AI to Judge AI Projects — Here’s What It Looks For
items.summary: A GitHub repository can say “Transformer,” “RAG,” or “Computer Vision” in the README. That does not tell you whether the work is technically deep, original, reproducible, or even really yours. I built AI-Atlas to look past the labels and inspect the evidence inside the code. The name of the “tool” There is a surprisingly difficult question hiding behind almost every technical portfolio: how good is this project, actually? Not how polished the README looks, how many stars it received, whether the repository name contains LLM , Agent , or Computer Vision , or whether its author wrote AI Engineer on LinkedIn. I mean something more specific: what does the implementation actually demonstrate? Imagine two repositories: The first fine-tunes a pretrained Transformer using an existing training script, changes a few hyperparameters, reports accuracy, and stops there. The second modifies the attention mechanism , implements the change manually, compares against several baselines, documents why the modification exists, stores reproducible experiment configurations, and includes an ablation showing whether the idea actually helped. There are differences… Both are legitimately Transformer projects. But they are not remotely the same piece of work. That problem became one of the most interesting parts of building AI-Atlas , the platform I have been developing to turn public GitHub work into an explainable map of demonstrated AI skills. AI-Atlas currently maps projects across Machine Learning, Computer Vision, Data Science, NLP & LLMs, AI Agents, and MLOps , but the domain classification itself is only the beginning. Once you decide to evaluate the work itself, you inherit a much harder problem: defining what good AI work actually means, distinguishing implementation from imported functionality, separating originality from complexity, and producing a judgment that is specific enough for the developer to inspect and disagree with. That last part became especially important to me. If an AI is going to judge someone’s work, “the model said so” is not a good enough explanation. A Project Is More Than Its Topic AI-Atlas separates public AI work into six evidence-backed domains rather than treating every repository as the same kind of project. A repository’s subject tells us surprisingly little about its quality. Take something as familiar as a ResNet implementation . One developer might import a pretrained architecture from torchvision , replace its classification head, fine-tune it on a dataset, and produce a perfectly functional project. Another might implement residual blocks independently, reproduce several ResNet variants , compare initialization strategies, build a reusable training pipeline, investigate how shortcut connections affect optimization, and document every experiment. Both repositories belong under Computer Vision. Their topic is nearly identical. The evidence of technical ability is not. Computer Vision — Source: DaaS Labs That is why AI-Atlas does not evaluate a project with one vague question like “Is this impressive?” Each relevant repository is examined across seven dimensions: Technical Depth, Conceptual Difficulty, Originality/Modification, Completeness, Practical/Research Usefulness, Documentation & Educational Value, and Engineering & Reproducibility. Those dimensions intentionally measure different things. A project can attempt a difficult idea but remain unfinished. It can be exceptionally well engineered without containing an original research contribution. A from-scratch educational implementation might be less novel than a new architecture , while still demonstrating considerably more understanding than a thin wrapper around an API. Even a sophisticated experiment becomes harder to trust if there is no reliable way to determine what configuration produced its result. Suppose AI-Atlas encounters an illustrative repository called vit-from-scratch . It finds attention.py , patch_embedding.py , a complete training loop, configuration files, experiment outputs, and a detailed architecture explanation . Now imagine another repository with the same title containing a short notebook that instantiates an existing Vision Transformer implementation and fine-tunes it . Both contain valid AI work, but the first exposes substantially more evidence about the developer's understanding of the architecture, training process, experimental decisions, and engineering choices. This is the distinction I wanted the evaluator to learn to make. The interesting question is not: “Does this repository contain a Transformer?” It is: “What did the developer actually do with the Transformer?” A Score Without Evidence Is Just Another Opinion AI-Atlas traces conclusions back toward implementation, training, and evaluation evidence rather than relying only on repository descriptions. This was probably the most important design constraint in the entire system. Imagine an automated evaluator returning Project Merit: 82 Why 82? Why not 74 or even another value??? Which part of the repository raised the score? Which missing component prevented it from reaching 90? If the explanation is simply “a language model analyzed the repository” , the number is almost meaningless . We would have replaced one shallow signal with another, except the new one looks more authoritative. AI-Atlas therefore separates interpretation from scoring . The evaluator reads the relevant implementation and returns judgments across the rubric together with its reasoning and supporting repository evidence. AI-Atlas then computes Project Merit through versioned scoring rules rather than allowing the language model to invent the final number directly. Conceptually, the process is much closer to this: The six-step path from public repository to evidence-grounded Project Merit score. That separation sounds subtle, but it matters. If I later decide that Technical Depth should contribute differently to Project Merit , that is a scoring-methodology change. If the evaluator incorrectly interprets a custom optimizer as ordinary library usage, that is an evidence-evaluation problem. Those are fundamentally different failure modes , and keeping them separate makes the system much easier to debug and criticize. The same principle applies to the public methodology. AI-Atlas exposes how repositories are discovered, understood, mapped, and explained, and the live site explicitly describes the central rule as “implementation, not labels,” “depth over repetition,” and “claims back to files.” This also means a high-level score is not intended to be the final destination. The interesting path is in the opposite direction: from the profile score to the domain, from the domain to the project, from the project to the rubric judgment, and eventually back toward the code that caused the judgment. The score becomes useful only when you can trace it back to something real. Sometimes the Correct Evaluation Is to Exclude the Repository I even mapped karpathy’s GitHub on here ! The public Atlas compresses repository evidence into a six-domain map, while the underlying projects remain the source of that profile. One of the easiest ways to make an AI portfolio evaluator appear impressive would be to discover AI expertise everywhere. That is also one of the easiest ways to destroy its usefulness. Real GitHub profiles contain forks, abandoned experiments, personal websites, coursework, profile READMEs, utilities, duplicate repositories, API wrappers, and projects that simply have nothing to do with artificial intelligence. Treating all of them as positive evidence would make larger and noisier profiles appear stronger almost automatically. AI-Atlas therefore performs filtering before deep evaluation: Forks do not become evidence of original work. Profile repositories do not count as AI projects simply because they describe someone’s skills. Obvious non-AI repositories can be listed as excluded rather than being forced into one of the six domains. The public site summarizes this as a Discover → Understand → Map → Explain pipeline: first remove obvious noise, then inspect what was actually built, then place genuine evidence into the appropriate domains. There is also a security reason for keeping this process conservative. Repository contents are treated as untrusted data . AI-Atlas reads public code as text, but it does not clone a stranger’s project and start executing installation scripts, Dockerfiles, tests, or arbitrary shell commands. The live trust section explicitly states that code is read, never run . Only read, never run the actual code! That means the evaluator is working from inspectable evidence rather than trusting the repository to demonstrate itself through execution. Popularity is deliberately kept separate too GitHub stars can indicate adoption, and forks can tell us that a project has attracted real usage, but those numbers answer a different question from technical quality. A simple developer tool can accumulate thousands of stars, while a difficult research reproduction written by one student can receive five. AI-Atlas therefore keeps the technical rubric based on the project itself, with only a small capped adoption adjustment for projects that cross meaningful usage thresholds. This matters particularly for students and independent developers. If popularity dominates the score, the evaluator is measuring audience size rather than engineering ability. What the Evaluator Is Actually Looking For AI-Atlas evaluates several independent qualities because a technically difficult project can still be incomplete, unoriginal, or difficult to reproduce. Technical Depth asks how much meaningful implementation exists beneath the project’s headline. Using PyTorch, Hugging Face , or scikit-learn does not make a project shallow; serious engineering almost always depends on libraries. The question is whether the developer made substantial technical decisions themselves. A repository containing custom model components, data pipelines, evaluation infrastructure, training logic, checkpointing, and careful experimental code demonstrates a different level of implementation depth from a notebook that calls a ready-made pipeline. Conceptual Difficulty concerns the problem itself. items.summary_html:
A GitHub repository can say “Transformer,” “RAG,” or “Computer Vision” in the README. That does not tell you whether the work is technically deep, original, reproducible, or even really yours. I built AI-Atlas to look past the labels and inspect the evidence inside the code.The name of the “tool”
There is a surprisingly difficult question hiding behind almost every technical portfolio: how good is this project, actually?

Not how polished the README looks, how many stars it received, whether the repository name contains LLM, Agent, or Computer Vision, or whether its author wrote AI Engineer on LinkedIn. I mean something more specific: what does the implementation actually demonstrate?

Imagine two repositories:
  • The first fine-tunes a pretrained Transformer using an existing training script, changes a few hyperparameters, reports accuracy, and stops there.
  • The second modifies the attention mechanism, implements the change manually, compares against several baselines, documents why the modification exists, stores reproducible experiment configurations, and includes an ablation showing whether the idea actually helped.
There are differences…
Both are legitimately Transformer projects. But they are not remotely the same piece of work.

That problem became one of the most interesting parts of building AI-Atlas, the platform I have been developing to turn public GitHub work into an explainable map of demonstrated AI skills. AI-Atlas currently maps projects across Machine Learning, Computer Vision, Data Science, NLP & LLMs, AI Agents, and MLOps, but the domain classification itself is only the beginning.

Once you decide to evaluate the work itself, you inherit a much harder problem: defining what good AI work actually means, distinguishing implementation from imported functionality, separating originality from complexity, and producing a judgment that is specific enough for the developer to inspect and disagree with.

That last part became especially important to me.

If an AI is going to judge someone’s work, “the model said so” is not a good enough explanation.
A Project Is More Than Its TopicAI-Atlas separates public AI work into six evidence-backed domains rather than treating every repository as the same kind of project.

A repository’s subject tells us surprisingly little about its quality. Take something as familiar as a ResNet implementation. One developer might import a pretrained architecture from torchvision, replace its classification head, fine-tune it on a dataset, and produce a perfectly functional project.

Another might implement residual blocks independently, reproduce several ResNet variants, compare initialization strategies, build a reusable training pipeline, investigate how shortcut connections affect optimization, and document every experiment.

Both repositories belong under Computer Vision. Their topic is nearly identical. The evidence of technical ability is not.

Computer Vision — Source: DaaS Labs

That is why AI-Atlas does not evaluate a project with one vague question like “Is this impressive?”

Each relevant repository is examined across seven dimensions: Technical Depth, Conceptual Difficulty, Originality/Modification, Completeness, Practical/Research Usefulness, Documentation & Educational Value, and Engineering & Reproducibility.

Those dimensions intentionally measure different things. A project can attempt a difficult idea but remain unfinished. It can be exceptionally well engineered without containing an original research contribution.

A from-scratch educational implementation might be less novel than a new architecture, while still demonstrating considerably more understanding than a thin wrapper around an API. Even a sophisticated experiment becomes harder to trust if there is no reliable way to determine what configuration produced its result.

Suppose AI-Atlas encounters an illustrative repository called vit-from-scratch.
  • It finds attention.py, patch_embedding.py, a complete training loop, configuration files, experiment outputs, and a detailed architecture explanation.

Now imagine another repository with the same title containing a short notebook that instantiates an existing Vision Transformer implementation and fine-tunes it.

Both contain valid AI work, but the first exposes substantially more evidence about the developer's understanding of the architecture, training process, experimental decisions, and engineering choices.

This is the distinction I wanted the evaluator to learn to make.

The interesting question is not:
  • “Does this repository contain a Transformer?”
It is:
  • “What did the developer actually do with the Transformer?”
A Score Without Evidence Is Just Another OpinionAI-Atlas traces conclusions back toward implementation, training, and evaluation evidence rather than relying only on repository descriptions.

This was probably the most important design constraint in the entire system.

Imagine an automated evaluator returning Project Merit: 82
  • Why 82? Why not 74 or even another value???
  • Which part of the repository raised the score?
  • Which missing component prevented it from reaching 90?

If the explanation is simply “a language model analyzed the repository”, the number is almost meaningless. We would have replaced one shallow signal with another, except the new one looks more authoritative.

AI-Atlas therefore separates interpretation from scoring. The evaluator reads the relevant implementation and returns judgments across the rubric together with its reasoning and supporting repository evidence. AI-Atlas then computes Project Merit through versioned scoring rules rather than allowing the language model to invent the final number directly.

Conceptually, the process is much closer to this:The six-step path from public repository to evidence-grounded Project Merit score.

That separation sounds subtle, but it matters.

If I later decide that Technical Depth should contribute differently to Project Merit, that is a scoring-methodology change.

If the evaluator incorrectly interprets a custom optimizer as ordinary library usage, that is an evidence-evaluation problem. Those are fundamentally different failure modes, and keeping them separate makes the system much easier to debug and criticize.

The same principle applies to the public methodology. AI-Atlas exposes how repositories are discovered, understood, mapped, and explained, and the live site explicitly describes the central rule as “implementation, not labels,” “depth over repetition,” and “claims back to files.”

This also means a high-level score is not intended to be the final destination. The interesting path is in the opposite direction: from the profile score to the domain, from the domain to the project, from the project to the rubric judgment, and eventually back toward the code that caused the judgment.

The score becomes useful only when you can trace it back to something real.
Sometimes the Correct Evaluation Is to Exclude the RepositoryI even mapped karpathy’s GitHub on here! The public Atlas compresses repository evidence into a six-domain map, while the underlying projects remain the source of that profile.
One of the easiest ways to make an AI portfolio evaluator appear impressive would be to discover AI expertise everywhere. That is also one of the easiest ways to destroy its usefulness.

Real GitHub profiles contain forks, abandoned experiments, personal websites, coursework, profile READMEs, utilities, duplicate repositories, API wrappers, and projects that simply have nothing to do with artificial intelligence. Treating all of them as positive evidence would make larger and noisier profiles appear stronger almost automatically.

AI-Atlas therefore performs filtering before deep evaluation:
  • Forks do not become evidence of original work.
  • Profile repositories do not count as AI projects simply because they describe someone’s skills.
  • Obvious non-AI repositories can be listed as excluded rather than being forced into one of the six domains.
The public site summarizes this as a Discover → Understand → Map → Explain pipeline: first remove obvious noise, then inspect what was actually built, then place genuine evidence into the appropriate domains.

There is also a security reason for keeping this process conservative. Repository contents are treated as untrusted data. AI-Atlas reads public code as text, but it does not clone a stranger’s project and start executing installation scripts, Dockerfiles, tests, or arbitrary shell commands. The live trust section explicitly states that code is read, never run.

Only read, never run the actual code!

That means the evaluator is working from inspectable evidence rather than trusting the repository to demonstrate itself through execution.

Popularity is deliberately kept separate too

GitHub stars can indicate adoption, and forks can tell us that a project has attracted real usage, but those numbers answer a different question from technical quality.

A simple developer tool can accumulate thousands of stars, while a difficult research reproduction written by one student can receive five.

AI-Atlas therefore keeps the technical rubric based on the project itself, with only a small capped adoption adjustment for projects that cross meaningful usage thresholds.

This matters particularly for students and independent developers. If popularity dominates the score, the evaluator is measuring audience size rather than engineering ability.

Technical Depth asks how much meaningful implementation exists beneath the project’s headline.

Using PyTorch, Hugging Face, or scikit-learn does not make a project shallow; serious engineering almost always depends on libraries.

The question is whether the developer made substantial technical decisions themselves. A repository containing custom model components, data pipelines, evaluation infrastructure, training logic, checkpointing, and careful experimental code demonstrates a different level of implementation depth from a notebook that calls a ready-made pipeline.

Conceptual Difficulty concerns the problem itself.

At the same time, complexity should not become a reward by itself. A difficult idea implemented incompletely should not receive full credit merely because the README contains advanced terminology.

Originality does not require producing a publishable paper. A careful reproduction can still be valuable. But reproducing and modifying demonstrate different abilities, so the evaluator should distinguish them.

A model implementation with no training entry point, no evaluation, and no instructions may demonstrate technical understanding, but it is still less complete than a repository where the components form an end-to-end experiment.

Practical/Research Usefulness asks whether the project accomplishes something meaningful.

Sometimes usefulness means supporting a real application. Sometimes it means testing a research hypothesis or making an important paper easier to understand. I deliberately do not equate usefulness with commercial value.

Why was this architecture chosen? Which assumptions were made? What failed? How are the reported results reproduced? Good documentation does not substitute for technical depth, but it makes technical depth inspectable.

Finally, Engineering & Reproducibility asks whether somebody else can reasonably verify or continue the work.

Configuration files, clear dependencies, random seeds, tests, evaluation scripts, dataset instructions, checkpoint conventions, and stored experiment settings all make a repository considerably stronger.

The seven dimensions AI-Atlas uses to reconstruct what an AI repository actually demonstrates

Not every project requires every item, but their presence communicates something important: the developer thought beyond making the code work once on their own machine.

That is ultimately what the evaluator is trying to reconstruct. Not a list of technologies, but the shape of the engineering demonstrated through their use.

Once I had a scoring system, I became increasingly interested in a different question.

Suppose the evaluator decides that a project is technically strong but its Engineering & Reproducibility is considerably weaker than the rest. What should the developer actually do with that information?

The least useful answer would be “raise the score.” That turns the entire system into a game. A much better question is: what real change to the repository would make the project better?

That is the idea behind the owner-only Start here recommendation. It does not simply select the repository with the lowest score.

“Start here“ recommendation

A project sitting at 40 because it is fundamentally small may have less useful growth potential than an already serious project whose experiments are difficult to reproduce.

From there, the optional roadmap can turn that weakness into 3–5 concrete improvements ranked by impact. Those improvements can be exported as a checklist or opened as GitHub issues, which turns the evaluation into actual repository work rather than another dashboard metric.

The Merit Predictor explores the same idea from a narrower direction.

The Merit Predictor

Instead of asking “How do I improve this entire project?”, you can choose one rubric dimension and ask what a realistic improvement might look like. The system can estimate a target, describe the work required, and show the resulting hypothetical Project Merit.

That final word is important.

A prediction does not change the real score. A generated roadmap does not change the real score either. Only modifying the project and rescanning new evidence can change what AI-Atlas says the repository demonstrates.

At that point, the evaluator becomes less like a ranking machine and more like a feedback loop between what you think you built and what your public repository can actually prove.

AI evaluation sounds simple until you actually try to define what should be evaluated.

A repository contains code, but code alone does not immediately tell us whether the project is difficult, original, complete, reproducible, or useful. Those judgments require interpretation. And the moment AI begins interpreting somebody’s work, I think the standard should become more transparent, not less.

That is the principle I am trying to preserve with AI-Atlas. The score should never be the end of the explanation.

Ideally, you should be able to travel from the overall Atlas score to a domain, from that domain to the projects that contributed to it, from the project to an individual rubric judgment, from the judgment to its reasoning, and eventually toward the files that caused the evaluator to reach that conclusion.

items.title: AI is writing patches, how much should we trust them?
items.summary: As AI-powered cyber attacks soar, CISOs have moved beyond using AI models to identify security vulnerabilities to deploying AI-generated patches. But those patches can create a whole new class of headaches. Research from 1Password’s Off-by-1 Labs published in August found more than half of LLM-written patches either failed to fix the issue or added a new one as well. “Many reports are saying that this year we'll get to about 66,000 reported vulnerabilities that we have to be concerned with,” IBM Enterprise Security Exec Jamie Thomas told The Stack in a recent interview. “Now it's not about finding the vulnerabilities - the remediation is really the difficult part.” The issue only seems to set to increase, in the short term at least, with Microsoft warning of a growing list of patches in each of its Patch Tuesday releases, and publishing more CVEs for October than it published in the entirety of 2025. Security defenders have increased their use of AI tools to address the gap between vulnerability discovery and their ability to patch them, with OpenAI launching a “ Patch the Planet ” initiative in June to supply AI tools for remediating vulnerabilities in open source projects. Notably, Google has also used its CodeMender AI agent for patching internally since October 2025. “CodeMender utilizes Agent Platform capabilities and Gemini models to find vulnerabilities in code, write fixes, and securely test them, giving developers final approval and control,” DeepMind’s Head of Gemini Security Raluca Ada Popa told The Stack .

items.summary_html:
TypeSafe AI has released Jev 1.14, a new version of its System One decision model. It is live now under the jev-preview alias. It adds 3 experimental ‘danger zone’ features: images, a box type and longer context. For developers, Jev 1.14 pushes a typed decision model toward vision tasks like inspection and localization. TypeSafe shares a note that none of the 3 features are ready for production yet.

TL;DR: Jev 1.14
  • Size: Parameters not disclosed. Context is 64k tokens per request and 32k per question by default, or 262k with an opt-in header.
  • Runs on: TypeSafe’s hosted API only (POST /v1/systemone). No open weights. Hardware and quantized variants not disclosed.
  • Performance: Small gains everywhere, largest in multilingual support (TypeSafe’s claim, no public scores).
  • Best: In TypeSafe’s Box test, 4 edge-check questions caught 30 of 36 cut-off crops.
  • Worst: Images and Box are not production-ready, and Box has no “not found” answer.
What is Jev 1.14?

Jev is a System One model from TypeSafe AI that returns typed decisions instead of generated text. You send a state along with typed questions: Choice, Score or Noul. Jev answers each with a typed value, probabilities and a confidence score. TypeSafe trains it with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD).

The new version, jev-1.14.0, brings small, subtle improvements to almost everything, according to the release post. TypeSafe expects the largest gain in multilingual support.

How does image input work in Jev?

Images are composable. Each image is listed once in a top-level assets map under a reference string. You then place that reference anywhere in state, instructions or criteria. The API swaps each reference for the image before the model reads it.

TypeSafe says jev-1.13.0 was multimodal all along. Per the Images docs, both Jev 1.13 and Jev 1.14 now accept images. Each request needs the header TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true.

Key image limits:

  • PNG or JPEG still images only, up to 16 MiB per file
  • 256 to 1568 pixels per side
  • 32 MiB per request body
  • Images bill as input tokens at the normal price, with no separate charge

TypeSafe warns that all models, Jev included, perform worse on images than on pure text. It recommends the simplest possible questions.

What is the new Box type?

Box is a new question type that returns 1 bounding box per question. The answer gives top, bottom, left and right edges as fractions from 0 to 1. It also returns a confidence score. Box needs jev-1.14.0 or jev-preview, plus the images header.

Box always returns a box. A question about an absent object still returns 4 edges. TypeSafe suggests pairing it with a Noul question that checks whether the target exists.

TypeSafe also shared a small test on 36 painting crops, each cutting off part of the target. 4 per-edge Noul questions caught 30 cuts. A single “is all of it inside” question caught 26. Drawing the box as an outline and asking about it caught 20.

How long is Jev’s context window now?

By default, both models keep 64k tokens per request and 32k per question. Sending TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true raises both limits to 262k tokens, per the Models docs. TypeSafe states that Jev always supported longer context internally. It capped context on purpose because Jev, like all models, is less reliable on long inputs. The dev team still recommends short contexts.

What do the benchmarks show?

TypeSafe published internal intelligence charts in the release post. They compare Jev only against open-weight models. The post does not include a numeric score table. TypeSafe says the measurement is likely biased toward its own models. It tells developers to favor their own evals.

&&

Pricing, availability and migration

Pricing is unchanged at $42 per billion input tokens, or $0.042 per million. Output tokens are free, per the Models docs.

The rollout plan from the release post:

  • jev-preview points to jev-1.14.0 now.
  • jev-latest moves to jev-1.14.0 in a week.
  • jev-1.13.0 stays available, with 60 days notice before deprecation.
  • jev-1.14.0 will get 30 days notice before its own deprecation.
How does Jev 1.14 compare? FeatureJev 1.14Jev 1.13Gemini 3.5 Flash-LiteModel IDjev-1.14.0jev-1.13.0gemini-3.5-flash-liteModel typeTyped decision modelTyped decision modelGeneral LLMParametersNot disclosedNot disclosedNot disclosedDefault context64k per request / 32k per question64k per request / 32k per question1,048,576 input tokensLong context262k (opt-in header)262k (opt-in header)Not applicableImage inputYes, experimental headerYes, experimental headerYes (text, images, video, audio, PDF)Bounding boxesNative box type, edges 0 to 1NoPrompted JSON box_2d, scaled 0 to 1000 (docs)OutputTyped answers with confidenceTyped answers with confidenceText, up to 65,536 tokensInput price (per 1M tokens)$0.042$0.042$0.30Output price (per 1M tokens)FreeFree$2.50StatusPreview (jev-preview)Stable (jev-latest)Stable Key Takeaways
  • Jev 1.14 is live as jev-preview. jev-latest switches in a week.
  • Images work on Jev 1.13 and 1.14 behind a danger-zone header.
  • The new Box type returns 1 normalized bounding box per question.
  • Long-context mode lifts limits to 262k tokens, at a reliability cost.
  • Price holds at $0.042 per million input tokens, with free output.

Check out the release post, Models docs, Images docs and Box docs. All credit goes to the researcher of this project. SpaceXAI just released Grok Voice 3.0 . Grok Voice 3.0 is a SpaceXAI speech-to-speech model that listens, reasons, calls tools and speaks. It now ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Speech-to-Speech Index with a score of 86.9. For developers, the endpoint, events and $0.08 per minute price are unchanged from Grok Voice 2.0. TL;DR Runs on: SpaceXAI’s hosted Voice Agent API only. No open weights, no local or quantized variants. Performance: Highest Index score of any model Artificial Analysis currently ranks. Best: 86.9 on the AA Speech-to-Speech Index, ranked #1. Worst: 71.6% on τ-Voice, behind GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 74.5%. Bottom line: Best: top composite score at 0.81 s time to first audio. Worst: not the leader on agentic task resolution or raw speech reasoning. What is Grok Voice 3.0? Grok Voice 3.0 is SpaceXAI’s flagship realtime voice model, exposed as grok-voice-3.0 on the /v1/realtime WebSocket endpoint . The grok-voice-latest alias already points to it, so existing agents switched automatically. SpaceXAI has not published parameter counts or architecture details. Reasoning is on by default ( reasoning.effort: "high" ) and can be set to "none" for faster turns. Server-side voice activity detection handles barge-in. Tools run inside the session: collections search, web search, X search, remote MCP servers and custom functions. How does Grok Voice 3.0 perform on benchmarks? The AA Speech-to-Speech Index is an equal-weighted average of 4 components. Those are Big Bench Audio reasoning, τ-Voice agentic performance, Speech Agent Arena preference and task success rate. Grok Voice 3.0 scores 86.9. GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) scores 83.2, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking 82.6. Grok Voice 2.0 scored 81.3. Component results are strong, not uniformly first: Big Bench Audio: 98.5%, ranked 4th. StepAudio 3 Realtime leads at 99.7%. Full Duplex Bench: 97.0%, ranked 4th. StepAudio 3 Realtime leads at 98.9%. Task success rate: 94.8%, up from 94.6% for Grok Voice 2.0. Speech Agent Arena Elo: 1070, the highest among the 4 models compared here. τ-Voice: 71.6%, up from 56.5%, but below GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 74.5%. ServiceNow’s EVA-Bench scores enterprise voice agents on accuracy and experience. SpaceXAI reports a top accuracy score of 74%. Is Grok Voice 3.0 fast and cheap? Artificial Analysis measures 0.81 s time to first audio. GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) measures 1.34 s, so SpaceXAI’s “40% lower latency” claim checks out. Grok Voice 2.0 was faster, though, at 0.70 s. On cost, SpaceXAI cites Artificial Analysis cost per Big Bench Audio task. Grok Voice 3.0 costs $0.025 per task, versus $0.030 for GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) and $0.055 for GPT-Realtime-2.1 (High). On AA’s cost per hour of input audio, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking is cheaper: $3.50 versus $4.80. List prices are not directly comparable. GPT-Live-1 costs $0.05 per minute, but backend model and tool usage is billed separately. Gemini 3.8 Live bills audio per minute plus text tokens. Grok Voice 3.0 Explainer

items.summary_html:
SpaceXAI just released Grok Voice 3.0. Grok Voice 3.0 is a SpaceXAI speech-to-speech model that listens, reasons, calls tools and speaks. It now ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Speech-to-Speech Index with a score of 86.9. For developers, the endpoint, events and $0.08 per minute price are unchanged from Grok Voice 2.0.

TL;DR
  • Runs on: SpaceXAI’s hosted Voice Agent API only. No open weights, no local or quantized variants.
  • Performance: Highest Index score of any model Artificial Analysis currently ranks.
  • Best: 86.9 on the AA Speech-to-Speech Index, ranked #1.
  • Worst: 71.6% on τ-Voice, behind GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 74.5%.
  • Bottom line:
    • Best: top composite score at 0.81 s time to first audio.
    • Worst: not the leader on agentic task resolution or raw speech reasoning.
What is Grok Voice 3.0?

Grok Voice 3.0 is SpaceXAI’s flagship realtime voice model, exposed as grok-voice-3.0 on the /v1/realtime WebSocket endpoint. The grok-voice-latest alias already points to it, so existing agents switched automatically.

SpaceXAI has not published parameter counts or architecture details. Reasoning is on by default (reasoning.effort: "high") and can be set to "none" for faster turns. Server-side voice activity detection handles barge-in. Tools run inside the session: collections search, web search, X search, remote MCP servers and custom functions.

How does Grok Voice 3.0 perform on benchmarks?

The AA Speech-to-Speech Index is an equal-weighted average of 4 components. Those are Big Bench Audio reasoning, τ-Voice agentic performance, Speech Agent Arena preference and task success rate.

Grok Voice 3.0 scores 86.9. GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) scores 83.2, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking 82.6. Grok Voice 2.0 scored 81.3.

Component results are strong, not uniformly first:

  • Big Bench Audio: 98.5%, ranked 4th. StepAudio 3 Realtime leads at 99.7%.
  • Full Duplex Bench: 97.0%, ranked 4th. StepAudio 3 Realtime leads at 98.9%.
  • Task success rate: 94.8%, up from 94.6% for Grok Voice 2.0.
  • Speech Agent Arena Elo: 1070, the highest among the 4 models compared here.
  • τ-Voice: 71.6%, up from 56.5%, but below GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 74.5%.

ServiceNow’s EVA-Bench scores enterprise voice agents on accuracy and experience. SpaceXAI reports a top accuracy score of 74%.

Is Grok Voice 3.0 fast and cheap?

Artificial Analysis measures 0.81 s time to first audio. GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) measures 1.34 s, so SpaceXAI’s “40% lower latency” claim checks out. Grok Voice 2.0 was faster, though, at 0.70 s.

On cost, SpaceXAI cites Artificial Analysis cost per Big Bench Audio task. Grok Voice 3.0 costs $0.025 per task, versus $0.030 for GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) and $0.055 for GPT-Realtime-2.1 (High). On AA’s cost per hour of input audio, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking is cheaper: $3.50 versus $4.80.

List prices are not directly comparable. GPT-Live-1 costs $0.05 per minute, but backend model and tool usage is billed separately. Gemini 3.8 Live bills audio per minute plus text tokens.

Benchmark data: Artificial Analysis, accessed October 14, 2026. SpaceXAI’s blog lists frozen Arena Elo values of 1048 (GPT-Live-1) and 990 (Gemini).

How do developers deploy Grok Voice 3.0?

The API is compatible with the OpenAI Realtime API, so migration mostly means a new URL and key.

  • Transports: WebSocket, WebRTC demo apps, and SIP for phone and contact-center calls.
  • Audio: PCM at 8 to 48 kHz, G.711 μ-law and A-law, and Opus.
  • Voices: 28 built-in voices, plus custom voices cloned from a reference clip of up to 120 s.
  • Languages: 20 listed locales with automatic language detection.
  • Extensions: force_message for scripted lines, pronunciation replace maps, and 30-minute session resumption.
  • Compliance: SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA eligible with a BAA, and GDPR. SpaceXAI says audio is not stored or used for training.

Production teams should pin grok-voice-3.0 rather than the alias. Grok Voice 2.0 is now deprecated.

Key Takeaways
  • Grok Voice 3.0 ranks #1 on the AA Speech-to-Speech Index at 86.9.
  • It answers in 0.81 s, 40% lower latency than GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium).
  • τ-Voice jumped to 71.6%, but GPT-Live-1 still leads at 74.5%.
  • Price stays at $0.08 per minute, and grok-voice-latest upgraded automatically.
  • It is API only: no weights, no disclosed size.

items.title: From a vague idea to a system map: the workflow behind Zextha
items.summary: I’m building Zextha , a visual workspace for exploring the system around an idea. This is a short walkthrough of the product workflow and the decisions behind it. The problem: a prompt leaves things unsaid “I want to build a learning companion” describes an intention. It does not tell us who will use it, what environment it needs to work in, or how we will know it helps. Starting implementation immediately can hide those unknowns inside the design. Zextha gives the early thinking a visible structure: Describe the idea in your own words. Answer four questions tailored to that idea. Explore a map of perspectives and their relationships. Use the map to decide what to investigate or try next. Four questions should earn their place A fixed budget–goal–timeline checklist is convenient, but it can miss the questions that matter for a particular project. For a learning companion, device access and the learner’s context may be important. For a content creator, the audience and a sustainable format may matter more. These are examples of useful questions, not a promise that every generated session uses the same wording. The goal is to collect context that can change the map, while keeping the interaction short. A map is an interface for investigation A useful node should give you something to examine: a dependency, constraint, risk, choice, or next action. Connections help show why one decision affects another. For example, choosing an offline-first experience affects storage, synchronization, content updates, and how failures are explained. Treating “offline support” as a single checkbox would hide much of that work. The output still needs human review. A generated map is not an exhaustive architecture review or evidence that an idea will work. It is a way to make the next discussion more concrete. Reading and references have different jobs Zextha’s Notes area contains original field books with chapters that can be read inside the workspace. Documents helps readers understand why a reference matters and follow it to the original source. Keeping those experiences distinct matters: reading a chapter and evaluating a source are different tasks. An optional perspective for agents Zextha also exposes an MCP connection for compatible clients. An agent can request a read-only perspective on an idea, an approach, or next steps. It does not automatically inspect your files or take control of your project; the client supplies the context. The connection details are available in the MCP workspace . Try it with a real uncertainty If you explore Zextha , try an idea you are still unsure about. Look for one useful connection, then verify it against the real requirements. I’d welcome feedback from builders: what information would make a system map useful before you start implementation? Disclosure: I’m Zextha’s founder. This post was prepared with AI assistance.

The goal is to collect context that can change the map, while keeping the interaction short.

A map is an interface for investigation

A useful node should give you something to examine: a dependency, constraint, risk, choice, or next action. Connections help show why one decision affects another.

For example, choosing an offline-first experience affects storage, synchronization, content updates, and how failures are explained. Treating “offline support” as a single checkbox would hide much of that work.

The output still needs human review. A generated map is not an exhaustive architecture review or evidence that an idea will work. It is a way to make the next discussion more concrete.

Reading and references have different jobs

Zextha’s Notes area contains original field books with chapters that can be read inside the workspace. Documents helps readers understand why a reference matters and follow it to the original source.

Keeping those experiences distinct matters: reading a chapter and evaluating a source are different tasks.

An optional perspective for agents

Zextha also exposes an MCP connection for compatible clients. An agent can request a read-only perspective on an idea, an approach, or next steps. It does not automatically inspect your files or take control of your project; the client supplies the context.

The connection details are available in the MCP workspace.

Try it with a real uncertainty

If you explore Zextha, try an idea you are still unsure about. Look for one useful connection, then verify it against the real requirements.

I’d welcome feedback from builders: what information would make a system map useful before you start implementation?

Disclosure: I’m Zextha’s founder. This post was prepared with AI assistance.
