items.title: Typed Decision Models on Tabular Data
items.summary: Typed decision models are language models that answer a question with a fixed set of possible answers by returning a probability for each answer instead of generating text. We study them on tabular data and compare four decision models with three large language models (LLMs) on row classification, fact verification and anomaly detection. Every request is sent in its original form and under 21 types of rewrite that keep its content, such as renaming the options or writing the table in another format. The decision models perform as well as the LLMs at a lower cost. Three of them are also far more robust to how the question is formulated. No model we test is robust to how the table is organized. For every model, at least a third of the row decisions change under some rewrite of the table or the question. The decisions to which a decision model gives low probability are the ones most likely to change. Decision models are a practical choice for tabular decisions, but their robustness remains an open problem.

items.title: GraphRAG-LTM: A Layered Threat Modeling Framework for Attacks on Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary: Graph retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) uses document-derived knowledge graphs to assemble evidence for large language model (LLM) answers. Its security depends on both the seed chunks retrieved for a query and the graph evidence assembled from them, yet attacks on this evidence path remain underexplored. We introduce GraphRAG-LTM, a Layered Threat Modeling framework that tests three nested levels of attacker access. BB Query uses ranking feedback to make query edits under a semantic-similarity constraint and demote relevant seed chunks. WB Query uses retriever gradients for the same objective. Graph-aware WB keeps the white-box adversarial query and deletes bridge triplets from the query-specific evidence graph, disrupting multi-hop evidence propagation through localized graph edits. Across datasets, retrievers, and LLM backbones, rank feedback alone reduces answer quality, gradient access strengthens query attacks, and bridge-triplet deletion further impairs supporting-fact retrieval. Further analyses show how seed retrieval and graph evidence jointly contribute to these failures.

items.title: Evidence-Anchored Overdose Death Prediction from Death Investigation Reports
items.summary: Confirmation of overdose deaths in the United States is often delayed due to the complexities of certifying drug-involved deaths. Death investigation reports represent a rich but underutilized data source that could be used to predict whether a death is a suspected overdose (i.e., a death preliminarily identified as an overdose prior to the final cause and manner of death determination). We present an automated framework that classifies suspected overdoses from death investigation reports, while producing supporting explanations guided by expert knowledge. Through an expert-guided design process, we investigate 1) what type of explanations are best for model prediction performance, and 2) which architecture is better suited for this task: pipeline models that rationalize first and then predict, or self-rationalizing models that jointly predict and rationalize? Our experiments show that a pipeline model with explanations grounded in the input death investigation reports outperforms the other settings. Our best model also outperforms a rule-based system currently in deployment by 15%, while allowing expert interventions for final decisions.

items.title: REWIND: Uncertainty-Guided Trajectory Repair for Test-Time Reasoning
items.summary: An early mistake in the generated reasoning can constrain all subsequent reasoning. Repeated-generation methods, like MCMC-based approaches, attempt to improve output quality by sampling multiple generations, but their effectiveness can be limited by randomly selecting where to regenerate. On MATH500 with Qwen2.5-Math-7B, we find that incorrect responses have substantially higher mean token entropy than correct responses, with an average within-question relative increase of approximately 112%, suggesting that entropy can signal reasoning errors. Motivated by this finding, we introduce REWIND, a training-free controller that uses entropy dynamics to propose targeted suffix regenerations. Across three model families and five benchmarks, REWIND outperforms all baselines, with gains of 0.51-10.00 percentage points over the strongest baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of targeted, uncertainty-guided trajectory repair across models and tasks. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rewind-D310.

items.title: INTACT: Inducing Latent Reasoning on a Frozen Backbone
items.summary: Latent reasoning replaces natural-language chains of thought with compact continuous "soft-token" representations, reducing the number of intermediate tokens that must be decoded autoregressively. We use a small external encoder to induce latent reasoning in a frozen backbone model. The encoder iteratively maps the backbone's hidden states to new latent blocks, constructing a latent reasoning prefix, after which the frozen model writes its remaining reasoning and its answer as text. Our method, INTACT, trains this encoder through distillation to reproduce the effect of written reasoning steps while keeping the model's behavior close to that of the frozen backbone, and then reinforces it on answer correctness. Across four frozen backbones from 1B to 8B, INTACT improves both GSM8K and average out-of-domain accuracy, including GSM8K gains from 75.8% to 79.3% on Llama-3.2-3B and from 77.6% to 79.7% on Qwen2.5-3B. It also reduces end-to-end latency per problem by 19% on Llama-3.2-3B and outperforms the evaluated latent-reasoning baselines at the 3B and 8B scales. Beyond the mathematics setting, the same recipe trained on a multi-domain corpus improves the frozen backbone on twelve evaluation benchmarks spanning mathematics, science, and commonsense, without task-specific adaptation.

items.title: Moral Combat: Exploiting Moral Foundations Theory to Jailbreak LLMs
items.summary: Social psychology has long described how people can be persuaded to interpret a harmful act as moral. Recent research suggests that Large Language Models (LLMs) echo aspects of human psychology, from cognitive biases to social conformity. This raises a question with direct safety implications: can LLMs be moralized to bypass safety guardrails? We answer this question with a multi-agent framework grounded in Moral Foundations Theory (MFT). Given a harmful request that is initially refused, our agents diagnose which moral foundation (MF) the prompt is violating, identify a justifiable foundation under which the same request appears virtuous, rewrite the prompt accordingly, and reinforce it with generated precedents of comparable moral reframing. We evaluate our framework on harmful prompts from three well-known jailbreak datasets across five open-source and proprietary models. Our analysis reveals that models are highly susceptible to moralization, exhibiting high single-trial jailbreak rates with success increasing further under repeated attempts. We also find that safety benchmarks are imbalanced in the MFs they violate, concentrating on foundations toward which models already exhibit biases.

items.title: PA1-OPD: One-Step Prefix-Augmented On-Policy Distillation for Language Model Pretraining
items.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) improves language-model pretraining by matching teacher distributions at corpus prefixes, but provides no direct supervision at contexts induced by student predictions. We introduce PA1-OPD, which augments corpus-path distillation with teacher feedback after one student-sampled transition per selected prefix. This expands the supervised states while retaining next-token prediction and corpus-path KD. Data-anchored roots support parallel sampling, and differentiable tree attention shares prefix computation without changing inference. In two continued-pretraining settings, full coverage improves held-out cross-entropy over KD across C4, PG-19, and Pile at every evaluated checkpoint. In Stage2, selecting the 10% of roots with highest student surprisal adds 48.85% to KD's Macro cross-entropy gain over next-token training. Gains remain when branch supervision excludes successor states already on the corpus path, supporting the value of feedback beyond observed contexts. Additional depth or breadth improves aggregate results at unchanged per-term supervision weight, with benefits varying by corpus. These findings support local student-induced supervision as a complement to pretraining distillation.

items.title: Are We Really Measuring Forgetting? Pitfalls in Evaluating Machine Unlearning for Multimodal LLMs
items.summary: As machine unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) rapidly advances, rigorous evaluation of its effectiveness becomes increasingly important. However, existing benchmarks largely inherit evaluation protocols from text-only unlearning and overlook the unique challenges of unlearning in multimodal settings. In this work, we identify three major pitfalls that may lead to misleading conclusions: the lack of heldout evaluation to distinguish genuine concept-wise forgetting from instance-wise overfitting, the reliance on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge rather than real-world knowledge acquired during pre-training, and unfair method comparisons caused by applying the same training settings to different unlearning methods. To address these challenges, we introduce GEMMU (Generalizable Evaluation for Multimodal Machine Unlearning), a benchmark built on real-world knowledge and a principled evaluation protocol. Re-evaluating representative unlearning methods under GEMMU reveals substantial generalization gaps and challenges conclusions drawn from previous benchmarks. Our findings highlight the importance of rigorous evaluation for advancing multimodal machine unlearning and provide guidelines for future benchmark design.

items.title: DAGFormer: Global Topology Prediction for Transformer Cross-Layer Connections
items.summary: We propose DAGFormer, a Transformer language model whose cross-layer connections are planned by a jointly trained topology predictor. Beyond the residual connections in a standard Transformer, DAGFormer adds direct connections from earlier layers to later ones, and the predictor controls the strength of every connection based on input tokens. Unlike existing cross-layer routing architectures, which set each layer's connections separately, DAGFormer plans the routing of the whole model at once. On matched OLMo-2 pairs from 75M to 1B parameters, DAGFormer lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by 17% to 25% over the vanilla Transformer, and a 1B DAGFormer trained on 5B tokens outperforms the vanilla model trained on 10B. Against four routing baselines with the same data and budget, it reaches the lowest perplexity at 75M, 300M and 1B. The gain carries over to 13 commonsense, science, reading and math evaluation tasks (2.0 to 2.5 points higher mean accuracy at 300M and 1B) and to instruction finetuning (63% to 70% AlpacaEval win rate against the vanilla Transformer, leading every routing baseline), and under structured pruning DAGFormer degrades the least in five of six settings.

items.title: J-tau: A Fully Localized Japanese Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction
items.summary: We present J-tau, the first publicly available Japanese benchmark for evaluating tool-using LLM agents in interactive customer-support scenarios. While tau-bench is widely used to evaluate LLM agents, it is English-centric and cannot evaluate agents in other languages. Existing multilingual extensions offer no public Japanese version and rely primarily on machine translation, leaving locale-specific entities such as addresses and currencies inconsistent with the target region. To enable reliable evaluation in Japanese, we carefully localize tau-bench through machine translation, entity adaptation, and human review. During this process, we also uncover and fix two flaws in the original tau-bench: invalid tasks and a score aggregation error that inflates certain models' results. Experiments show that J-tau yields fewer evaluation errors than a naively machine-translated counterpart and that our fixes resolve both flaws.

items.title: Selective Reasoning for Typed Decision Models: When to Start, Read, and Stop
items.summary: Typed decision models need an interface that can use additional reasoning while retaining candidate outputs. We train a shared candidate-answer reader on a frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone to unify direct decisions with on-demand, interruptible reasoning. The reader returns distributions from empty and partial reasoning prefixes. A benefit gate starts reasoning, a natural-state trigger requests explicit reads, and an entropy rule accepts acquired answers and cancels generation. Measurements distinguish answer-query work, generated output, and pipeline time. Across 768 questions from ProofWriter, LogiQA 2.0, and ARC-Challenge, accuracy rises from 70.96% for direct reading to 84.38%. Relative to 512-token terminal reading, accuracy improves by 7.29 percentage points with 2.25% more mean output work. Relative to 1,024-token terminal reading, pipeline time falls by 46.30% with an accuracy difference of -1.17 points. Exact-prefix controls isolate the saving from interruption, while read-scheduling controls distinguish reduced observation work from shorter response time.

items.title: HACHIMI-II: From Role-Play to Learner Behavior Modeling for Faithful Student Simulation
items.summary: Simulated students let researchers test tutoring systems and teaching strategies before real learners are available, but only if the simulation reproduces where a particular learner succeeds and fails. The common approach asks a large language model to role-play a student, but a role does not model what this learner knows or will do next, so the model's own competence fills the gap. Simulated students perform at a level set by the model, differ little from one another, and seldom make the real learners' errors. We model the learner's behavior and recast student simulation as third-person prediction of the learner's next action. HACHIMI-II builds a student model from the learner's history, infers the learner's state for the current item or tutor turn, and compiles it into a behavior harness that constrains the next action. On three item-response datasets, the Wasserstein-1 distance between simulated and real student ability is 2.4--8.4$\times$ smaller than that of the strongest baseline. On two dialogue datasets, HACHIMI-II reproduces real student errors with the same knowledge type, locus, and mechanism 1.8--5.1$\times$ more often than the strongest baseline, and ablations trace the gains mainly to the explicit learner state. Predicting the learner makes capable models usable as simulated students.

items.title: Measuring and Reducing Unusable Replies of LLM Agents
items.summary: People delegate multi-step work to LLM agents and read only the reply that the agent hands back. Current evaluation scores task completion and the faithfulness of reports, and it leaves open whether the requester can understand and use the reply. We call this property reply usability and measure it with a reader model that takes the requester's position and tests whether the reply can be interpreted from what the requester has seen, is in the requester's language and answers the request. Its agreement with the majority of five annotators lies within the range of the individual annotators. Across eight models from seven families, 54% of 480 replies fail, and the best model still fails on 30%. Failed replies mostly point to material the requester has not seen or use labels that the agent coined during its work. Stating explicit requirements for the reply reduces the failure rate from 0.52 to 0.43 together with errors and omissions, and a secondary model that rewrites the reply reduces it to 0.36, which human annotators confirm in a blind comparison. Reply usability can thus be scored alongside task success and improved with one appended message or one call to a secondary model.

Its agreement with the majority of five annotators lies within the range of the individual annotators. Across eight models from seven families, 54% of 480 replies fail, and the best model still fails on 30%. Failed replies mostly point to material the requester has not seen or use labels that the agent coined during its work. Stating explicit requirements for the reply reduces the failure rate from 0.52 to 0.43 together with errors and omissions, and a secondary model that rewrites the reply reduces it to 0.36, which human annotators confirm in a blind comparison. Reply usability can thus be scored alongside task success and improved with one appended message or one call to a secondary model.

items.title: Interlock: From Local Correctness to Task Completion in Long-Horizon Agents
items.summary: Large language model agents increasingly undertake long-horizon tasks in complex environments characterized by fragmented evidence, partially completed states, and dependencies across resources and artifacts. Existing agents may satisfy individual requirements while failing to maintain these relationships, producing locally correct but incomplete outcomes. These failures arise because task completion depends on relationships among environmental evidence, consequential decisions, and required effects. To address this completion gap, we propose Interlock, a framework for task synthesis that represents each task as a typed completion graph. Grounding edges connect public evidence to decisions, coupling hyperedges impose joint constraints across components, and realization edges connect decisions to all required downstream effects. Interlock compiles this graph into a resettable workspace, a public request, and an evaluation rubric. A source-coverage review checks whether the original requirements survive generation, while a public-input review checks whether the rubric is supported by the materials available to the solver. An agent-as-judge inspects execution artifacts and runs verification scripts, retaining trajectories judged to satisfy all mandatory requirements. To evaluate training utility, we fine-tune two Qwen3.6 backbones on their own accepted trajectories. Across the two backbones, training improves AutomationBench task pass rates by 4.00-4.50 percentage points, JobBench weighted scores by 3.20-6.64 points, and Harvey LAB criterion pass rates by 3.89-4.16 percentage points. These results demonstrate the training utility of the synthesized experience across external task environments.

items.title: Share the Symbol, Not the Vector: Training-Free Fact Communication Across Language Models
items.summary: Multi-agent systems allow language models to solve tasks collaboratively by sharing complementary information. These systems typically communicate through text, while recent approaches also explore exchanging internal model states. However, sharing these states across architectures often requires learned translators or assumptions about model compatibility. We introduce SYNC (Symbol-Indexed Neural Communication), a word-indexed interface that connects heterogeneous models without fine-tuning or a learned translator. From descriptions only it can see, the sender selects words from a shared list and sends their indices for each object, without seeing the questions. The receiver writes the described facts into its hidden states using its own word directions, vectors fitted once from its activations. We test selective use by swapping one attribute between two objects and requiring correct answers about both changed and unchanged attributes before and after the swap, four answers in total. We choose an early write layer on four development receivers and then fix it. With three different senders and nine newer receivers from five families, four-answer success on new scenes reaches 72.0-98.3%, up to 96 percentage points above middle-layer writing, and the two largest receivers match plain text. A task-free probe predicted in advance which depths each new receiver can use (45 of 45 cases). Without retuning, messages listing every fact keep 89.6-100% success under new layouts, and sender messages reach 23.9-64.0% on a landmark task with multi-token symbols, below text but from 0% without a message. These results show that shared word indices and receiver-local directions can support selective fact use across model families without additional training.

items.title: BANGLAPLAN: A Benchmark for Constraint-Based Planning and Decision-Making in Bangla
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly help users arrange appointments, plan journeys, and allocate limited resources. These tasks require models to satisfy constraints on time, cost, capacity, and order, or determine that no feasible solution exists. Bangla is the world's seventh most widely spoken language, and existing benchmarks cover many language and reasoning tasks. However, benchmarks for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla under explicit constraints remain lacking. We introduce BANGLAPLAN, a benchmark of 1,000 problems across ten task families grounded in everyday life and institutions in Bangladesh. It includes feasible and infeasible problems in four language registers: everyday, formal, colloquial, and Bangla--English mixed. Answers cover eight structured types, including schedules, routes, allocations, and ordered steps, in a common JSON format. We construct the benchmark through language-model-assisted drafting and independent human validation. We evaluate 11 open-weight and proprietary model configurations using exact match, separately reporting feasible-case accuracy, infeasibility detection, and format errors. We find a large performance gap: GPT-6.1 Sol achieves 98.7% accuracy and Qwen3.5-27B with thinking reaches 80.3%, while direct-answer configurations score at most 30.9%. Seven of eleven configurations perform below the always-``infeasible'' baseline. Our findings also suggest that harder problems primarily reduce plan-construction accuracy, while infeasibility detection remains more robust. BANGLAPLAN provides a reproducible basis for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla. BANGLAPLAN is available at: https://github.com/mrayhanulmasud/banglaplan.

items.title: RouteWeaver: Weaving Mode Selection and Execution into Unified LLM Routing
items.summary: LLM routing dynamically selects and coordinates heterogeneous language models across diverse tasks. However, existing approaches are largely built around a predefined execution paradigm, such as single-round, multi-round, or agentic routing, which fixes how model calls are organized and limits adaptation to different query needs. We propose RouteWeaver, a unified routing framework that integrates these routing modes within a single LLM policy, jointly learning which mode to use and how to select models within that mode. To jointly optimize mode selection and within-mode execution, we develop COMET-GRPO (COordinated Mode-Execution Training), which decouples the trajectory-level advantage into separate signals for mode selection and within-mode execution, enabling more targeted credit assignment to each decision level. We further introduce progressive exploration, which gradually shifts training from externally assigned modes to autonomous selection, so that the router first learns how to execute each mode before deciding when to use it. We evaluate RouteWeaver across mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall. RouteWeaver achieves an average accuracy of 61.4%, an 11.03% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, and outperforms all compared baselines in each of the five domains. Ablations show that both COMET-GRPO and progressive exploration are important for adaptive routing; without progressive exploration, the routing policy collapses entirely to single-round execution.

items.title: Beyond State Capacity: Why Retrieval Breaks in Mamba
items.summary: Mamba models underperform Transformers on in-context retrieval. This gap is usually attributed to Mamba's fixed-size recurrent state, which loses information as the context grows. We challenge this assumption by focusing on query-first retrieval, a setup in which the query precedes the context and state capacity should not be the binding constraint. We show that even in this setting Mamba lags substantially behind Transformers, despite its selection mechanism, which was designed to distinguish relevant content from distractors. We then demonstrate that the Mamba selection gates have sufficient control over the state updates to influence the model output: intervening on specific gates alone can swing accuracy between extremes. However, as gates are input-dependent, they require the incoming token's representation to encode its relevance to the query. We therefore probe token representations across layers, and find that the relevance signal emerges only gradually with model depth, and that the gates begin to reflect it only several layers deeper. Crucially, we find that gates in retrieval-critical layers are not yet aligned with relevance. The selection mechanism is thus expressive enough to solve the task, but it commonly operates on a relevance signal that has not yet arrived. Mamba's retrieval bottleneck therefore extends beyond state capacity: even when capacity is sufficient, the delayed emergence of relevance information across depth often prevents successful retrieval.

items.title: Recognizing Dialogue Ambiguity via Candidate Set Visual Grounding
items.summary: Interpreting an ambiguous utterance in real-world interactions often requires context beyond a single utterance. When the utterance refers to objects in a visual scene, it is necessary to maintain and update the set of plausible referents as context accumulates, without assuming that the available information identifies a unique object. However, prior work on interactive visual grounding, which localizes objects referred to by linguistic expressions, has focused on identifying a unique object once sufficient dialogue context becomes available. To address this gap, we propose Candidate Set Visual Grounding (CSVG), a task for estimating the set of objects consistent with the given dialogue context. We further introduce CandVG, a benchmark that evaluates how the candidate set changes across dialogue turns. Our evaluation of vision-language models shows that stronger visual grounding capability does not necessarily yield better CSVG performance. In particular, models have difficulty predicting the complete candidate set, owing to challenges in candidate generation and premature commitment to a small set of candidates in early turns. Nevertheless, we find that this limitation can be partially mitigated in the evaluated large-scale models using instructions designed for CSVG.

items.title: MakSafe: A Spatiotemporal Semantic Framework for Formal Specification and Compliance Checking of Road Vehicle Safety Rules
items.summary: Scenario-based validation is essential for automated road vehicles but cannot cover the full variability of openworld traffic. We present MakSafe, a formal spatiotemporal framework for specifying and checking road vehicle safety rules through semantic zones, action-based forecasting, and trace-tree reasoning, avoiding uniform time discretization. We formalize the road network, vehicle states, and occupancy zones, then build executable rules for front-vehicle identification and timeto-collision (TTC) verification. The evaluation combines a tracedependent case study with a scalability benchmark over traffic density (N ), horizon (H), and branch factor (B). MakSafe yields branch-specific verdicts, deriving safe and unsafe outcomes from the same initial scene, and re-evaluates a scenario after a control update. A single rule check stays well below a millisecond across the reported sweep, and longer horizons slow the TTC check.

items.title: Does the Linguistic Register of Thinking Matter? Wenyan as a Compact Reasoning Register for Chinese LLMs
items.summary: Visible reasoning traces of Chinese reasoning-oriented LLMs are typically written in modern vernacular Chinese, which may be verbose under limited decoding budgets. We ask whether the linguistic register of reasoning can be used to improve efficiency. We propose Wenyan Thinking, which emits intermediate reasoning in Classical Chinese (wenyanwen) while retaining a short direct-answer output. Starting from modern-Chinese reasoning traces, we rewrite only the reasoning field into wenyan and fine-tune Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 on the rewritten supervision. To distinguish register shift from generic compression, we construct a compact modern-Chinese control using the same source data, teacher family, base model, and SFT recipe. Across budget-sensitive evaluations on MMLU-ProX-Lite-ZH, CEVAL, and AGIEval-CN, Wenyan Thinking substantially reduces reasoning length and missing-answer rates under constrained decoding. Compact rewriting explains much of the efficiency gain, while wenyan consistently outperforms the compact modern-Chinese control on the primary benchmark and remains competitive across the additional benchmarks. These results identify linguistic register as a practical design axis for efficient visible reasoning in Chinese LLMs.

items.title: Beyond Reachability: A Relation-Semantic Reasoning Framework for Biomedical Multi-hop QA
items.summary: Biomedical multi-hop reasoning over knowledge graphs requires identifying a semantically valid relation sequence that supports the answer. Existing methods can retrieve correct answers, yet often rank them poorly within a large pool of seemingly relevant candidates. Even when a correct answer is retrieved, its associated evidence and reasoning path may fail to support the relation composition required by the question. We term this disconnect between answer reachability and evidential validity the reachable-but-invalid problem. We present ReSemReason, which shares a question-induced distribution over typed, directed relation schemas between candidate discovery and evidence selection. Schema compatibility guides graph search; ReSemAttn then uses relation-conditioned key/value projections and an uncertainty-weighted path prior to attend to candidate-specific evidence. A separate absolute-support score complements normalized attention when all retrieved paths are weak. The reported experiments on BioHopR, PrimeKGQA, and MedReason show improvements in answer ranking and answer-set quality. Path-discrimination analyses examine the distinction between endpoint correctness and evidential support. We also specify matched controls for search, attention, and schema uncertainty.

items.title: Qwen-MT-Lumen at WMT2026: Instruction-Specialized Translation via Quality-Aware Training and On-Policy Distillation
items.summary: We present Lumen, The open-source model is available at, our submission to the WMT 2026 General Machine Translation Shared Task. We focus on instruction-specialized translation, where systems must produce accurate translations while satisfying fine-grained requirements on style, terminology, and structured output. Lumen follows a four-stage pipeline. First, continued pre-training and supervised fine-tuning jointly strengthen multilingual translation competence and the ability to follow translation-specific instructions, such as terminology, style, and format constraints. Second, we extend the originally offline M^{2}PO preference-optimization framework into an online preference-optimization stage: the current policy samples candidate translations, an LLM judge assigns continuous direct-assessment scores, and the resulting multi-pair preferences are used to update the model. Third, on-policy distillation transfers stronger translation-instruction-following behavior from a larger teacher model to the Qwen3-14B student, improving translation-instruction adherence while retaining a 14B primary translation backbone. Finally, structure-aware inference and postprocessing preserve required formats, while selective repair addresses clear structural or decoding failures before submission. We participate in 23 translation directions. Under an absolute 1--5 LLM-judge rubric that evaluates translation-instruction following and translation quality separately, Lumen reaches an overall mean score of 4.60. Despite using a 14B translation backbone, it achieves performance comparable to leading proprietary systems in both translation quality and translation-instruction following.

items.title: PRISMATIC : Prescription Risk Inspection System for Multi-Agent Treatment Interaction in Clinical Decision-Making
items.summary: Medical prescribing errors for multimorbid patients, who require complex drug regimens, are a major patient safety concern. These errors often stem from fragmented decision-making across medical specialties, a critical coordination failure that leads to adverse drug events and rehospitalizations. To address this coordination challenge, we introduce PRISMATIC, a multi-agent architecture where specialized agents, each representing a workflow role, collaboratively generate and refine treatment plans. Operating on a blackboard architecture, the system first structures patient information from clinical notes, then iteratively develops safe, rational, and interpretable drug regimens. The agents' collaboration is governed by two novel adaptive coordination mechanisms: (1) Dynamic Self-Updating Weight Adjustment (DSWA), a long-term mechanism that adjusts the influence weights of agents based on historical case outcomes, enabling the system to adapt and trust more reliable specialists over time. (2) Discrepancy Feedback Precise Calibration (DFPC), a short-term mechanism where agents provide iterative feedback to resolve disagreements and eliminate prescription conflicts for the current patient. Experiments on patient records from the MIMIC-IV database show that PRISMATIC significantly reduces drug conflicts, improves prescription coverage, and enhances treatment consistency compared to strong LLM baselines. Our work demonstrates that structuring clinical co-treatment as a multi-agent coordination problem offers a promising path toward safer and more coherent multidisease management.

items.title: Likelihood Is Not Authorship: Can We Reliably Measure Human Contribution in AI-Assisted Writing?
items.summary: AI-text detection generally asks whether a machine wrote a text. As AI becomes an increasingly integral and accepted part of writing, the more relevant question is no longer whether AI was used, but how much of the text reflects human contribution. A prominent line of work estimates this by measuring how predictive a person's prompt is of the final text. We show that this measure can be easily manipulated. We introduce SPECIFICITY PADDING that simply asks the model to copy a few random IDs from the prompt, and that alone makes a title-only request look more human than one that supplies the article's key ideas. A context-swap audit then holds each document fixed, and only shows or hides the IDs to the evaluator. The score of the unchanged text swings by a third to half of its scale, and it rises for every document we test, on news and scientific abstracts, across varied LLMs from 3.8B to 753B parameters. The same articles can average 85\% human or 15\% human depending only on which prompt is on record, and even with no prompt at all, the output-only variant rewards the random strings themselves. An exact identity, the credit ledger, explains why. The score is a surprisal-weighted average over the text, so rare strings that the context makes copyable collect the credit, whatever they mean. A two-point bound marks a deeper limit. If the prompt could have been machine-written, every transcript-only method must, in the worst case, miss by half the contribution at stake. Likelihood-based scores alone cannot reliably establish human contribution without evidence of what the person added and how the text was produced.

Abstract: AI-text detection generally asks whether a machine wrote a text. As AI becomes an increasingly integral and accepted part of writing, the more relevant question is no longer whether AI was used, but how much of the text reflects human contribution. A prominent line of work estimates this by measuring how predictive a person's prompt is of the final text. We show that this measure can be easily manipulated. We introduce SPECIFICITY PADDING that simply asks the model to copy a few random IDs from the prompt, and that alone makes a title-only request look more human than one that supplies the article's key ideas. A context-swap audit then holds each document fixed, and only shows or hides the IDs to the evaluator. The score of the unchanged text swings by a third to half of its scale, and it rises for every document we test, on news and scientific abstracts, across varied LLMs from 3.8B to 753B parameters. The same articles can average 85\% human or 15\% human depending only on which prompt is on record, and even with no prompt at all, the output-only variant rewards the random strings themselves. An exact identity, the credit ledger, explains why. The score is a surprisal-weighted average over the text, so rare strings that the context makes copyable collect the credit, whatever they mean. A two-point bound marks a deeper limit. If the prompt could have been machine-written, every transcript-only method must, in the worst case, miss by half the contribution at stake. Likelihood-based scores alone cannot reliably establish human contribution without evidence of what the person added and how the text was produced.

items.title: More Methods, Better Agents? A Reality Check on Self-Distillation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Self-distillation in agentic reinforcement learning has produced a growing number of methods. However, existing evaluations often reuse published baseline scores under differing experimental conditions, provide few direct comparisons among contemporaneous methods, and give limited attention to training stability and computational cost. These limitations obscure the source of reported gains and the practical strengths and weaknesses of competing methods. Costly agent training further motivates a common basis for comparison. To address these gaps, we compare ten representative methods against GRPO on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, Search-QA, and WebShop across three model sizes. Our study comprises 132 training runs totaling 12,124.4 recorded H800 GPU-hours, with repeated evaluations over eight rollout seeds for the pretrained backbones and all eleven trained methods. Beyond final task performance, we examine training progress, stability, and measured computational cost. Our evaluation yields three key findings. First, gains over GRPO remain limited in scope, with no method consistently outperforming it across settings. Second, strong final performance can mask unstable training. Third, additional training cost does not consistently translate into better performance. We establish this benchmark to support fair, comprehensive comparison and guide future research toward reliable and cost-effective improvements in agent training. Project page: https://aim-uofa.github.io/Self-Distillation-AgentRL/

items.title: JetSpec++: Foresight Parallel Drafting with Self Refinements
items.summary: Speculative decoding's effectiveness is governed by two quantities: the acceptance rate of drafted tokens and the cost of producing them. We show the two objectives can be co-optimized with algorithm-system co-design, and present JetSpec++, which retains a strong learned draft model while hiding its cost almost entirely. JetSpec++ combines three components: intra-block self refinement, which trains the draft model to iteratively correct its own parallel predictions within a block of tokens; inter-block foresight drafting, which begins the next block before the current one is verified; and pipelined drafting and verification, which overlaps the two stages so drafting's marginal wall-clock cost approaches zero. In comparison with state-of-the-art speculative decoding methods, JetSpec++ attains a wall-clock speedup of up to $7.45\times$ over autoregressive (AR) decoding and $1.54\times$ over DSpark, with up to 1,361 tokens per second for a single request on GB200, and an average acceptance length of 8.94 across seven benchmarks, while preserving the target model's output distribution. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/JetSpec.

items.title: Evolve Together, Fall into Place: How Social Scaffolding Shapes Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
items.summary: Recent work lets LLM agents evolve their own harness, up to the team itself. Yet in human groups, the same abilities achieve different outcomes under different social conditions. Borrowing the notion of scaffolding from developmental psychology, we investigate whether the social scaffolding of a self-evolving multi-agent system (MAS), namely its team composition and structure of interdependence (e.g., collaboration, conformity, or competition), shapes how the team evolves. We present AGORA (Agents Growing through Organization and Relational Arrangements), a framework that varies the two axes independently across three evolution mechanisms. Across web search, codebase understanding, and document QA, we find that (1) evolution alone rarely helps, while the right scaffolding surpasses a strong agent evolved alone by up to 25 points; (2) it does so by moving authority to the most capable member while the others step back; and (3) this member, having grown within the team, outperforms the same model alone. Designing a self-evolving MAS thus requires designing its social scaffolding, which shapes not only how its agents learn, but who gets to lead.

items.title: Delta Tokenizer: Reference-Identical Tokenization of Session Deltas and Segment-Parallelism for Long Prompts on Multicore CPUs
items.summary: An agent that drives an LLM sends the model the same conversation again and again, and each turn adds only a little text at the end. Inference engines reuse the KV cache of the shared prefix, so only the new tokens pass through the model. However, tokenization has no such shortcut. The CPU front end of the serving engine converts every request back into token IDs from its first character, which lengthens the time to first token (TTFT) and consumes CPU on every turn. We present Delta Tokenizer, a CPU tokenization front end that tokenizes only the delta between a request and the previous request of the same session. It retains the earlier token sequence, encodes again only the appended text and the short tail whose tokens the append could affect, and joins the two only at a position the tokenizer's splitting rules themselves cannot move, which keeps the result exact. For long requests with no state to reuse, it cuts the text where practical tokenizers already keep neighboring pieces independent, encodes the pieces on several cores at once, and concatenates the outputs into the reference encoding, exactly. A shared CPU pool schedules these chunks together with the short incremental updates, so an update runs between two chunks rather than behind an entire long job. The incremental path shortens the tokenization of a session turn by roughly 40x relative to the Hugging Face reference tokenizer, and on 16 cores the chunk-parallel path encodes a four-million-character request 8.2x faster than a serial encode and 1.6-2.1x faster than LoPT. Inside SGLang, Delta Tokenizer reduces the median TTFT through the chat interface by 59% at 100K tokens and brings the P99 TTFT of agent sessions down 9.5x under load and 23x when long requests tie up the front end. Every output we checked matches the reference, among them 41.8 billion documents encoded by its fast encoder.

items.title: Model vs. User: Whose Values Prevail? Inference-Time Value Alignment in Multi-Turn Conversations
items.summary: Human values shape how we expect language models to behave. Dominant alignment approaches treat values as global objectives, although the appropriate value orientation is personal and contextual. Training-free alignment can steer models toward target values at inference time, yet has been largely evaluated in single-turn settings and with a single steering direction (e.g., toward safety). We evaluate four prompt- and activation-based steering methods in multi-turn conversations, where user and assistant models push toward the same or opposing, equally desirable values. We track alignment with a linear probe across three models and two value trade-offs. When assistant and user pull in opposite directions, the side matching the assistant's baseline bias often prevails, and effects that look successful early often fade or reverse after a few turns. Steering should therefore be evaluated over full conversations and in both directions of a value trade-off.

items.title: EGCForest: Structured Agent Memory Organization for Enterprise Group Chats
items.summary: Enterprise group chats record project progress, decisions, task ownership, and other organizational information valuable to enterprise agents. Reliable retrieval is challenging because evidence spans interleaved threads, channels, and time, with meaning and authority conditioned on the speaker. Neither RAG's independent chunk retrieval nor memory systems' summary-based consolidation can reliably recover such distributed evidence. We present EGCForest, a novel multi-view hierarchical memory framework for enterprise group chats. EGCForest organizes an immutable message log into three complementary forests: a Channel forest for temporal workflows, an Actor forest for speaker-conditioned context, and an Artifact forest for deliverable lifecycles. Cross-view connections are enabled by a Placement Map and sparse structural bridges. Built on this memory backbone, EGCForest retrieves and assembles evidence by jointly leveraging message-level relevance, hierarchical context from forest summaries, and cross-view links, recovering distributed evidence. Experiments on three enterprise-chat benchmarks show that EGCForest consistently outperforms RAG and memory-system baselines, improving answer accuracy by up to 20.85 points over MemOS while supporting efficient online retrieval.

items.title: OpenTWBench (Open Taiwan Benchmark): Taiwan-Domain Knowledge Evaluation for Large Language Models, and How the Measurement Apparatus Shapes the Score
items.summary: We present OpenTWBench, an open evaluation suite for Taiwan-domain knowledge in large language models, built around two benchmarks. tw-exam-bench contains 255,854 four-option questions across 148 academic subjects, from fifteen years of Taiwan's national examinations published as open data by the Ministry of Examination; answer keys agree across 31,312 duplicated question groups at 99.91%, with all 27 disagreements accounted for. A reviewed second pass withdrew 2,180 items whose stems depend on a figure the text does not carry; all scores use the remaining 253,674. tw-formosa-bench contains 1,696 difficulty-curated questions about everyday and contemporary Taiwan - the Taiwan that licensing examinations never ask about - generated from a community-curated corpus under a discipline in which no model writes a ground truth, and curated against a frozen seven-model pool so that the pool scored at the passing margin (46.9-74.6%, median ~54%); a leave-one-out experiment shows the selection preserves model ranking (near-zero bias). Within six weeks the frontier had cleared that band: of 108 models now on the public board, 22 score above its ceiling, the best 91.6%. We also document how much of a score comes from the apparatus rather than the model. On identical questions, switching answer extraction from pattern matching to an explicit \boxed{} answer moves accuracy from 20.8% to 93.9%; a single placeholder character in a system prompt moved one model from last (58.2%) to first (83.9%) on the same benchmark; doubling the thinking budget from 8k to 16k tokens bought 0.2% while shuffling which questions failed; and a three-judge validation panel proved to be one judge in disguise, two members approving 92-99% of everything shown. We release all datasets, per-item difficulty data, curation manifests and a leaderboard at https://opentwbench.ai

items.title: Rationale Distribution Distillation via Flow Matching for Distributional Continuous Latent Reasoning
items.summary: Sampling multiple chain-of-thought rationales from a language model can uncover correct solutions missed by a single attempt. However, these rationales are typically lengthy, making repeated autoregressive generation costly. Continuous latent reasoning offers a compact alternative, but point-valued methods condition repeated answer sampling on a single rationale, which can limit exploration of diverse paths and answer coverage. We thus propose rationale distribution distillation (RDD), training a conditional flow over fixed-length latent sequences by distilling from multiple textual reasoning paths. Furthermore, we expand the distillation targets through within-query mixup, interpolating between complete latent rationales for the same query. The flow nonautoregressively generates the entire latent sequence, and a frozen language model autoregressively decodes answers from sampled rationale contexts. Empirically, the resulting distributional reasoner achieves higher answer coverage than the evaluated point-valued latent reasoning baselines, particularly on advanced mathematical tasks.

items.title: RCCM: Diagnosing Gains and Harms in Reasoning-Prompt Transfer
items.summary: A reasoning prompt can improve one deployment and degrade another. RCCM (Reasoning-Control Capability Mismatch) examines these reversals by pairing answers to the same questions with records of how generation ends. Across five open-weight deployments and nine strategies, aggregate accuracy hides substantial question-level gains and harms; a common-budget MATH500 evaluation examines transfer on a separate sample. On 60 additional questions, concise reasoning improves Phi's automatic answer matching at a 2,048-token cap across three collections, but sharply reduces Qwen's. Author-reviewed final-answer commitments give a smaller, statistically unresolved Phi gain. Reserving an answer stage also improves matching, with additional input and call costs. These results show why a prompt benefit must be interpreted alongside its execution and evaluation: matching a reference answer need not mean delivering it, and an apparent compression benefit may admit another explanation. RCCM records this evidence for reproducible transfer comparisons.

items.title: Frustratingly Easy Majority Voting Using Length Conditioning
items.summary: Majority Voting (MV) is a simple and widely used strategy which improves the reasoning accuracy of Large Language Models (LLMs) by allocating additional inference-time computation. Specifically, in MV multiple Chain-of-Thoughts (CoTs) are independently sampled and the most frequent final answer is selected. In this work, we propose Length-Conditioned Majority Voting (LCMV), a Test-Time Training approach which improves MV leveraging an empirical observation that has recently been established in several studies: longer CoTs tend to be associated with a lower probability of correctness. We formulate this inductive bias as a length-conditioned prior probability, which is modeled by a simple logistic function. Moreover, we adapt this prior at test time using only unlabeled testing data and without fine-tuning the LLM. Finally, the adapted prior is used to weight the vote of each sampled answer. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and reasoning benchmarks show that LCMV consistently improves over both standard MV and existing length-based and confidence-based aggregation strategies, while retaining the simplicity and model-agnostic nature of MV. Our code is available at: https://github.com/aimagelab/LCMV.

items.title: Beyond Benchmark Accuracy: A Diagnostic Test for LLM Chemical Prediction
items.summary: LLMs have achieved strong performance on chemical prediction benchmarks. However, existing evaluation methods typically provide target entity identity information directly, making it difficult to determine whether model predictions arise from transferable structure-property reasoning capabilities or rely on target-related contextual information or memory retrieval. We propose the Identity-Blinded Reasoning Diagnostic framework to evaluate chemical prediction models when target entity identity information is hidden. In this framework, the target is no longer directly defined by its entity identity, but instead by a known source entity and an explicit structural edit operation. This setting preserves the information required to determine the target while reducing the opportunity for models to access target identity cues. We evaluate this framework across six tasks spanning odor prediction, molecular property prediction, retrosynthesis, and reaction yield prediction. The results show that models generally achieve better prediction performance when source and target entity properties are consistent. Providing explicit source entity labels further strengthens this dependence. Moreover, while keeping the target entity, structural change, and ground-truth label unchanged, replacing only the source entity label causes some model predictions to systematically shift toward the substituted source labels. These results indicate that high benchmark accuracy in chemical prediction tasks does not necessarily imply that LLMs possess reliable structure-property reasoning capabilities. Our diagnostic framework provides a controlled evaluation approach for testing whether models can genuinely update predictions according to entity changes. The framework can be extended to other AI for Science tasks, particularly those where targets can be defined through transformations of known entities.

items.title: Not All Criteria Matter: Importance-Aware Criteria Weighting for Rubric-Based LLM Evaluation
items.summary: Rubric-based evaluation assesses the responses of large language models (LLMs) by aggregating the verification results of explicit criteria, yet not all criteria matter equally. However, existing methods commonly aggregate the verification results with uniform weighting, which assigns minor and overlapping criteria the same weight as essential ones and thus produces misleading evaluation scores. Although some methods prompt an LLM to directly assign weights, direct weighting requires a holistic judgment over all criteria that LLMs struggle to make reliably. To address these limitations, we propose Importance-Aware Criteria Weighting (ICW), which derives the weights of criteria from pairwise importance comparisons made by an LLM. Specifically, ICW transforms the holistic judgment over all criteria into a series of pairwise importance comparisons, checks and revises inconsistent comparisons, and derives the weights from the principal eigenvector of the comparison matrix. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ICW consistently outperforms uniform weighting and competitive weighting methods, and translates into better policy models in downstream reinforcement learning.

items.title: MemDuet: Learning Dual-Process Memory for Long-Context Reasoning
items.summary: Reasoning over infinitely long documents is becoming a reality with recurrent memory agents. However, increasing context length exacerbates the trade-off between reasoning performance and inference efficiency. Inspired by Kahneman's account of fast and slow thinking, we propose MemDuet, a dual-process memory framework that learns to coordinate a small language model for fast, parallel evidence selection from raw context chunks (System 1) with a large language model for memory-update verification and memory updates in document order (System 2). We train MemDuet in three stages: supervised fine-tuning of System 1 for evidence selection, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) of System 2 for verification and memory rewriting, and joint optimization of both policies to coordinate selection and updating for long-context reasoning. Experiments on diverse long-context reasoning benchmarks (RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and 2WikiMultiHopQA) demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off as context length grows. Averaged across evaluation settings on the three datasets, MemDuet achieves an end-to-end inference speedup of 9.74x and an output-token reduction of 73.91% relative to RL-MemAgent.

items.title: To Reason but Not to Stop: Understanding and Recovering Pruned Large Reasoning Models
items.summary: Weight pruning can degrade the accuracy of large reasoning models (LRMs), yet it remains unclear whether it damages reasoning itself. We find that much of this degradation stems from a failure to stop rather than to reason. As sparsity increases, pruned LRMs increasingly fail to terminate within the token budget, often after the correct answer has appeared in their reasoning, instead falling into repetitive loops, even though they still recognize where the dense model would stop. We further find that the hidden-state difference between terminating and looping continuations is consistent across pruned checkpoints, suggesting a shared direction associated with committing to an answer. Building on this, we propose Termination-Guided Activation Steering (TGAS), a training-free method that adds this direction to the residual stream at inference time. Across six LRMs, three pruning pipelines, and math and code benchmarks, TGAS improves termination and overall accuracy while reducing repetitive reasoning and generation length, showing that this failure is actionable.

items.title: Does Machine Translation Retain Media Bias?
items.summary: Within the most recent two decades, machine translation (MT) has been advanced from a research area to a mature, deployed technology for prose text and most language pairs. However, language has different dimensions of meaning, and the alluded progress has primarily been demonstrated for propositional meaning. In this small exploratory study, we investigate whether one type of affective meaning, namely different types of linguistically expressed media bias, are retained under automatic translation for two language pairs, English and German as the source languages, and Bulgarian as the target language. We evaluate four state-of-the-art translation methods to answer the question whether and to what degree a loss of non-neutral language (specifically, 27 types of media bias) can occur as a result of applying MT. Our empirical findings are consistent with the claim that MT does not fully retain existing news bias of its input source text, but also may add extra bias of its own. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first experimental study of MT media bias retention.

items.title: AtomSearch: Evidence-Grounded Tree Search for Agent Skill Optimization
items.summary: Agent skills adapt frozen models through editable external instructions. Revising several rules at once makes changes difficult to inspect, while judging each local edit only by its immediate score can discard useful intermediate states. We introduce AtomSearch, which keeps revision actions local while using subsequent skill states to guide search. Contrastive atomic editing links each primitive rule edit to failed and successful executions, a behavioral hypothesis, and an intended scope. Skill-State Tree Search (STS) evaluates short edit compositions and selectively retains them as executable states that can be revisited and extended. Outcome memory supplies later proposals with observed repair and regression statistics. We evaluate AtomSearch across four tasks and five target models. With deepseek-v4-flash, it exceeds SkillOpt on three of four tasks, including a 9.68-percentage-point gain on LiveMathematicianBench, and SkillOpt's final skills contain 2.3-19.7 times as many characters. In 67% of completed searches, the best validation state passes through an ancestor that was not highest-scoring at its depth. These results show how local rule edits can support the exploration of useful revision paths and yield compact skills, with additional offline evaluations used to explore alternative states.

items.title: Choosing the Number of Attention Heads from Intrinsic Dimension: A Small-Scale Study
items.summary: The number of attention heads in a transformer is usually set by convention or grid search. We test a simple heuristic for setting it in advance: estimate the intrinsic dimension of token representations without labels, and use roughly that many heads. We estimate intrinsic dimension with a nested-dropout VAE trained on DistilBERT embeddings of WikiText-2, choosing the KL weight at the knee of the VAE's rate-distortion curve rather than by hand. This gives $k^*=9.2$ (95% CI [8.6, 9.8]). In a small 4-layer transformer trained from scratch, 10 heads and 32 heads are statistically equivalent on SST-2 and on MRPC (paired TOST over 10 seeds, $\pm1$ point margin), with 69% fewer attention parameters for the 10-head model. Training 10 heads from the start also slightly outperforms training 32 heads and pruning to 10 (0.6 points, $p=0.008$). The evidence is narrow: two classification tasks, one small architecture, no pretrained models, and no formal link between intrinsic dimension and head count. We present the result as a practical heuristic worth testing at larger scale, not as a general principle.

items.title: SoK: Grading Open-Text Legal Answers, from Law School Exams to Trustworthy Rubric Judges
items.summary: Law students are examined through open-text answers: case solutions, essays and memos that apply the law to a set of facts. Such answers are expensive to grade, human graders disagree widely on them, and large language models (LLMs) now offer to grade them at scale, both in teaching and in the benchmarks that test legal AI. This paper systematizes how open-text legal answers can be evaluated. We derive eight desiderata from educational measurement and from the law that governs exams, among them validity, reliability, reasons, credit for defensible alternative solutions, robustness to gaming and human oversight. We then compare eight evaluation paradigms against them, from unstructured human grading to LLM judges with instance-specific rubrics and pairwise comparison. Three findings stand out. A rubric written for the task is the strongest lever for agreement between an LLM judge and human graders, but the reported figures answer different questions and rarely come with the human agreement they must be read against. The central validation gap lies where examination law is most demanding: defensible alternative solutions, follow-on errors, and the examiner's correction of model judgments. And rubric-centred grading is the most auditable family, because it makes the standard, its application and the final decision checkable. From this we derive the trustworthy rubric judge: an instance rubric that credits arguments and alternative paths,evidence checked in code, probes, repeated runs, calibration against independent human grades,logging, and an examiner who reads every script. We state what each safeguard rests on, what remains to be tested, and the uses the evidence supports today.

items.title: Gray-Box Hallucination Detection in LLMs with Token Identities
items.summary: Large language models often produce fluent but factually incorrect output. Gray-box detectors identify such hallucinations from the token-probability statistics emitted during generation, avoiding the need for white-box access to hidden states that frontier models do not provide. These detectors, however, typically rely only on probability-derived representations and ignore the identities of the candidate tokens. They can therefore observe how uncertain the model is, but not what it is uncertain about. Consequently, they cannot distinguish between a model that is torn between "big" and "small" and one that is torn between "big" and "huge" when the two pairs receive the same probability distribution. We introduce GURI (Gray-box Uncertainty Representations with Identity), a lightweight gray-box hallucination detector that combines candidate-token probabilities with per-token vector identifiers. This exposes which alternatives the model considered while preserving the accessibility and transferability of the gray-box setting. Across three open-weight models and three question-answering benchmarks, GURI increases mean test ROC-AUC from 72.09% to 79.09% over a probability-only baseline. On the closed-source GPT-4.1 model, mean ROC-AUC increases from 67.39% to 71.84%. Among the three open-weight models, GURI outperforms transferred probability-only baseline in 17 of 18 directed cross-model transfers without fine-tuning. For the three open-weight models, cross-dataset transfer between HotpotQA and TriviaQA with the model held fixed improves mean ROC-AUC over transferred LOS-Net by 3.76 points.

items.title: A Strong Harness Narrows the Model Gap: A Comparative Evaluation for Legislative Document-to-XML Conversion
items.summary: Legal-content reproduction requires matching the source exactly in section hierarchy, verbatim text, citations, and amendment spans; a dropped citation or mislabeled amendment carries into the products lawyers rely on. We report an industrial pipeline converting U.S. state legislation into strict, schema-constrained XML, and hypothesize that its accuracy comes from harness engineering, the deterministic tooling built around a model, more than the model itself. Our controlled ablation crosses three harnesses (zero-shot, a single tool-using agent, and a decomposed multi-agent pipeline) with three Claude models on 153 gold bills from two jurisdictions. The harness narrows the model gap: the weakest model in the full pipeline beats the strongest model alone (0.948 versus 0.806, paired bootstrap p less than 0.001). Because the two agentic harnesses share identical tools, their gap comes from orchestration: decomposition plus the persisted state and per-agent context it brings. Across four scored dimensions, the model spread at zero-shot (0.68 to 0.81) narrows to 0.95 at the full pipeline; the residual sits almost entirely in citation normalization, where the canonical identifier is retrieved from an external authority rather than generated from the weights, so a deterministic lookup tool supplies the exactness that a larger model does not.

items.title: FACES: Fine-grained Gated Semantic Alignment for Multimodal Emotional Support Conversation
items.summary: In recent years, with advances in multimodal interaction technologies and the growing demand for intelligent emotional support, Multimodal Emotional Support Conversation (MESC) has emerged as an important task. However, existing systems still suffer from shallow responses and inappropriate support strategies due to weak semantic feedback, cross-dimension reward compensation, and coarse reasoning supervision. To address these challenges, we propose FACES, a fine-grained gated semantic alignment framework for MESC. Specifically, FACES integrates multi-source rewards to construct multidimensional semantic and functional alignment signals, employs a non-compensatory gated fusion mechanism to reduce cross-dimension reward offset, and leverages structured Chain-of-Thought (CoT) anchors to perform token-level credit assignment. Under a controlled response-length protocol, FACES improves the average MLLM-based evaluation score from 3.61 to 4.04 and achieves an 80.22% pairwise win rate over SOTA. Human evaluation under the same protocol yields a 75.3% preference rate. Results on three external datasets further support transferability. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/OCT-ARR/arr.

items.title: What Is a Clarification? Estimating Model-Dependent Input Ambiguity
items.summary: Ambiguous inputs can admit multiple interpretations, each potentially yielding a different answer. Existing work largely treats this ambiguity as a property of the input, yet for a particular language model, only some alternatives may be known and answerable. We therefore distinguish world ambiguity, capturing all alternatives admitted by an input, from model ambiguity, capturing those accessible to the responding model. To characterize these alternatives, we formalize natural-language clarifications through three desiderata: \emph{uniqueness}, \emph{faithfulness}, and \emph{answer equivalence}. We show that these desiderata induce a one-to-one correspondence between valid answers and equivalence classes of clarifications, implying that any interpretation can be represented either by its answer or by the clarifications that uniquely express it. We leverage this correspondence to introduce \circleclar{}, a black-box method that estimates the set of answers available to a model by checking consistency along an answer--clarification--answer cycle. Across open-domain QA and executable Text-to-SQL, \circleclar{} achieves strong recovery of these answer sets. In QA, the recovered support yields the strongest overall performance in model-dependent ambiguity detection and enables effective selection among answering, clarifying, and abstaining. Together, these results demonstrate the practical value of a model-dependent view of ambiguity and its characterization through an answer-clarification correspondence.

items.title: Which Knowledge Should LLMs Trust? Uncovering a Generalizable Steering Direction Across Knowledge Conflicts
items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently encounter conflicts between internal parametric knowledge and external contextual knowledge, yet the mechanisms governing this selection remain unclear. We show that the choice between context and parametric knowledge is linearly represented and can be controlled along a single direction in the model's residual stream. We first demonstrate that this direction generalizes across factual-conflict settings, including context formats, knowledge categories, and datasets, while consistently shifting behavior between parametric and contextual answers. We then transfer a direction learned from simple factual conflicts to three more complex task families: RAG, memory, and rule following, where models must acquire information from retrieved documents, interaction histories, or explicit rules. Across four model families and multiple transfer settings, steering consistently improves the use of prompt-provided information over the unsteered model. These results suggest that the direction captures a transferable preference for external knowledge rather than a mechanism specific to factual conflicts.

items.title: AFCS: Atomic-Fact-Conditioned Synthesis for Factual Knowledge Pretraining
items.summary: Synthetic data is increasingly used in language-model pretraining. Existing knowledge-corpus synthesis pipelines, including WRAP and Nemotron-CC, usually take a source passage or document segment as input and generate rewritten or QA-style samples from that text. This can improve surface form and prompt diversity, but it does not explicitly require fine-grained source facts -- especially secondary entities, list/table entries, and precise temporal attributes -- to appear in the synthesized corpus. We propose AFCS (Atomic-Fact-Conditioned Synthesis), a pipeline that first extracts source-supported atomic facts and then uses each retained fact to drive generation. AFCS uses structure-aware extraction over the document tree, source-grounded verification, local context expansion, and multi-format generation. In continued-pretraining experiments with OLMo-3-7B and a 32B base on the same FineWiki source corpus, AFCS outperforms WRAP and Nemotron-CC on SimpleQA, SimpleQA Verified, PopQA, and HotpotQA. Granularity ablations show that fact-level synthesis improves over chunk-level, paragraph-level, and entity-level synthesis; and a 100B-token mid-training integration improves factual benchmarks and raises the 12-task general benchmark average by +1.09.

items.title: Language Exposure Matters: Distribution and Order in Multilingual BabyLM Pre-training
items.summary: We investigate two aspects of multilingual pre-training with limited data, namely how language exposure is distributed across English, Dutch, and Chinese, and how that exposure is ordered during training. In particular, we compare balanced multilingual exposure to language-dominant exposure, where one language is exposed with more training data than the others. We also compare mixed training, where multilingual training data is used throughout training, with curriculum training, where monolingual exposure of the dominant language is followed by balanced multilingual exposure. Our results show that multilingual BabyLM performance varies with both the amount and order of language exposure. Mixed training outperforms curriculum learning across all 15 matched configurations, indicating that simultaneous multilingual exposure is more effective than staged exposure in our setting. Several language-dominant mixed training configurations achieve higher scores than the balanced configuration, suggesting that a balanced distribution is not necessarily the highest-performing configuration in our setting. Interestingly, the Dutch-primary configurations achieve the best overall performance.

items.title: Why Generate a Click? Plug-in Decision Heads for Web Agents
items.summary: Web agents built on vision language models decide every action by generating text such as click(12), although most of that text encodes a choice among a few action types and a few dozen marked elements. We read these choices directly from the hidden states that the generator computes while it reads the goal and the screenshot. Plug-in decision heads on a frozen generator predict the action type, pool the visual tokens inside each numbered box to pick the target, and point at a listed text option or at a WRITE slot that leaves the writing of new text to the generator. A confidence cascade executes the heads' action when they are sure and otherwise lets the generator decode from the KV cache of the same forward pass. With Qwen3-VL 4B and 8B generators trained on 213k web steps, a strict threshold keeps the cascade between 0.3 points below and 1.4 points above the generator on seven offline test sets while the heads decide 12 to 64% of the steps. A looser threshold raises step success on unseen Mind2Web websites by 3.1 and 1.8 points, costs up to 2 points on GUIAct and MiniWoB++, and lifts WebArena task success from 12.5 to 13.8% (4B) and from 13.6 to 14.6% (8B) with less than half of the generated tokens. Training the heads jointly with the generator lowers the generator's own step success by up to 4.9 points; heads on a frozen generator avoid this cost.

items.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Mechanistic Interpretability in NLP: A Critical Survey of Recoverability, Interpretability, and Utility
items.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach to mechanistic interpretability by decomposing language-model activations into sparse, potentially interpretable features. However, differences in design assumptions, evaluation objectives, and experimental settings complicate conclusions about their effectiveness. We present a critical survey of 138 studies on SAEs in natural language processing. Our contributions are fourfold: (1) we propose a task-grounded taxonomy connecting dictionary design, feature operations, and NLP functions; (2) we examine how sparsity allocation, geometry, data coverage, and inference affect feature recoverability; (3) we assess evidence for semantic interpretability, mechanistic faithfulness, and behavioral utility; and (4) we synthesize findings across multilingual processing, retrieval, reasoning, classification, and behavioral regulation, highlighting the roles of objectives, baselines, supervision, and intervention pipelines. Through comparative analyses of published results, we reconcile apparent disagreements, identify unresolved questions, and propose directions for more rigorous evaluation. An anonymous research register https://anonymous.4open.science/r/sae-research-register-C331/register.html accompanies the survey.

items.title: Gap Detection: Mitigating Homogenization through Demand and Defensibility
items.summary: Language models often produce semantically similar answers to open-ended questions, even when many plausible alternatives exist. Generating useful alternatives requires identifying both what the query calls for and what existing responses already cover. We introduce Gap Detection, a framework that searches for relevant but unoccupied directions in a shared text embedding space. Its objective, GapScore, combines query relevance (Demand) with dissimilarity to the nearest existing item (Defensibility). The framework optimizes this product on the unit sphere, maps candidate directions to concept words with a language model, and uses task-specific filtering and constrained prompting to turn those concepts into text. On five curated topics and 90 INFINITY-CHAT queries, the reported mean relative reductions in output Collision are 12.8% and 10.8%, respectively. We also instantiate the framework for generative engine optimization over four product markets and for iterative synthetic-data augmentation. In the latter setting, with 100 training examples per method, Gap Detection reduces Collision from 0.324 to 0.298 relative to undirected accumulation and increases the Vendi Score from 27.16 to 29.20; the accuracy difference is one example on a 40-example test set. Component ablations expose the trade-off between semantic separation and relevance, while also showing that better direction scores do not uniformly yield better downstream metrics. These results support explicit gap search as a practical mechanism for diversifying content, with task validity checked separately from geometric novelty.
